### 2.53 The neighbour property of Farey sequences

Let n ≥ 1 and let a/b < c/d be consecutive terms of `F_n` (in lowest terms). Then bc − ad = 1 and b + d > n.

Consecutive: no term of `F_n` lies strictly between them.

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.1, Proposition 1.1, printed p. 23.) The determinant criterion; consecutive terms of `F_n` are joined by an edge (the Farey series is the part of the square diagram above height 1/n, p. 30).

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.2, printed p. 30.) The inductive passage from `F_n` to `F_{n+1}` used in the proof steps.

To prove this, induct on n. F₁ = {0/1, 1/1}: 1·1 − 0·1 = 1 and 1 + 1 > 1.

Passing from `F_n` to `F_{n+1}`: new terms have denominator n + 1 and lie strictly between consecutive a/b < c/d of `F_n` with bc − ad = 1; by [Fractions between neighbours have denominator at least b + d](#layer-2-topic-35) they have denominator ≥ b + d > n, so a new term exists only if b + d = n + 1 and it is then the mediant, unique.

The new consecutive pairs (a/b, (a + c)/(b + d)) and ((a + c)/(b + d), c/d) have determinant 1 (b(a + c) − a(b + d) = bc − ad) and denominator sums > n + 1; untouched pairs have b + d ≥ n + 2 > n + 1.

**Checks.**

- In F₇, 2/5 and 3/7 are consecutive: 5·3 − 2·7 = 1 and 5 + 7 > 7.
- Hatcher, Proposition 1.1: edges of the Farey diagram are exactly the pairs with determinant ±1.

*Needs:* [The Farey sequence `F_n`](#layer-2-topic-12); [Fractions between neighbours have denominator at least b + d](#layer-2-topic-35); [The mediant of two fractions](#layer-2-topic-11).

### 2.54 Every positive rational occurs exactly once in the Stern–Brocot tree

The map w ↦ sternBrocot w from finite left/right paths to ℚ is injective and its image is the set of positive rationals.

Paths are finite words; values are positive rationals in lowest terms.

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.1, Proposition 1.3, printed p. 26.) Surjectivity.

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.1, printed p. 21.) The order property that gives injectivity.

To prove this, determinant-one bounds: for the raw lower (a,b) and upper (c,d), including the initial upper bound (1,0), bc−ad=1. The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) is reduced and lies strictly between the two bounds. Prove these using integer cross-products, without applying the positive-denominator Rat.mediant API to the infinite bound.

Injectivity: nodes in the left and right descendant subtrees lie strictly to the left and right of the parent mediant. Distinct paths either diverge into disjoint subtrees or one is a proper ancestor of the other; in both cases their values differ.

Surjectivity: fix a reduced positive target p/q between the current bounds and set U=bp−aq and V=cq−dp. Both are positive integers; initially (U,V)=(p,q). If U<V the target lies left of the mediant and updating the upper bound to (a+c,b+d) changes (U,V) to (U,V−U). If U>V the right update changes it to (U−V,V). Thus U+V strictly decreases at every update.

At U=V, p(b+d)=q(a+c), so the reduced target equals the reduced mediant. Well-founded induction on the positive integer U+V proves every positive rational occurs. A denominator-only measure is invalid: the right spine enumerates positive integers with denominator1.

**Checks.**

- 3/8 = [0; 2, 1, 2] is the result along left, left, right, left (through 1, 1/2, 1/3, 2/5); its depth 4 is below its denominator 8.
- The positive rationals are listed in increasing order by the in-order traversal.

*Needs:* [The Stern–Brocot tree](#layer-2-topic-36); [The mediant of two fractions](#layer-2-topic-11).

### 2.55 Every eventually periodic sequence is automatic

For any k≥1, a sequence f:ℕ→Δ satisfying f(t+p)=f(t) for all t≥N, with p≥1, is k-automatic in the existing canonical-digit convention. It is the API lemma `isAutomatic_of_eventually_periodic` of [k-automatic sequences](#layer-2-topic-33), stated here as a separate result; it introduces no second definition.

Base 1 uses Mathlib’s unary digit-list convention and is treated separately. No finiteness assumption on Δ is needed.

(Thijmen J. P. Krebs, [A more reasonable proof of Cobham's theorem](#reference-krebs-cobham-2018), Theorem 1, p.1; §3, p.2, converse omitted as usual.) The source leaves the converse to the standard argument. This supplies that argument explicitly, including the base-one case of [k-automatic sequences](#layer-2-topic-33).

To prove this, the sequence is determined by its first N+p values, so its range is finite.

For k ≥ 2 use the direct automaton of [k-automatic sequences](#layer-2-topic-33). Its finite state holds the value represented by the prefix and the current place value `k^L`, each cut off at N and also reduced modulo p. A digit d adds d times the place value and multiplies the place value by k; these equations define the finite transition map. The output is f at the value if it is below N, and otherwise f at the representative in [N, N+p) of its residue. Induction on the least-significant-first digits proves correctness without the finite-kernel theorem, so the declaration stays before Eilenberg's theorem.

For k=1, Nat.digits 1 t has length t. Mapping into Fin 1 makes every input digit zero. A finite counter with states 0,…,N+p−1 advances through the prefix then cycles through N,…,N+p−1, outputting the corresponding value of f. It computes the unary word of length t exactly.

**Checks.**

- The sequence with value 7 at zero and n mod 2 at positive n has period 2 on n≥1 but its values at 0 and 2 differ.
- The sequence with value 7 at zero and n mod 2 at positive n is 1-automatic in the existing unary convention.
- A special initial value followed by a periodic tail is allowed.
- Base 1 is not covered by the kernel criterion and is handled by its unary counter.
- For N=0,p=1 the counter is the one-state constant automaton.

*Needs:* [k-automatic sequences](#layer-2-topic-33); [Deterministic finite automata with output](#layer-2-topic-8); Mathlib `Nat.digits_one`.

### 2.56 Unimodality of the rows of Eulerian numbers

For n ∈ ℕ and q with 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1: A(n, q) ≤ A(n, q + 1). With the symmetry A(n, q) = A(n, n − 1 − q), each row A(n, 0), …, A(n, n − 1) rises weakly to its middle and falls symmetrically after it.

2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 means q + 1 ≤ (n − 1)/2, the left half of the row; for n = 0 the hypothesis never holds.

(Richard P. Stanley, [Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1, second edition](#reference-stanley-ec1), Chapter 1, Exercise 1.50(e), p. 124, with its solution, p. 178; Exercises 1.49 and 1.50(a)–(b), p. 124, with the solutions of 1.49 and 1.50(b), p. 177.) Asks to show that `Σ_{w ∈ S_n} x^{des(w)}` is symmetric and unimodal, and solves it from the real-rootedness of the Eulerian polynomial (Exercise 1.49) and Newton's inequalities (Exercise 1.50(a),(b)); cites Gasharov for a combinatorial proof.

(Brian Lawrence and Will Sawin, [The Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties](#reference-lawrence-sawin-2025), Appendix C, proof of Lemma C.4, p. 117.) Uses, without stating it as a lemma, that A(n, r) ≥ A(n, r₀) for r₀ ≤ r ≤ n/2, which is this unimodality.

To prove this, induction on n with the recurrence of [Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39) (c): A(n, q + 1) − A(n, q) = (q + 2)A(n − 1, q + 1) + (n − 2q − 2)A(n − 1, q) − (n − q)A(n − 1, q − 1) for 1 ≤ q (and the analogous expression at q = 0).

Under 2(q + 1) ≤ n − 1 the index q + 1 is at most the middle (n − 2)/2 of row n − 1, or equals it up to the symmetric partner when n is odd; by the induction hypothesis and the symmetry, A(n − 1, q + 1) ≥ A(n − 1, q) ≥ A(n − 1, q − 1).

Hence the difference is at least ((q + 2) + (n − 2q − 2) − (n − q))·A(n − 1, q − 1) = 0, all coefficients other than the last being nonnegative because n − 2q − 2 ≥ 1.

Alternatively (Stanley, Exercise 1.50(e) with its solution): the Eulerian polynomial has only real zeros (Exercise 1.49), hence log-concave coefficients by Newton's inequalities, hence unimodal; symmetry places the peak in the middle.

**Checks.**

- Row 6 is 1, 57, 302, 302, 57, 1; row 7 is 1, 120, 1191, 2416, 1191, 120, 1.


*Needs:* [Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39).

### 2.57 Power and factorial bounds for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemmas C.1–C.2)

For n ≥ 1 and q ≥ 0: (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ (the left side computed in ℤ), and A(n, q) ≤ n!. The upper bound (q + 1)ⁿ and A(n, q) ≤ n! hold for n = 0 as well.

n ≥ 1 for the lower bound, as in the source; q ∈ ℕ arbitrary (for q ≥ n the bounds are consistent with A(n, q) = 0).

(Brian Lawrence and Will Sawin, [The Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties](#reference-lawrence-sawin-2025), Appendix C, Lemma C.1 with its proof, p. 116.) States (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ for n ≥ 1, q ≥ 0, and proves both halves by the labelling argument.

(Brian Lawrence and Will Sawin, [The Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties](#reference-lawrence-sawin-2025), Appendix C, Lemma C.2 with its proof, p. 116.) States A(n, q) ≤ n! and derives it from the factorial sum.

To prove this, upper bound: by Worpitzky's identity ([Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39) (d)) (q + 1)ⁿ is a sum of nonnegative terms one of which is A(n, q)·C(n, n) = A(n, q). (Lawrence–Sawin's argument: labelling [n] by 1, …, q + 1 and listing each label class in decreasing order gives every permutation with at most q ascents.)

Lower bound (Lawrence–Sawin's argument): the labellings producing a permutation with fewer than q ascents have two adjacent labels whose classes are separated; recording the position j ∈ {0, …, n} of the cut and merging the labels injects them into (n + 1)·qⁿ data, so the number of permutations with exactly q ascents is at least (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ.

A(n, q) ≤ n! from `Σ_q A(n, q) = n!` ([Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39) (a)).

Ascents and descents give the same numbers ([Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39) (f)), so the source's ascent count is A(n, q).

**Checks.**

- n = 3, q = 1: 2³ − 4·1 = 4 ≤ A(3, 1) = 4 ≤ 8: the lower bound is attained.
- n = 4, q = 2: 3⁴ − 5·2⁴ = 1 ≤ 11 ≤ 81.
- For q ≥ n the lower bound is ≤ 0, consistent with A(n, q) = 0.

*Needs:* [Basic identities of Eulerian numbers](#layer-2-topic-39).

### 2.58 Ward's strong divisibility theorem for elliptic divisibility sequences

Let b, c, d ∈ ℤ with b ≠ 0 and c ≠ 0, and W = normEDS b c d, the nondegenerate integral EDS with W₀ = 0, W₁ = 1, W₂ = b, W₃ = c, W₄ = db (so W₂ | W₄). Then W is a strong divisibility sequence, `gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}|` for all m, n ∈ ℤ, if and only if gcd(W₃, W₄) = 1, i.e. c is coprime to db. Equivalently n ↦ |Wₙ| is a strong divisibility sequence on ℕ (Mathlib's Nat.IsStrongDvdSequence).

b, c, d ∈ ℤ with bc ≠ 0 (nondegenerate: W₂W₃ ≠ 0). The coprimality gcd(W₃, W₄) = 1 is necessary: strong divisibility at (3, 4) says gcd(W₃, W₄) = |W₁| = 1. It cannot be dropped: normEDS 1 (−6) (−6) = 0, 1, 1, −6, −6, 210, −1044, … has gcd(W₃, W₄) = 6. Absolute values are needed: Wₙ can be negative (W₃ = −1 for the curve 37a1).

(Joseph H. Silverman and Katherine E. Stange, [Terms in elliptic divisibility sequences divisible by their indices](#reference-silverman-stange-2010), Remark 28, p. 24 (arXiv:1001.5303v1).) Recalls Ward's recursive EDS, normalised by W₁ = 1 and W₂ | W₄, and Ward's association with a curve; the arithmetic theory is attributed to Ward's memoir.

(Joseph H. Silverman, [p-adic properties of elliptic divisibility sequences (lecture slides)](#reference-silverman-icms-2007), slide 1, 'Elliptic Divisibility Sequences As Recursions' (ICMS workshop, Edinburgh, 27 June 2007).) States that an integral EDS with W₂W₃ ≠ 0 and W₂ | W₄ is a strong divisibility sequence; the coprimality of W₃ and W₄ is missing there; the Checks show it is necessary.

(Subham Bhakta, Daniel Loughran, Simon L. Rydin Myerson and Masahiro Nakahara, [The elliptic sieve and Brauer groups](#reference-bhakta-loughran-rydin-myerson-nakahara-2023), §3.1, Lemma 3.5 and the remark after it, p. 9 (arXiv:2109.03746).) Strong divisibility of the normalised denominator sequence, with the warning that the division-polynomial sequence need not be strongly divisible when P has bad reduction — the primes this theorem's gap concerns.

(Joseph H. Silverman and Nelson Stephens, [The sign of an elliptic divisibility sequence](#reference-silverman-stephens-2004), §1, p. 3 (arXiv:math/0402415v1).) An EDS is determined by W₂, W₃, W₄ through its two duplication recursions, and a triple with W₂W₃ ≠ 0 gives an EDS exactly when W₂ | W₄ (attributed to Ward).

To prove this, ward's sequences are the normEDS: normEDS b c d satisfies the elliptic net relations (Tau Ceti `isEllipticNet_normEDS`), hence the EDS recursion, with W₀, …, W₄ = 0, 1, b, c, db; an EDS with W₁ = 1 and W₂W₃ ≠ 0 is determined by W₂, W₃, W₄, and such a triple gives an integral EDS exactly when W₂ | W₄ (Silverman–Stephens, §1, p. 3), so every normalised nondegenerate integral EDS is normEDS b c d for some b, c, d ∈ ℤ with bc ≠ 0.

Necessity: put m = 3, n = 4.

Sufficiency, prime by prime: it suffices that for every prime p, `min(v_p W_m, v_p Wₙ) = v_p W_{gcd(m,n)}`. The inequality ≥ in the other direction is divisibility (Tau Ceti `isDvdSequence_normEDS`).

Primes p ∤ bc with `Δ(E_{b,c,d}) ≠ 0`: [Strong divisibility of an integral EDS at primes not dividing W₂W₃](#layer-2-topic-43).

Primes p | bc: by the coprimality, p divides exactly one of b, c, and p ∤ d when p | c. At such primes the point P = (0, 0) can have singular reduction on every integral model of `E_{b,c,d}`, and the valuations `v_p(Wₙ)` are then not filtration levels of nP (for b = 1, c = 3, d = 1 and p = 3, where 3 ∤ d + b⁴, no integral model carries P as an integral nonsingular point with Wₙ = ψₙ(P) up to a unit, and v₃(Wₙ) is 0 for 3 ∤ n, 1 for n ≡ 3 (mod 6) and 4 + v₃(n/6) for 6 | n — the sets `{n : 3^V | Wₙ}` are 3ℤ, 6ℤ, 6ℤ, 6ℤ, 18ℤ, … but the jump from 1 to 4 is not a formal-group pattern). The theorem asserts that the sets `{n : p^V | Wₙ}` are still subgroups; this case and the singular case `Δ(E_{b,c,d}) = 0` are the required auxiliary target 'Ward's strong divisibility at primes dividing W₂W₃ and for singular attached curves'.

Assemble over all primes: `|W_{gcd(m,n)}|` and `gcd(W_m, Wₙ)` have the same p-adic valuation for every p and are nonnegative.

**Checks.**

- normEDS 2 3 2 = id: the theorem reads gcd(m, n) = gcd(m, n).
- normEDS 1 (−1) 1 (curve 37a1): W₅ = 2, W₁₀ = −4, W₁₅ = −314, and gcd(W₁₀, W₁₅) = 2 = |W₅|.
- normEDS 1 (−6) (−6): gcd(W₃, W₄) = 6 ≠ 1 = |W₁|, so the coprimality hypothesis is sharp.
- Numerically: for b ∈ [−6, 6] ∖ {0} and c, d ∈ [−8, 8], c ≠ 0, the 1552 sequences with gcd(c, db) = 1 satisfy `gcd(W_m, Wₙ) = |W_{gcd(m,n)}|` for 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 24.

**Auxiliary proof target.** The good-prime filtration proves the subgroup property of `{n:p^V∣W_n}` only when p∤bc and the attached curve is nonsingular. The endpoint must also prove it for primes dividing b or c, and for singular attached curves. For b=1,c=3,d=1 at p=3, the required valuations are 1 at n≡3 modulo 6 and 4+v₃(n/6) at multiples of 6; an integral nonsingular-point argument cannot be assumed there. The singular example normEDS 2 3 2 n=n must remain included. A recursion proof or a complete singular-reduction valuation argument is needed before invoking the full Ward theorem.

### 2.59 Rational generating functions, linear recurrences and closed forms (Stanley, Theorem 4.1.1)

Fix complex numbers α₁, …, `α_d` with d ≥ 1 and `α_d ≠ 0`, and put `Q(x) = 1 + α₁x + ⋯ + α_dx^d`. For f : ℕ → ℂ the following are equivalent: (i) ∑ f(n)xⁿ = P(x)/Q(x) with P a polynomial of degree less than d; (ii) for every n ≥ 0, `f(n + d) + α₁f(n + d − 1) + ⋯ + α_d f(n) = 0`; (iii) for every n ≥ 0, f(n) = ∑ᵢ Pᵢ(n)γᵢⁿ, where `Q(x) = ∏ᵢ(1 − γᵢx)^{dᵢ}` with the γᵢ distinct and nonzero, and Pᵢ is a polynomial of degree less than dᵢ.

The αᵢ are complex, `α_d ≠ 0`: Q has degree exactly d and Q(0) = 1. The γᵢ are the reciprocals of the roots of Q and dᵢ their multiplicities. (iii) has polynomial coefficients; constants suffice only when Q has distinct roots.

(Richard P. Stanley, [Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1, second edition](#reference-stanley-ec1), Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1.1, p. 535.) The hypotheses of the result; conditions (i) and (ii) follow on p. 535 and (iii) on p. 536.

(Richard P. Stanley, [Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1, second edition](#reference-stanley-ec1), Theorem 4.1.1(i), (ii), p. 535.) Conditions (i) and (ii) of the result's TFAE.

(Richard P. Stanley, [Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1, second edition](#reference-stanley-ec1), Proof of Theorem 4.1.1, p. 536.) The dimension count, which the proof here replaces by the closed-form results of this layer.

To prove this, (i) ⇔ (ii): multiplying ∑ f(n)xⁿ by Q and comparing coefficients, the coefficient of `x^{n+d}` of Q·∑ f(n)xⁿ is the left side of (ii); it vanishes for all n iff the product is a polynomial of degree < d (`PowerSeries.coeff_mul`; [The rationality predicate for a formal power series](#layer-2-topic-26)).

(ii) is the recurrence ofMonic (reverse Q), where reverse `Q = X^d Q(1/X) = X^d + α₁X^{d−1} + ⋯ + α_d` is monic (its leading coefficient is Q(0) = 1) with constant term `α_d ≠ 0` and roots exactly the γᵢ with multiplicities dᵢ (`Polynomial.reverse`).

(ii) ⇔ (iii): by closed-form-of-a-complex-linear-recurrence (existence) and [Exponential polynomials are linear recurrence sequences](#layer-2-topic-45) (converse) applied to the recurrence of reverse(Q).

Stanley's proof instead compares the four spaces V₁ to V₄ of dimension d, the independence of the partial fractions being [Exponential polynomials in distinct nonzero bases are linearly independent](#layer-2-topic-3); both routes use the dimension d of the solution space.

**Checks.**

- The closed form has polynomial coefficients of degree < multiplicity; with Q = (1 − x)² the solutions are f(n) = a + bn, and constant coefficients would be wrong.
- Fibonacci (Stanley Example 4.1.2): Q = 1 − x − x², P = x, Fₙ = (φⁿ − φ̄ⁿ)/√5.
- Stanley Example 4.1.3: f(n) = 2f(n − 1) + f(n − 2), f(0) = 1, f(1) = 3 gives (1 + x)/(1 − 2x − x²) and `f(n) = ((1 + √2)^{n+1} + (1 − √2)^{n+1})/2`.

### 2.60 The characteristic polynomial of the companion matrix

For every commutative ring R and every monic p ∈ R[X], the characteristic polynomial of C(p) is p: det(X·I − C(p)) = p.

p monic; R any commutative ring (no field, no extension of scalars).

(Jim Hefferon, [Linear Algebra, fourth edition](#reference-hefferon-linearalgebra-2020), Topic: Linear Recurrences, printed p. 477.) The theorem, for the recurrence matrix (a transpose-and-reversal of C(p)); the sign `±(−λ^k + ⋯)` of det(A − λI) is the sign convention det(λI − A) of Mathlib's charpoly.

(Jim Hefferon, [Linear Algebra, fourth edition](#reference-hefferon-linearalgebra-2020), Topic: Linear Recurrences, Exercise 5, printed p. 480.) The proof steps.

To prove this, induct on d = natDegree p. For d = 0, p = 1 and C(p) is the empty matrix with charpoly 1.

For d = 1, p = X + c and XI − C(p) is the 1×1 matrix (X + c). For d ≥ 2 write p = X·p₁ + p.coeff 0 with p₁ monic of degree d − 1. Expand det(X·I − C(p)) along the first row (`Matrix.det_succ_row_zero`), whose entries are X in position (0,0), p.coeff 0 in position (0, d − 1) and 0 elsewhere: the (0, 0) minor is X·I − C(p₁) shifted, contributing X·charpoly C(p₁) = X·p₁ by induction, and the (0, d − 1) entry p.coeff 0 has triangular minor with determinant `(−1)^{d−1}·(−1)^{d−1}`, contributing p.coeff 0.

Hefferon's hint (expanding down the final column and using induction) is the transposed form of the same computation; Mathlib's `Matrix.charpoly_transpose` identifies the two.

Over a field an alternative is `charpoly_leftMulMatrix`: C(p) is the matrix of multiplication by the root of AdjoinRoot p, whose minimal polynomial is p.

**Checks.**

- charpoly C(X² − X − 1) = X² − X − 1; charpoly C(X − a) = X − a; charpoly C(1) = 1.
- Rank 2: charpoly [[0, −d], [1, t]] = X² − tX + d, matching `TauCeti.det_companionFinTwo` (det = d) and `TauCeti.trace_companionFinTwo` (trace = t).

*Needs:* [The companion matrix of a polynomial](#layer-2-topic-46); Mathlib `Matrix.charpoly`; Mathlib `Matrix.det_succ_row_zero`; Mathlib `Matrix.charpoly_transpose`; Mathlib `Matrix.charpoly_monic`; Mathlib `charpoly_leftMulMatrix`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.det_companionFinTwo`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.trace_companionFinTwo`.

### 2.61 Solutions of a recurrence are orbits of the transposed companion matrix

Let R be a commutative ring, p ∈ R[X] with d = natDegree p ≥ 1, and u : ℕ → R. Write `s_n = (u(n), u(n + 1), …, u(n + d − 1)) ∈ R^d`. Then u solves `ofMonic p iff s_n = (C(p)ᵀ)ⁿ s₀` for every n ≥ 0; in that case u(n) is the first coordinate of (C(p)ᵀ)ⁿ s₀.

d ≥ 1 (for d = 0 the state space is 0 and the equivalence fails: only u = 0 solves ofMonic 1). The state vector is ordered oldest first, as Mathlib's `LinearRecurrence.tupleSucc`.

(Jim Hefferon, [Linear Algebra, fourth edition](#reference-hefferon-linearalgebra-2020), Topic: Linear Recurrences, printed p. 475.) The theorem for Fibonacci; the result states it for every monic p with the oldest-first state vector.

(Victor Shoup, [A Computational Introduction to Number Theory and Algebra (Version 2)](#reference-shoup-v2), Section 18.1, Example 18.1, printed p. 488.) The register is the state vector sₙ; its update is C(p)ᵀ.

To prove this, `c(p)ᵀ s_n = (u(n + 1), …, u(n + d − 1), −∑ p.coeff i u(n + i))` by the companion-matrix API (`toLin'_companion_transpose`, `Matrix.mulVec`).

So `s_{n+1} = C(p)ᵀ s_n` for all n iff the last coordinates agree, which is the recurrence u(n + d) = −∑ p.coeff i u(n + i); induct on n for the power form.

Conversely `s_n = (C(p)ᵀ)ⁿ s₀` for all n gives `s_{n+1} = C(p)ᵀ s_n` and hence the recurrence.

**Checks.**

- Fibonacci: `(F_n, F_{n+1}) = ([[0, 1], [1, 1]])ⁿ (0, 1)`, the matrix being C(X² − X − 1)ᵀ = C(X² − X − 1).
- Hefferon's form `v_n = T^{n−1} v₁` is the same statement with the coordinates in reverse order.

*Needs:* [The companion matrix of a polynomial](#layer-2-topic-46); [The linear recurrence of a monic polynomial](#layer-2-topic-27); Mathlib `LinearRecurrence.IsSolution`; Mathlib `LinearRecurrence.tupleSucc`; Mathlib `Matrix.mulVec`.

### 2.62 The Lucas sequence of the second kind Vₙ(P, Q)

For a commutative ring R and P, Q ∈ R: V₀ = 2, V₁ = P, `V_{n+2} = P·V_{n+1} − Q·Vₙ`. If α + β = P and αβ = Q then Vₙ = αⁿ + βⁿ (Carmichael's Sₙ), and Vₙ² − (P² − 4Q)Uₙ² = 4Qⁿ.

R any commutative ring; P, Q arbitrary.

The supporting API comprises:

- `lucasV`: Vₙ(P, Q): V₀ = 2, V₁ = P, `V_{n+2} = P V_{n+1} − Q Vₙ`.
- `lucasV_zero`: V₀ = 2.
- `lucasV_one`: V₁ = P.
- `lucasV_add_two`: `V_{n+2} = P V_{n+1} − Q Vₙ`.
- `lucasV_eq_add_pow`: If α + β = P and αβ = Q then Vₙ = αⁿ + βⁿ.
- `lucasV_eq_eval_dickson`: Vₙ(P, Q) = (dickson 1 Q n)(P), Mathlib's Dickson polynomial of the first kind.
- `lucasV_sq_sub`: Vₙ² − (P² − 4Q)Uₙ² = 4Qⁿ.
- `map_lucasV`: f (Vₙ(P, Q)) = Vₙ(f P, f Q) for a ring homomorphism f.

(R. D. Carmichael, [On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms αⁿ ± βⁿ](#reference-carmichael-arithmeticforms-1913), Introduction, p. 30, and Section 2, p. 36.) The definition (Carmichael's Sₙ) and the lemma `lucasV_sq_sub`, with (α − β)² = P² − 4Q.

To prove this, define lucasV P Q by the recursion.

Vₙ = αⁿ + βⁿ: both sides satisfy the recursion and agree at n = 0, 1.

Vₙ² − (P² − 4Q)Uₙ² = 4Qⁿ: in the universal ring where α, β exist, (α − β)² = P² − 4Q and (αⁿ + βⁿ)² − (αⁿ − βⁿ)² = 4αⁿβⁿ (Carmichael p. 36); the identity is polynomial in P, Q, so it holds over every commutative ring by specialising from ℤ[P, Q].

Vₙ(P, Q) = (dickson 1 Q n)(P): same recursion and initial values 2, P (`Polynomial.dickson_add_two`).

**Checks.**

- Vₙ(3, 2) = 2ⁿ + 1 over ℤ.
- Vₙ(2, 1) = 2 for every n (repeated root).
- V₀, …, V₅ of (1, −1) are 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11.
- Vₙ(P, Q) = (dickson 1 Q n)(P) for P, Q ∈ ℤ (Mathlib's Dickson polynomial of the first kind).
- `V_{2^i}(4, 1) = LucasLehmer.s i`, Mathlib's Lucas–Lehmer sequence 4, 14, 194, ….
- Vₙ(1, −1) are the Lucas numbers 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11; Vₙ(3, 2) = 2ⁿ + 1; Vₙ(2, 1) = 2.
- The Lucas–Lehmer numbers are `V_{2^i}(4, 1)`: Mathlib's `LucasLehmer.s i`.

### 2.63 The addition formula for Lucas sequences

For every commutative ring R, P, Q ∈ R and m, n ≥ 0: `U_{m+n+1} = U_{m+1}U_{n+1} − Q·U_mU_n`.

No hypothesis on P, Q.

(Peter Bala, [Divisibility sequences from strong divisibility sequences](#reference-bala-strongdivisibility-2014), Appendix, Proposition A3, p. 9.) The target with b = −Q, k = m, and n shifted by one so that no negative index appears.

To prove this, induct on m (Bala's Proposition A3 with a = P, b = −Q): the case m = 0 is `U_{n+1} = U_{n+1}`; the step uses `U_{m+n+2} = P U_{m+n+1} − Q U_{m+n}` and the recursion for `U_{m+2}`.

For P = 1, Q = −1 this is Mathlib's `Nat.fib_add`.

**Checks.**

- For Fibonacci, `F_{m+n+1} = F_{m+1}F_{n+1} + F_mF_n`.
- For m = n it gives `U_{2n+1} = U_{n+1}² − QUₙ²`.

<a id="layer-2-topic-64"></a>

### 2.64 Coprimality properties of Lucas sequences

Let P, Q ∈ ℤ be coprime. Then for every n ≥ 0, `U_{n+1}(P, Q)` is coprime to Q and to Uₙ(P, Q).

P and Q coprime (IsCoprime P Q); P = 0 or Q = 0 is allowed (then Q or P is a unit).

(Peter Bala, [Divisibility sequences from strong divisibility sequences](#reference-bala-strongdivisibility-2014), Appendix, Proposition A2, p. 9.) The lemma with b = −Q and the index shifted.

(R. D. Carmichael, [On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms αⁿ ± βⁿ](#reference-carmichael-arithmeticforms-1913), Section 2, Theorem I, p. 35.) The first part (Uₙ coprime to Q = αβ).

To prove this, induct on n. U₁ = 1 is coprime to everything.

`U_{n+2} = P U_{n+1} − Q Uₙ ≡ P U_{n+1} (mod Q)`, and P is coprime to Q, so `gcd(U_{n+2}, Q) = gcd(U_{n+1}, Q) = 1` (`IsCoprime.mul_right`, `IsCoprime.of_mul_right_left`).

`gcd(U_{n+2}, U_{n+1}) = gcd(Q Uₙ, U_{n+1}) = gcd(Uₙ, U_{n+1}) = 1` using the previous point for `U_{n+1}`.

**Checks.**

- For P = 1, Q = −1: consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime (Mathlib's `Nat.fib_coprime_fib_succ`).
- Without coprimality it fails: P = 2, Q = 2 gives U₂ = 2, not coprime to Q.

### 2.65 k-automatic `iff k^m`-automatic

Let k ≥ 2 and m ≥ 1. A sequence is `k^m`-automatic iff it is k-automatic.

k ≥ 2, m ≥ 1.

(Andrew Bridy, [Automatic sequences and curves over finite fields](#reference-bridy-automaticcurves-2016), Section 2.3, before Proposition 2.16, p. 9.) The theorem.

To prove this, by Eilenberg's theorem it suffices to compare kernels. The `k^m`-kernel is contained in the k-kernel (exponent me).

Conversely, write a k-kernel element with exponent e = mq + j (0 ≤ j < m) and `r = r₀ + k^{mq}r₁` with `r₀ < k^{mq}`, `r₁ < k^j`: then `k^e n + r = k^{mq}(k^j n + r₁) + r₀`, so it is `n ↦ b(k^j n + r₁)` with `b = (n ↦ a(k^{mq}n + r₀))` in the `k^m`-kernel; finitely many b, j < m and `r₁ < k^j` give finitely many elements.

**Checks.**

- The Thue–Morse sequence is 4-automatic (and `2^m`-automatic for every m).
- It is not 3-automatic (Cobham's theorem, which this result does not use).

### 2.66 Cobham's characterisation by uniform morphisms

Let k ≥ 2. A sequence a : ℕ → Δ is k-automatic iff there are a finite alphabet Γ, a k-uniform morphism φ : `Γ → Γ^k`, a letter-to-letter coding τ : Γ → Δ and a fixed point s of φ (`s(kn + r) = φ(s(n))_r` for all n and r < k, in particular φ(s(0))₀ = s(0)) with a = τ ∘ s.

k ≥ 2; the fixed point is encoded by the equations s(kn + r) = φ(s n) r, which determine s from s(0).

(G. Christol, T. Kamae, M. Mendès France, G. Rauzy, [Suites algébriques, automates et substitutions](#reference-christol-suitesalgebriques-1980), Section 5, Theorem 1 and the remark after it, p. 406.) The theorem (i) ⇔ (ii) for every base k; Cobham's proof is not reproduced in the source, the proof steps give it.

(G. Christol, T. Kamae, M. Mendès France, G. Rauzy, [Suites algébriques, automates et substitutions](#reference-christol-suitesalgebriques-1980), Section 3, p. 404.) The fixed point of a k-uniform morphism, encoded in the result by `s(kn + r) = φ(s n)_r`.

To prove this, (⇐) Read the digits of n most significant first: `s(n) = δ*(s(0), (n)_k^R)` for the automaton with transitions `δ(x, r) = φ(x)_r`, since `s(kn + r) = φ(s n)_r`; leading zeros are harmless because φ(s(0))₀ = s(0). Output τ; conclude by [Automaticity does not depend on the reading direction](#layer-2-topic-51).

(⇒) Take a most-significant-first automaton (σ, δ, q₀, τ) with δ(q₀, 0) = q₀: the reversal ([Automaticity does not depend on the reading direction](#layer-2-topic-51)) of the kernel automaton of [Eilenberg's theorem: automatic iff finite kernel](#layer-2-topic-50) has this property, because its initial state is the output map b ↦ b(0) and b(k·0) = b(0). Put Γ = σ, `φ(q)_r = δ(q, r)` and s(n) = δ*(q₀, `(n)_k` reversed); then `s(kn + r) = φ(s n)_r` and a = τ ∘ s.

**Checks.**

- Thue–Morse: Γ = {0, 1}, φ(0) = 01, φ(1) = 10, τ = id, s = 0110 1001 ….
- The Baum–Sweet sequence: Γ = {a, b, c, d}, φ(a) = ab, φ(b) = cb, φ(c) = bd, φ(d) = dd, τ(a) = τ(b) = 1, τ(c) = τ(d) = 0 (Christol–Kamae–Mendès France–Rauzy, p. 404).

### 2.67 Algebraic power series over `𝔽_q` have q-automatic coefficients

Let K be a finite field with q elements and f = ∑ aₙXⁿ ∈ K⟦X⟧ algebraic over K[X]. Then (aₙ) is q-automatic.

K finite, q = |K|.

(G. Christol, T. Kamae, M. Mendès France, G. Rauzy, [Suites algébriques, automates et substitutions](#reference-christol-suitesalgebriques-1980), Section 7, p. 409.) The first step.

(G. Christol, T. Kamae, M. Mendès France, G. Rauzy, [Suites algébriques, automates et substitutions](#reference-christol-suitesalgebriques-1980), Section 7, p. 409.) The finite stable set and the conclusion through the kernel.

To prove this, by [Ore relations for algebraic power series over a finite field](#layer-2-topic-34), `∑_{i=0}^k aᵢf^{qⁱ} = 0` with a₀ ≠ 0. Put g = f/a₀ ∈ K⸨X⸩; then `g = ∑_{i=1}^k bᵢ g^{qⁱ}` with `bᵢ = −aᵢa₀^{qⁱ−2} ∈ K[X]`.

Let N = max(deg a₀, deg bᵢ) and `H = {∑_{i=0}^k cᵢg^{qⁱ} : cᵢ ∈ K[X], deg cᵢ ≤ N}`, a finite set (K finite). f = a₀g ∈ H.

H is stable under every `Λ_r`: for `h = ∑ cᵢg^{qⁱ}`, substituting `g = ∑ bᵢg^{qⁱ}` in the i = 0 term gives `h = ∑_{i≥1}(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ)g^{qⁱ}`, so `Λ_r(h) = ∑_{i≥1} Λ_r(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ)g^{q^{i−1}}` ([The Cartier operators on Laurent series](#layer-2-topic-10)), with `deg Λ_r(c₀bᵢ + cᵢ) ≤ 2N/q ≤ N`.

Hence the Λ-orbit of f, which is the set of generating series of the q-kernel of (aₙ) (`LaurentSeries.cartier_ofPowerSeries`), is finite; by [Eilenberg's theorem: automatic iff finite kernel](#layer-2-topic-50), (aₙ) is q-automatic.

**Checks.**

- Thue–Morse: the relation (1 + X)³T² + (1 + X)²T + X = 0 yields a finite Λ-stable set; the kernel has 2 elements.
- Rational series (degree 1) give eventually periodic, in particular automatic, sequences.

### 2.68 Power series over `𝔽_q` with q-automatic coefficients are algebraic

Let K be a finite field with q elements and a : ℕ → K q-automatic. Then f = ∑ aₙXⁿ is algebraic over K[X]; if the q-kernel has m elements, the degree of f is at most `q^m − 1`.

K finite, q = |K|.

(Andrew Bridy, [Automatic sequences and curves over finite fields](#reference-bridy-automaticcurves-2016), Section 2.3, Proposition 2.13, p. 7.) The theorem (the height bound is not part of the result).

(Andrew Bridy, [Automatic sequences and curves over finite fields](#reference-bridy-automaticcurves-2016), Section 2.3, proof of Proposition 2.13, p. 7.) The proof steps.

To prove this, let y₁, …, `y_m` be the generating series of the q-kernel of a (finite by [Eilenberg's theorem: automatic iff finite kernel](#layer-2-topic-50)); it is stable under the `Λ_r` (`LaurentSeries.cartier_ofPowerSeries`).

By `f = ∑_r X^r(Λ_r f)^q` ([The Cartier operators on Laurent series](#layer-2-topic-10)), each yᵢ lies in the K(X)-span of `y₁^q`, …, `y_m^q`; raising to q-th powers (a K(X)-semilinear bijection onto its image), `y_i^{q^j}` lies in the span of the `y^{q^{j+1}}`, and by induction `{yᵢ, yᵢ^q, …, yᵢ^{q^m}}` lies in the span of `y₁^{q^{m+1}}`, …, `y_m^{q^{m+1}}`, of dimension ≤ m.

So yᵢ, `yᵢ^q`, …, `yᵢ^{q^m}` are K(X)-linearly dependent: a nonzero polynomial `∑ cⱼT^{qʲ}` over K(X) vanishes at yᵢ, and clearing denominators f = y₁ is algebraic over K[X]; dividing by T when f ≠ 0 bounds the degree by `q^m − 1`.

**Checks.**

- The Thue–Morse kernel has 2 elements, and T has degree 2 ≤ 2² − 1.
- Eventually periodic sequences give rational series.

### 2.69 The mediant property of Farey sequences

Let n ≥ 1 and let a/b < c/d < e/f be three consecutive terms of `F_n`. Then c/d = (a + e)/(b + f), the mediant of its neighbours reduced to lowest terms.

Three consecutive terms of `F_n`; the mediant need not be in lowest terms (in F₇, 1/5, 1/4, 2/7 gives 3/12 = 1/4).

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.2, printed p. 31.) The theorem, with edges supplied by the neighbour property.

(Allen Hatcher, [Topology of Numbers](#reference-hatcher-topologyofnumbers-2024), Section 1.2, printed p. 28.) The worked example of the Checks.

To prove this, by [The neighbour property of Farey sequences](#layer-2-topic-53), bc − ad = 1 and de − cf = 1.

Then c(b + f) − d(a + e) = (bc − ad) − (de − cf) = 0, so (a + e)/(b + f) = c/d as rational numbers: this is the mediant reduced to lowest terms, the cancelled factor being be − af (Hatcher p. 31).

### 2.70 Finite carries for arbitrary bounded digits

Let k≥2, d≥0 and f:ℕ→Δ be k-automatic. There is a finite-state DFAO M on Fin(d+1) such that M.output(M.eval(w)) = f(Nat.ofDigits k (the list of digit values of w)) for every word w, read least significant digit first. Digits are allowed to exceed k−1.

The existing canonical least-significant-first definition of IsAutomatic is retained. The output alphabet is arbitrary; no independent finiteness assumption is added.

(Thijmen J. P. Krebs, [A more reasonable proof of Cobham's theorem](#reference-krebs-cobham-2018), Lemma 5, p.1, normalization step; explicit bounded-carry proof supplied here.) The source cites two books for normalization. The displayed invariant is a self-contained deduction on the k-kernel.

To prove this, by [Eilenberg's theorem: automatic iff finite kernel](#layer-2-topic-50) the k-kernel K of f is finite. Use states (g,c) with g∈K and 0≤c≤d, initial state (f,0), output g(c).

For digit e≤d set r=(c+e) mod k and c′=⌊(c+e)/k⌋, and replace g by g′(n)=g(kn+r). Since c+e≤2d and k≥2, c′≤d. Writing `g(n)=f(k^j n+s)` shows directly that g′ is again a kernel element, with residue `k^j r+s<k^(j+1)`.

After a word of length L and little-endian value V, prove the invariant `g(n+c)=f(k^L n+V)` for every n≥0. The transition uses kc′+r=c+e, and appending the new high digit changes V to `V+ek^L`. At n=0 the output is f(V), including any unflushed final carry.

The state set is finite and can be encoded by Fin of its cardinality. No assumption that the last digit is nonzero is used.

**Checks.**

- The next carry for base 2, carry 3 and digit 4 is ⌊7/2⌋=3, so the bound 2 would fail.
- At k=2, d=4, carry 3 and digit 4 give next carry 3; a carry bound of 2 fails.
- The empty word has V=0 and output f(0).
- At k=3 the little-endian words [3] and [0,1] both output f(3).
- Trailing zero digits preserve the represented integer and the output.

### 2.71 Eulerian numbers with few descents (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemma C.3)

For n ≥ 2 and q ∈ ℕ with q < n/(log(n + 1) + 1) − 1 (natural logarithm, real comparison): (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ ≤ A(n, q) ≤ (q + 1)ⁿ.

n ≥ 2; the hypothesis on q is the real inequality q + 1 < n/(log(n + 1) + 1).

(Brian Lawrence and Will Sawin, [The Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties](#reference-lawrence-sawin-2025), Appendix C, Lemma C.3 with its proof, pp. 116–117.) Insert this into the lower bound of [Power and factorial bounds for Eulerian numbers (Lawrence–Sawin, Lemmas C.1–C.2)](#layer-2-topic-57): A(n, q) ≥ (q + 1)ⁿ − (n + 1)qⁿ > (1 − 1/e)(q + 1)ⁿ; the upper bound is the upper half of that result.

### 2.72 Roots of p are eigenvalues of the companion matrix, without extending scalars

Let R be a commutative ring, p ∈ R[X] monic with d = natDegree p ≥ 1, and q ∈ R. Then p(q) = 0 iff the vector `(1, q, …, q^{d−1})` is an eigenvector of C(p)ᵀ with eigenvalue q. Over a field K, q ∈ K is an eigenvalue of C(p) iff p(q) = 0. No extension of scalars is made: eigenvalues are taken in R (or K) itself.

### 2.73 Lucas sequences are divisibility sequences

For every commutative ring R, P, Q ∈ R and m, n ≥ 0: `U_{mn}(P, Q) = U_m(P, Q)·Uₙ(V_m(P, Q), Q^m)`. In particular `U_m` divides `U_{mn}`, so n ↦ Uₙ(P, Q) is an `IsDvdSequence`.

No hypothesis on P, Q; the identity is universal.

(R. D. Carmichael, [On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms αⁿ ± βⁿ](#reference-carmichael-arithmeticforms-1913), Section 2, Theorem IV, p. 37.) The divisibility statement for integers; the result gives the explicit quotient `Uₙ(V_m, Q^m)`, which is Carmichael's product formula grouped by the pair `(α^m, β^m)`, and proves it over every commutative ring.

To prove this, work in the universal ring A = ℤ[P, Q][α]/(α² − Pα + Q) with β = P − α, where α + β = P, αβ = Q; A is free over ℤ[P, Q] with basis 1, α.

`α^m` and `β^m` satisfy `α^m + β^m = V_m` and `α^mβ^m = Q^m`, so `Uₙ(V_m, Q^m)·(α^m − β^m) = α^{mn} − β^{mn}` (Binet for the pair `(α^m, β^m)`); multiplying `U_m(α − β) = α^m − β^m` gives `(α − β)·U_mUₙ(V_m, Q^m) = (α − β)U_{mn}`.

multiplication by α − β = 2α − P is injective on ℤ[P, Q] ⊂ A (A is free with basis 1, α, and c(2α − P) = 0 forces 2c = 0, hence c = 0 in the torsion-free ℤ[P, Q]), so `U_{mn} = U_mUₙ(V_m, Q^m)` in ℤ[P, Q]; specialise along ℤ[P, Q] → R (`map_lucasU`, `map_lucasV`).

**Checks.**

- Fibonacci: F₆ = 8 = F₃·U₂(V₃, −1) = 2·4.
- `U_m ∣ U_{mn}` holds over every commutative ring, with no coprimality hypothesis.

*Needs:* [The Lucas sequence of the first kind Uₙ(P, Q)](#layer-2-topic-47); [The Lucas sequence of the second kind Vₙ(P, Q)](#layer-2-topic-62); Mathlib `IsDvdSequence`.

### 2.74 Strong divisibility of Lucas sequences

Let P, Q ∈ ℤ be coprime. Then for all m, n ≥ 0, `gcd(U_m(P, Q), Uₙ(P, Q)) = |U_{gcd(m, n)}(P, Q)|`. Equivalently n ↦ |Uₙ(P, Q)| is a strong divisibility sequence (Mathlib's `Nat.IsStrongDvdSequence`).

P, Q coprime integers, otherwise arbitrary: degenerate cases (α/β a root of unity, P = 0, Q = 0) are included, with gcd(0, 0) = 0. gcd is `Int.gcd` (a natural number), compared with the absolute value `Int.natAbs`.

(R. D. Carmichael, [On the numerical factors of the arithmetic forms αⁿ ± βⁿ](#reference-carmichael-arithmeticforms-1913), Section 2, Theorem VI, p. 38.) The theorem for P, Q nonzero coprime integers with α, β not roots of unity (Carmichael's standing exclusion, p. 36); the result removes that exclusion.

(Peter Bala, [Divisibility sequences from strong divisibility sequences](#reference-bala-strongdivisibility-2014), Appendix, proof of Proposition 2.2, pp. 9 to 10.) The proof steps, which use only Propositions A2 and A3 and so cover the degenerate cases.

(Peter Bala, [Divisibility sequences from strong divisibility sequences](#reference-bala-strongdivisibility-2014), Section 2, Proposition 2.2, p. 3.) The statement over a GCD domain; the result is the case D = ℤ, a = P, b = −Q, and also allows P = 0 or Q = 0.

To prove this, if m = n, or one index is 0, the claim is immediate (U₀ = 0). Assume n > m ≥ 1 and write n = m + k.

By the addition formula, `Uₙ = U_{k+1}U_m − Q U_kU_{m−1}`, so `gcd(Uₙ, U_m) = gcd(Q U_k U_{m−1}, U_m) = gcd(U_k, U_m)`, removing Q and `U_{m−1}` by coprimality ([Coprimality properties of Lucas sequences](#layer-2-topic-64)).

Hence `gcd(U_m, Uₙ) = gcd(U_m, U_{n−m})`; use strong induction on m+n on the indices to reach `gcd(U_{gcd(m,n)}, U₀) = |U_{gcd(m,n)}|`.

**Checks.**

- Fibonacci: `gcd(F_m, Fₙ) = F_{gcd(m,n)}` is Mathlib's `Nat.fib_gcd`.
- U(3, 2) = 2ⁿ − 1: `gcd(2^m − 1, 2ⁿ − 1) = 2^{gcd(m,n)} − 1`.
- The coprimality hypothesis is needed: P = Q = 2 gives U₂ = 2, U₃ = 2, gcd 2 ≠ |U₁| = 1.
- Degenerate case P = Q = 1 (sixth roots of unity): U = 0, 1, 1, 0, −1, −1, …, and gcd(U₃, U₆) = 0 = U₃.

### 2.80 Cobham’s theorem: independent automatic bases force periodicity

Apply [Relatively close positive powers of two bases](#layer-2-topic-14) with C=6ξ to obtain m,n≥1 and `A=a^m`,`B=b^n` with 6ξ|A−B|≤B. Multiplicative independence gives A≠B.

For each x≥N take its representatives u,v. The `C_b` comparisons at exponent n supply the two wide B-block equalities, and the `C_a` comparison at exponent m supplies the A-block equality.

**Checks.**

- 2≠4 but `2^2=4^1`, so unequal bases do not establish the theorem’s hypothesis.
- The bases 2 and 3 meet the hypothesis; the conclusion is eventual periodicity, not periodicity from zero.
- The bases 2 and 4 fail the hypothesis even though they are unequal.
- A constant sequence has period 1.

*Needs:* [Finite prefix colours control wide radix blocks](#layer-2-topic-79); [Uniform repeated representatives for a finite colouring](#layer-2-topic-15); [Relatively close positive powers of two bases](#layer-2-topic-14); [A nonzero local period from two close radix scales](#layer-2-topic-17); [Overlapping radix windows force a single tail period](#layer-2-topic-38).

<a id="layer-2-topic-81"></a>

### 2.81 Cobham’s base-independence theorem

For multiplicatively independent integers a,b≥2 and any f:ℕ→Δ, the conjunction that f is a-automatic and b-automatic is equivalent to the existence of N∈ℕ and p≥1 with f(t+p)=f(t) for every t≥N.

Multiplicative independence means `a^m≠b^n` for all positive m,n. Use IsAutomatic for automaticity.

(Thijmen J. P. Krebs, [A more reasonable proof of Cobham's theorem](#reference-krebs-cobham-2018), Theorem 1, p.1.) This is the complete equivalence of the source, on the automaton carrier fixed here and with the converse exposed as a reusable prerequisite.

To prove this, the forward implication is [Cobham’s theorem: independent automatic bases force periodicity](#layer-2-topic-80).

For the converse apply [Every eventually periodic sequence is automatic](#layer-2-topic-55) to each of the two bases, with the same tail and period.

**Checks.**

- The sequence with value 7 at zero and n mod 2 at positive n is both 2-automatic and 3-automatic.
- A sequence with a finite exceptional prefix and a periodic tail is automatic in bases 2 and 3.
- No assertion is made that an arbitrary automatic sequence is periodic in its single base.
- The theorem does not apply to the dependent pair 2,4.

*Needs:* [Cobham’s theorem: independent automatic bases force periodicity](#layer-2-topic-80); [Every eventually periodic sequence is automatic](#layer-2-topic-55).

### Examples

The Fibonacci rational series has denominator 1−X−X² and numerator X. Repeated characteristic roots require polynomial coefficients, as the sequence n for (X−1)² shows. Finite-characteristic tests keep Christol separate from characteristic-zero rationality. Every computed value and negative control attached to a result above is part of its required interface.

## Layer 3: polynomial and matrix arithmetic

Prove existence and uniqueness of matrix normal forms, then develop integer-valued polynomial arithmetic and root-based irreducibility criteria. Place the quadratic-order index comparison before the imaginary quadratic Pólya classification that uses it.

<a id="layer-3-topic-1"></a>

### 3.1 No unit-circle zero in Perron's equality case

Let f ∈ ℝ[X] be monic of degree n ≥ 2, write `a = a_{n−1}` and `S = Σ_{i=0}^{n−2}|a_i|`, and assume 1 + S ≤ |a| and f(1) ≠ 0 ≠ f(−1). For every z ∈ ℂ with |z| = 1, the complexification `f_ℂ(z)` is nonzero.

All coefficients are real; the complex polynomial is obtained by the canonical embedding ℝ → ℂ. The two endpoint exclusions are separate hypotheses. No nonzero-constant assumption is needed for this boundary lemma.

(V. V. Prasolov, [Многочлены (Polynomials)](#reference-prasolov-polynomials-russian-2003), Chapter 2, §7.2, Theorem 7.2(b), last paragraph of proof, printed/PDF p. 69.) Isolates the boundary argument in the proof. The source theorem uses integer coefficients; its boundary argument uses only their reality, so this lemma records that precise generalization.

To prove this, `expand f_ℂ(z) = z^{n−1}(z+a) + r(z)` with `r(z) = Σ_{i=0}^{n−2} a_i z^i`, using the finite coefficient expansion. On |z|=1, the triangle inequality gives |r(z)| ≤ S.

If `f_ℂ(z)=0`, then |z+a| = |r(z)| ≤ S ≤ |a|−1. Put A=|a|≥1. Squaring and using |z|²=1 gives a Re(z) ≤ −A. Since −1≤Re(z)≤1 and a is real with a≠0, this forces Re(z)=−1 when a>0 and Re(z)=1 when a<0.

In either case |z|²=(Re z)²+(Im z)²=1 forces Im(z)=0. Thus z=−1 or z=1. Evaluation commutes with ℝ→ℂ, contradicting the relevant endpoint hypothesis. This is the real-coefficient equality argument, not a claim for arbitrary complex coefficients.

**Checks.**

- X²+2X−1 satisfies equality and has f(1)=2, f(−1)=−2; neither root is on the unit circle.
- X²−2X+1 and X²+2X+1 satisfy the coefficient inequality but have a root at 1 or −1 respectively, so deleting either endpoint condition is unsound.
- For (X−i)² ∈ ℂ[X], the same norm inequality and both endpoint exclusions hold but i is a unit-circle root; real coefficients are essential.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.as_sum_range_C_mul_X_pow`; Mathlib `Complex.normSq_apply`; Mathlib `Complex.normSq_eq_norm_sq`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-2"></a>

### 3.2 Irreducibility from one outer root counted with multiplicity

Let f ∈ ℤ[X] be monic of positive degree with f(0)≠0. If its complex root multiset contains exactly one root with |z|≥1, counting multiplicity, then f is irreducible in ℤ[X].

Positive degree excludes the unit polynomial; f(0)≠0 excludes a factor X; the hypothesis counts a multiset, not distinct roots.

(V. V. Prasolov, [Многочлены (Polynomials)](#reference-prasolov-polynomials-russian-2003), Chapter 2, §7.2, Theorem 7.2(a), factorization argument, printed/PDF p. 69.) Extracts the source's integral-factor argument as a reusable declaration for both Perron variants; only the single-outer-root conclusion of the analytic argument is used.

To prove this, use `Polynomial.Monic.irreducible_iff_natDegree`. Positive degree gives f≠1. It remains to rule out f=g h with g,h monic integer polynomials both of positive degree.

The nonzero constant term of f forces both g(0) and h(0) nonzero, and their integer absolute values are at least 1.

Map the factors to ℂ. Each splits and remains monic with positive degree. The signed product-of-roots formula gives `|g(0)|=∏_{α∈roots(g)}|α|` and the analogous formula for h. If all roots of g had norm <1, their nonempty finite product of nonnegative norms would be <1, a contradiction. Thus each factor has at least one outer root.

`Polynomial.roots_mul` identifies the roots of f with the multiset sum of the roots of g and h. Filtering by |z|≥1 and taking cardinality adds the counts, giving at least two. This contradicts the assumed cardinality one, even if the two selected roots are equal.

The existing strict Perron criterion and the weak criterion both consume this common algebraic argument. No alternative root carrier or irreducibility predicate is defined.

**Checks.**

- The degree-one polynomial X−2 has one outer root and is irreducible; no n≥2 restriction belongs on this algebraic adapter.
- X²−2X has exactly one outer root but is reducible: its constant term is zero.
- (X−2)² has one distinct outer root but two with multiplicity and is reducible; replacing the multiset count by a set cardinality is invalid.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.Monic.irreducible_iff_natDegree`; Mathlib `Polynomial.Splits.coeff_zero_eq_prod_roots_of_monic`; Mathlib `IsAlgClosed`; Mathlib `IsAlgClosed.card_roots_eq_natDegree`; Mathlib `Complex.isAlgClosed`; Mathlib `Polynomial.roots_mul`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-3"></a>

### 3.3 The Smith normal form decomposition of an integer matrix

For an integer matrix A with m rows and n columns, a Smith normal form decomposition consists of integer matrices P, P′ (m × m) and Q, Q′ (n × n) with P P′ = P′ P = 1 and Q Q′ = Q′ Q = 1, a natural number r ≤ min(m, n) and positive integers `d_0`, …, `d_{r−1}` with `d_i | d_j` for i ≤ j, such that the reconstruction equation `P A Q = D_{m,n}(d)` holds, where `D_{m,n}(d)` is the m × n matrix with `d_i` in position (i, i) for i < r and zeros elsewhere. The inverse equations express unimodularity over ℤ, and the reconstruction equation fixes the original matrix.

A is an arbitrary integer matrix: not assumed square, and its determinant (when square) is not assumed nonzero. The `d_i` are positive integers (natural numbers), so the decomposition pins the sign that a divisibility chain alone leaves open. Both products P P′ and P′ P are recorded; over ℤ one of them implies the other, but the decomposition carries both so that no determinant argument is needed to use it.

The supporting API comprises:

- `IntMatrix.smithDiag`: `D_{m,n}(d)`: the m × n integer matrix with `d_i` at (i, i) for i < r and 0 elsewhere.
- `IntMatrix.IsSmithDecomposition`: the displayed relation on A, P, Q and d, retaining the positivity, chain, inverse equations and `P A Q = D_{m,n}(d)`.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_eq_reconstruct`: `A = P′ · D_{m,n}(d) · Q′`.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_isUnit_det_P`: det P is a unit of ℤ, i.e. ±1.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_isUnit_det_Q`: det Q is a unit of ℤ, i.e. ±1.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_toGLP`: The row transformation as an element of `GL_m(ℤ)`.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_rank_eq_rank`: r equals the rank of A over ℚ (Mathlib Matrix.rank of the image of A in ℚ).
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_d_zero_eq_gcd`: If r > 0 then `d_0` is the gcd of the entries of A; agrees with Tau Ceti `Matrix.invariant_factor_zero_eq_gcd` in the square nonsingular case.
- `IntMatrix.smithDecomposition_transpose`: A decomposition of A gives a decomposition of Aᵀ with the same d, with Qᵀ, Q′ᵀ as row and Pᵀ, P′ᵀ as column transformations.

(William Stein, [Algebraic Number Theory, a Computational Approach](#reference-stein-ant), Proposition 2.1.5, Section 2.1, printed p. 17.) The decomposition packages exactly the data of the proposition (P, Q, the diagonal and the chain) with the inverses of P and Q made explicit; the source says P and Q are invertible as integer matrices, and the decomposition expresses invertibility by the inverse equations.

To prove this, define `D_{m,n}(d)` entrywise: the (i, j) entry is `d_i` when i = j < r and 0 otherwise.

Define `IntMatrix.IsSmithDecomposition A P Q d` as the conjunction of the displayed rank bounds, positivity, divisibility chain, unimodularity and matrix equation. Its arguments are existing matrices and a finite natural-number family; the inverse matrices may equivalently be quantified in the unimodularity conditions.

Derive the reconstruction `A = P′ D_{m,n}(d) Q′` by multiplying the reconstruction equation on the left by P′ and on the right by Q′ and using the four inverse equations `(Matrix.mul_assoc)`.

Derive that P and Q are invertible (det P · det P′ = 1 from `Matrix.det_mul`), so each decomposition yields elements of `GL_m(ℤ)` and `GL_n(ℤ) (Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup)`.

Transpose: (P A Q)ᵀ = Qᵀ Aᵀ Pᵀ and `D_{m,n}(d)ᵀ = D_{n,m}(d)`, so a decomposition of A gives one of Aᵀ with the roles of P and Q exchanged.

**Checks.**

- Every decomposition of the matrix with rows (2, 4, 6) and (3, 6, 9) has r = 1 and `d_0 = 1`.
- Every decomposition of diag(2, 3) has r = 2 and d = (1, 6); the diagonal (2, 3) fails the chain.
- Every decomposition of the zero 2 × 3 matrix has r = 0.
- diag(1/2, 1/3) · diag(2, 3) = 1 over ℚ, but no integer decomposition of diag(2, 3) has all `d_i = 1`.
- For A = diag(2, 3) no decomposition has d = (2, 3): 2 does not divide 3. Every decomposition has d = (1, 6).
- For the zero matrix every decomposition has r = 0.
- A decomposition over ℚ is not a decomposition: the rational matrices diag(1/2, 1/3) turn diag(2, 3) into the identity, but no integer decomposition has d = (1, 1).

*Needs:* Mathlib `Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup`; Mathlib `Matrix.det`; Mathlib `Matrix.rank`; Mathlib `Matrix.rank_mul_eq_left_of_isUnit_det`; Mathlib `Matrix.rank_mul_eq_right_of_isUnit_det`.

*Lean:* `smithDiag` in namespace Certificates.

<a id="layer-3-topic-4"></a>

### 3.4 Uniqueness of invariant factors over a principal ideal domain

Let R be a principal ideal domain and M an R-module with `M ≅ R^r ⊕ ⊕_{i≤k} R/(a_i) ≅ R^{r′} ⊕ ⊕_{j≤k′} R/(b_j)`, where the `a_i` and `b_j` are nonzero nonunits forming divisibility chains. Then r = r′, k = k′ and `a_i` is associated to `b_i` for every i.

The `a_i` and `b_j` are nonzero and nonunits; without excluding units the statement is false (summands R/(1) = 0 can be added). Divisibility chains on both sides.

(Keith Conrad, [Modules over a PID](#reference-conrad-modulespid-2025), Theorem 5.7, p. 16.) The source's proof counts dimensions of `π^{i−1}T/π^iT` over A/(π), which is the step used here; the result applies the count exponent by exponent to get the whole chain, not only the product.

(William Stein, [Algebraic Number Theory, a Computational Approach](#reference-stein-ant), Proof of Theorem 2.1.2, Section 2.1, printed/PDF p. 20.) The ℤ case with a different invariant (minimal numbers of generators of nG); both routes determine the chain.

To prove this, r is the rank of `M / M_tors` (both torsion parts are the torsion submodule), so r = r′.

For an irreducible π, the dimension over R/(π) of `π^{s−1} T / π^s T` (T the torsion submodule) is the number of i with `π^s | a_i`; this number is intrinsic to T.

Knowing these numbers for all π and s determines, for each i counted from the top of the chain, the exponent of π in `a_i`; since the chains are ordered, `a_i` and `b_i` have the same π-adic valuations for every π, hence are associated (a PID is a UFD); k = k′ is the number of i with some π dividing `a_i`.

**Checks.**

- ℤ/2 ⊕ ℤ/4 and ℤ/8 have the same order but different invariant factors (2, 4) and (8).
- ℤ/6 and ℤ/2 ⊕ ℤ/3: the second is not in invariant-factor form (2 ∤ 3); its invariant-factor form is ℤ/6.
- The number of cyclic factors of a finite abelian group G in invariant-factor form is the minimal number of generators of G.

*Needs:* Mathlib `IsPrincipalIdealRing`; Mathlib `Module.equiv_free_prod_directSum`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-5"></a>

### 3.5 Hermite normal form (column-style, upper)

An m × k integer matrix H is in Hermite normal form if there is a strictly increasing map p : {0, …, k−1} → {0, …, m−1} (the pivot rows) such that for every column j: `H_{p(j), j} > 0`; `H_{i, j} = 0` for i > p(j) (the pivot is the lowest nonzero entry of the column); and for every column j′ > j to its right, `0 ≤ H_{p(j), j′} < H_{p(j), j}` (entries to the right of a pivot in its row are reduced modulo it). A matrix in Hermite normal form has no zero column. The column lattice of H is the ℤ-span of its columns in ℤᵐ.

Convention pinned: columns generate the lattice (Mathlib's mulVec and Basis.toMatrix convention), pivots are the lowest nonzero entries, and the triangle is upper. This is the convention of Cohen used by Belabas and of Micciancio's Definition 7 for square matrices; Micciancio's Definition 1 of lecture 4 and Damer use the lower-triangular mirror image, obtained by reversing the order of rows and of columns, and Stein's exercise uses rows (the transpose). No zero columns: k is the rank of the lattice; a Hermite decomposition records the zero columns separately.

The supporting API comprises:

- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm`: The predicate of the statement.
- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm.pivot_unique`: The pivot rows are determined by H: p(j) is the largest row with a nonzero entry in column j.
- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm.linearIndependent_cols`: The columns of H are ℤ-linearly independent.
- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm.isUpperTriangular`: For a square H in Hermite normal form, H is upper triangular in Mathlib's sense (Matrix.IsUpperTriangular) with positive diagonal.
- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm.det_eq_prod_diag`: For square H in Hermite normal form, `det H = ∏ H_{i,i} > 0`.
- `IntMatrix.IsHermiteNormalForm.one`: The identity matrix is in Hermite normal form.

(Daniele Micciancio, [CSE 206A: Lattice Algorithms and Applications, lecture 1 (Introduction to lattices)](#reference-micciancio-hnf-2014), Definition 7, p. 6.) The square nonsingular case of the result, with the same orientation; the result extends it to rank-deficient and rectangular lattices by moving pivots down strictly.

(Karim Belabas, [Topics in computational algebraic number theory](#reference-belabas-computational-2004), Section 4.3, printed p. 28.) The convention adopted for ideals of number fields (columns, upper triangular), which Layer 5 uses. The upper form uses column operations and positive diagonal pivots.

(William Stein (with an appendix by Paul E. Gunnells), [Modular Forms, a Computational Approach](#reference-stein-modularforms-2007), Chapter 7, Exercise 7.5, printed p. 120.) The row-style transpose of the same notion; its third condition is misprinted , and the result does not follow it.

To prove this, define the predicate as in the statement, with p existentially quantified.

p is determined by H: p(j) is the largest i with `H_{i,j} ≠ 0 (IsHermiteNormalForm.pivot_unique)`.

The columns are linearly independent: in a vanishing combination `Σ c_j H_{·,j}`, look at row p(k−1): every column j < k−1 has p(j) < p(k−1) and so vanishes in that row, and column k−1 has the positive entry `H_{p(k−1),k−1}` there, so `c_{k−1} = 0`; induct downwards.

For m = k the pivots are p(j) = j, so H is upper triangular with positive diagonal, and `det H = ∏ H_{i,i}` (Mathlib `Matrix.det_of_isUpperTriangular`).

**Checks.**

- The matrix with columns (3, 0) and (2, 1) is in Hermite normal form.
- The matrix with columns (3, 0) and (4, 1) is not in Hermite normal form.
- diag(2, −1) is not in Hermite normal form.
- The m × 0 matrix is in Hermite normal form (the zero lattice).
- The matrix with columns (3, 0) and (2, 1) is in Hermite normal form (Micciancio's example).
- The matrix with columns (3, 0) and (4, 1) is not: 4 is not reduced modulo the pivot 3.
- diag(2, −1) is not: the pivot −1 is negative.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Matrix.IsUpperTriangular`; Mathlib `Matrix.det_of_isUpperTriangular`; Mathlib `Matrix.mulVecLin`.

### 3.6 The ring Int(D) of integer-valued polynomials

Let D be an integral domain with fraction field K. Int(D) is the set of f ∈ K[X] with f(a) ∈ D for every a ∈ D. It is a D-subalgebra of K[X] containing D[X]. The main case is Int(ℤ) ⊆ ℚ[X]; for a number field, `Int(𝓞_K) ⊆ K[X]`.

D an integral domain, K its fraction field (Mathlib IsFractionRing D K); D is identified with its image in K.

The supporting API comprises:

- `intValuedPolynomials`: Int(D) as a D-subalgebra of K[X].
- `IntValuedPolynomials.mem_iff`: f ∈ Int(D) iff f(a) ∈ D for all a ∈ D.
- `IntValuedPolynomials.map_mem`: Polynomials with coefficients in D are integer-valued: D[X] ⊆ Int(D).
- `IntValuedPolynomials.C_mem_iff`: A constant c is integer-valued iff c ∈ D.
- `IntValuedPolynomials.comp_mem`: Int(D) is closed under composition.
- `IntValuedPolynomials.ringChoose_X_mem`: Every binomial polynomial (X choose n) lies in Int(ℤ).
- `IntValuedPolynomials.eq_top_of_field`: Over a field D = K, Int(K) = K[X].

(Paul-Jean Cahen and Jean-Luc Chabert, [What You Should Know About Integer-Valued Polynomials](#reference-cahen-chabert-intvalued-2016), Section 1, printed p. 312.) The target is this definition, as a D-subalgebra.

(Jesse Elliott, [Presentations and module bases of integer-valued polynomial rings](#reference-elliott-intvalued-2011), Section 1, p. 1.) The same definition in the same generality.

To prove this, carrier: {f ∈ K[X] | ∀ a ∈ D, f(a) ∈ D}.

Closure: (f g)(a) = f(a) g(a), (f + g)(a) = f(a) + g(a), constants c ∈ D are integer-valued (`Polynomial.eval_mul` and its siblings).

D[X] ⊆ Int(D): a polynomial with coefficients in D takes values in D on D.

Composition: if f, g ∈ Int(D) then f ∘ g ∈ Int(D), since g(a) ∈ D.

The binomial polynomials Ring.choose X n lie in Int(ℤ): their values at integers are binomial coefficients (Mathlib Ring.choose on ℤ).

**Checks.**

- X(X − 1)/2 ∈ Int(ℤ), and it is not the image of any polynomial in ℤ[X].
- X/2 ∉ Int(ℤ).
- (X³ − X)/3 ∈ Int(ℤ).
- The constant 1/2 is not in Int(ℤ).
- X(X − 1)/2 ∈ Int(ℤ) but ∉ ℤ[X].
- (X³ − X)/3 ∈ Int(ℤ) by Fermat's little theorem.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Subalgebra`; Mathlib `IsFractionRing`; Mathlib `Polynomial.eval`; Mathlib `Ring.choose`; Mathlib `BinomialRing`; Mathlib `Polynomial.map`; Mathlib `Ring.map_choose`.

### 3.7 The two-power case of Capelli's theorem

Let K be a field and a ∈ K with a not a square in K and a ∉ −4K⁴. Then `X^{2^k} − a` is irreducible over K for every k ≥ 0.

K any field (the characteristic-2 case is included: there −4K⁴ = {0}). Both conditions are needed: X⁴ + 4 = (X² + 2X + 2)(X² − 2X + 2) although −4 is not a square in ℚ.

(Fernando Szechtman, [On the degree of repeated radical extensions](#reference-szechtman-radical-2021), Section 1, Irreducibility Criterion (C), p. 1.) The target is the case `n = 2^k` of the criterion, over an arbitrary field as in the source (which attributes it to Vahlen, Capelli and Rédei and does not prove it); the proof steps give the norm argument.

(Biswajit Koley and A. Satyanarayana Reddy, [Irreducibility of xⁿ − a](#reference-koley-reddy-capelli-2020), Lemma 10, p. 4.) The corresponding step over ℚ in the source's elementary proof; it locates the −4b⁴ exception in the two-power part.

To prove this, k = 0, 1: X − a is irreducible; X² − a is irreducible since a is not a square (Mathlib `X_pow_sub_C_irreducible_of_prime` with p = 2).

Characteristic 2 uses the same quadratic induction as the next step. Let beta be a root of the irreducible `X^2-a` and L=K(beta). If `beta=gamma^2`, the quadratic norm gives `a=N(beta)=N(gamma)^2`, contradicting nonsquareness of a. Also -`4L^4={0}`, and beta is nonzero since a is not a square. Thus both hypotheses for the induction over L hold, with no unproved assertion about degrees of inseparable factors. The remaining norm computation is the characteristic-not-two case.

Induction (Mathlib `X_pow_mul_sub_C_irreducible`): with β a root of X² − a and L = K(β) of degree 2, `X^{2^k} − a` is irreducible over K once `X^{2^{k−1}} − β` is irreducible over L. By induction on k (applied to L and β) it suffices that β is not a square in L and, when k − 1 ≥ 2, β ∉ −4L⁴.

(char K ≠ 2; in characteristic 2 the norm argument of the previous step already settles the case.) If β = γ² with γ ∈ L, take norms: `N_{L/K}(β) = −a` (the norm of a power-basis generator is ± the constant coefficient of its minimal polynomial, Mathlib `Algebra.PowerBasis.norm_gen_eq_coeff_zero_minpoly`), so −a = N(γ)² = c² with c ∈ K, c ≠ 0. Then i := β/c ∈ L satisfies i² = a/c² = −1, and {1, i} is a K-basis of L. Writing γ = x + y i with x, y ∈ K, γ² = x² − y² + 2xy i = β = c i forces x² = y² and c = 2xy = ±2x², so a = −c² = −4x⁴ ∈ −4K⁴, a contradiction. Hence β is not a square in L.

(char K ≠ 2; in characteristic 2 the norm argument of the previous step already settles the case.) If β = −4δ⁴ with δ ∈ L, then −β = (2δ²)² is a square, so −a = N(β) = N(−β) = N(2δ²)² = c² with c ≠ 0, and i := β/c ∈ L has i² = −1 as before; then β = (2iδ²)² (since (2iδ²)² = −4δ⁴) is a square in L, which the previous step excludes. Hence β ∉ −4L⁴, and the induction hypothesis applies to `X^{2^{k−1}} − β` over L.

**Checks.**

- X⁴ + 1 is irreducible over ℚ (a = −1 is not a square and −1 ∉ −4ℚ⁴).
- X⁴ + 4 = X⁴ − (−4) is reducible: −4 = −4·1⁴.
- X⁸ − 2 is irreducible over ℚ.

*Needs:* Mathlib `X_pow_sub_C_irreducible_of_prime`; Mathlib `X_pow_mul_sub_C_irreducible`; Mathlib `Algebra.PowerBasis.norm_gen_eq_coeff_zero_minpoly`; Mathlib `Algebra.norm_algebraMap`; Mathlib `Algebra.norm`.

### 3.8 The analytic order of a complex polynomial is its root multiplicity

For a nonzero p ∈ ℂ[X] and z ∈ ℂ, the order of vanishing at z of the entire function w ↦ p(w) equals the multiplicity of z as a root of p.

p ≠ 0.

(Edward J. Barbeau, [Polynomials, Chapter Six: Irreducibility and factorization (draft)](#reference-barbeau-irreducibility-2010), Section 2, Perron's criterion, printed p. 49.) Rouché counts zeros with multiplicity as analytic orders; this lemma converts that count to the root count of a polynomial, a step the source takes for granted.

To prove this, write `p = (X − z)^m q` with m = rootMultiplicity z p and q(z) ≠ 0 (Mathlib `Polynomial.exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd`).

Then `p(w) = (w − z)^m q(w)` near z with q analytic and q(z) ≠ 0, which is the characterisation of analytic order m (Mathlib `AnalyticAt.analyticOrderAt_eq_natCast`).

**Checks.**

- For p = (X − 1)² (X + 1) the order at 1 is 2 and at 0 is 0.
- For p = X³ the order at 0 is 3.
- Summing over a disc counts roots with multiplicity, which is how Rouché's theorem is applied to polynomials.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.exists_eq_pow_rootMultiplicity_mul_and_not_dvd`; Mathlib `AnalyticAt.analyticOrderAt_eq_natCast`; Mathlib `analyticOrderNatAt`; Mathlib `Polynomial.rootMultiplicity`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-9"></a>

### 3.9 A prime value far from the roots forces irreducibility

Let f ∈ ℤ[X] and b ∈ ℤ with f(b) prime, f(b − 1) ≠ 0, and Re α < b − 1/2 for every complex root α of f. Then f is irreducible in ℤ[X].

f(b) is a prime (up to sign) of ℤ; f(b − 1) ≠ 0.

(John Brillhart, Michael Filaseta and Andrew Odlyzko, [On an irreducibility theorem of A. Cohn](#reference-brillhart-cohn-1981), Theorem 2, printed p. 1055.) The target is Theorem 2 (credited there to Pólya and Szegő) with its proof.

To prove this, if deg f = 0 then f = f(b) is a prime constant, irreducible. Assume deg f ≥ 1 and f = g h with neither factor a unit.

Key inequality: for a nonconstant g ∈ ℤ[X] whose roots α satisfy Re α < b − 1/2, |g(b − 1/2 − t)| < |g(b − 1/2 + t)| for t > 0 (each linear factor satisfies |b − 1/2 − t − α| < |b − 1/2 + t − α|). At t = 1/2: |g(b − 1)| < |g(b)|; since g(b − 1) is a nonzero integer, |g(b)| ≥ 2.

A constant factor c with |c| ≥ 2 and a nonconstant cofactor g gives |f(b)| = |c||g(b)| ≥ 4 composite; two nonconstant factors give |f(b)| = |g(b)||h(b)| with both ≥ 2. Either contradicts primality.

**Checks.**

- f = X² + 1, b = 2: f(2) = 5 prime, f(1) = 2 ≠ 0, roots ±i with real part 0 < 3/2: irreducible.
- X³ − 9X² − 9X + 1 = (X + 1)(X² − 10X + 1) has the prime value 11 at 10 but a root 5 + √24 ≈ 9.9 with real part > 9.5: the root condition is essential.
- f(b − 1) ≠ 0 is needed to get |g(b − 1)| ≥ 1.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.roots`; Mathlib `Polynomial.eval_mul`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-10"></a>

### 3.10 The roots of a digit polynomial

Let b ≥ 2 and let `f = Σ a_k X^k ∈ ℤ[X]` be nonzero with `0 ≤ a_k ≤ b − 1` for all k. Then every complex root α of f satisfies Re α < b − 1/2.

Digits: all coefficients in [0, b − 1]; f ≠ 0.

(John Brillhart, Michael Filaseta and Andrew Odlyzko, [On an irreducibility theorem of A. Cohn](#reference-brillhart-cohn-1981), Theorem 3 and Corollary 1, printed pp. 1056–1057.) The target is the root-location content of Theorem 3 and Corollary 1 specialised to digits.

To prove this, degree 0 has no roots; degree 1: the root `−a_0/a_1 ≤ 0 < b − 1/2`.

Degree n ≥ 2: the leading digit `a_n ≥ 1` and `a_{n−1}`, `a_{n−2} ≥ 0`, and `m := max_{k≤n−2} |a_k|/a_n ≤ b − 1 ≤ B`, where B = 1 for b = 2 and B = ⌊(2b − 1)(2b − 1 − √2)/2⌋ for b ≥ 3.

Theorem 3 of Brillhart–Filaseta–Odlyzko: all roots lie in `Re z ≤ max(r_1/√2, r_2)`, where `r_1` is the positive root of x² − x − m and `r_2` that of x³ − x² − m (estimate |f(z)/zⁿ| from below on the two regions `|z| > r_1`, and `|z| ≤ r_1` with |arg z| < π/4).

`r_1 ≤ r_1*`, `r_2 ≤ r_2*` for the roots with m replaced by B, and h(b − 1/2) = (2b − 1)(2b − 1 − √2)/2 − B > 0, g(b − 1/2) = (b − 1/2)²(b − 3/2) − B > 0 give `b − 1/2 > max(r_1*/√2, r_2*)`.

**Checks.**

- For b = 10 and f = 3X² + 9X + 7 (the digits of 397) the roots have real part −1.5 < 9.5.
- For b = 2 the bound B = 1 equals b − 1.
- Negative digits break it: X³ − 9X² − 9X + 1 has a root near 9.9.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Polynomial.roots`.

### 3.11 The sloped valuation of a polynomial over a valued field

Let K be a field with an additive valuation v : K → ℝ ∪ {∞} (v(0) = ∞, v(xy) = v(x) + v(y), v(x + y) ≥ min(v(x), v(y))). For r ∈ ℝ and `f = Σ a_i X^i ∈ K[X]`, the sloped valuation is `v_r(f) = min_{i : a_i ≠ 0} (v(a_i) + r i)`, and `v_r(0) = ∞`. It is the intercept of the supporting line of slope r of the Newton polygon.

Valuation with values in ℝ ∪ {∞} (Mathlib AddValuation K (WithTop ℝ)); the minimum over the support of f.

For Laurent fields this is the supporting-line interface of FormalLaurentPuiseux L5's polygon, under §3.18's comparison.

The supporting API comprises:

- `slopedValuation`: `v_r(f)`.
- `SlopedValuation.zero`: `v_r(0) = ⊤`.
- `SlopedValuation.C_mul_X_pow`: `v_r(c Xⁿ) = v(c) + r n` for c ≠ 0.
- `SlopedValuation.le_coeff`: `v_r(f) ≤ v(a_i) + r i` for every i.
- `SlopedValuation.min_le_add`: `min(v_r f, v_r g) ≤ v_r(f + g)`.
- `SlopedValuation.zero_slope`: `v_0` is the Gauss valuation `min_i v(a_i)`.

(Kiran S. Kedlaya, [p-adic differential equations (18.787, MIT, fall 2007): Newton polygons](#reference-kedlaya-newtonpolygons-2007), Section 2, p. 2.) The target is this definition for ordinary (untwisted) polynomials, the case d = 0 of the source.

To prove this, define `v_r(f)` as the infimum over the support of f in WithTop ℝ (Finset.inf), so `v_r(0) = ⊤`.

Monomial: `v_r(c X^n) = v(c) + r n`.

Each term bounds it: `v_r(f) ≤ v(a_i) + r i`.

Ultrametric: `v_r(f + g) ≥ min(v_r(f), v_r(g))`.

r = 0 gives the Gauss valuation `min_i v(a_i)`.

**Checks.**

- `v_r(X) = r`.
- `v_r(X − c) = min(v(c), r)` for c ≠ 0.
- `v_r(0) = ⊤`.
- `v_r(0) = ∞`.

*Needs:* Mathlib `AddValuation`; Mathlib `AddValuation.map_mul`; Mathlib `AddValuation.map_add`; Mathlib `Polynomial.support`.

### 3.12 The index of ℤ[√d] in the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)

Let d ≠ 0, 1 be squarefree, K = ℚ(θ) with θ² = d (minpoly ℤ θ = X² − d). Then `[𝓞_K : ℤ[θ]] = 2` if d ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 1 otherwise.

d squarefree, d ≠ 0, 1; θ generates K.

(Keith Conrad, [Factoring in quadratic fields](#reference-conrad-quadraticfields-2021), Section 3, Theorem 3.4, p. 2.) The two rings of integers whose comparison with ℤ[√d] the result records as an index.

(William Stein, [Algebraic Number Theory, a Computational Approach](#reference-stein-ant), Proposition 6.2.6, Section 6.2, printed p. 73.) Applied to O = ℤ[√d].

To prove this, θ is an integral primitive element; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.NumberField.IntegralPrimitiveElement.discr_minpoly_eq_index_sq_mul_discr` gives `disc(X² − d) = 4d = index(θ)² · d_K`.

Tau Ceti `NumberField.discr_eq_of_squarefree_of_mod_four_eq_one` and `NumberField.discr_eq_four_mul_of_mod_four_ne_one` give `d_K = d` or 4d.

Hence index(θ)² = 4 or 1.

**Checks.**

- d = 5: ℤ[√5] has index 2 in ℤ[(1 + √5)/2].
- d = −1: `ℤ[i] = 𝓞_{ℚ(i)}`.
- d = −3: ℤ[√−3] has index 2 in ℤ[(1 + √−3)/2], the ring containing the primitive cube roots of unity.

*Needs:* Tau Ceti `TauCeti.NumberField.IntegralPrimitiveElement.discr_minpoly_eq_index_sq_mul_discr`; Tau Ceti `TauCeti.NumberField.IntegralPrimitiveElement.index`; Tau Ceti `NumberField.discr_eq_of_squarefree_of_mod_four_eq_one`; Tau Ceti `NumberField.discr_eq_four_mul_of_mod_four_ne_one`; Mathlib `Polynomial.discr`.

### 3.13 The Legendre exponent `w_q(n)`

For an integer q ≥ 2 and n ∈ ℕ, `w_q(n) = Σ_{k≥1} ⌊n/q^k⌋`, a finite sum since its terms vanish once `q^k > n`. Equivalently `w_q(n) = Σ_{l=1}^{n} v_q(l)`, where `v_q(l)` is the largest h with `q^h | l`. For a prime p, `w_p(n) = v_p(n!)` (Legendre's formula); for a prime power `q = p^f` with f ≥ 2, `w_q(n)` is not a p-adic valuation of n!.

q ≥ 2 an integer (q = 1 is excluded: the sum would diverge).

The supporting API comprises:

- `legendreExponent`: `w_q(n) := Σ_{k ∈ [1, n]} n / q^k` for q ≥ 2.
- `LegendreExponent.eq_sum_multiplicity`: `w_q(n) = Σ_{l=1}^{n} v_q(l)`, with `v_q(l)` the largest h such that `q^h | l`.
- `LegendreExponent.succ`: `w_q(n + 1) = w_q(n) + v_q(n + 1)`.
- `LegendreExponent.eq_zero_iff`: For q ≥ 2: `w_q(n) = 0 ↔ n < q`.
- `LegendreExponent.self`: `w_q(q) = 1`.
- `LegendreExponent.add_le`: `w_q(m) + w_q(n) ≤ w_q(m + n)`.
- `LegendreExponent.prime_eq_padicValNat`: For p prime: `w_p(n) = padicValNat p n!` (Mathlib `padicValNat_factorial`).

(Paul-Jean Cahen and Jean-Luc Chabert, [What You Should Know About Integer-Valued Polynomials](#reference-cahen-chabert-intvalued-2016), Section 6, the v-ordering formula for `w_q(n)`, printed pp. 331–332.) Defines `w_q(n)` as the valuation of the v-ordering products and shows it equals `Σ_{l≤n} v_q(l) = Σ_k ⌊n/q^k⌋`, noting the analogy with Legendre's formula.

(Amandine Leriche, [Pólya fields, Pólya groups and Pólya extensions: a question of capitulation](#reference-leriche-polya-2011), Section 2, the function `w_m` and the remark on K = ℚ, p. 239.) The same function indexed by the norm of a maximal ideal, with `w_p(n) = v_p(n!)` for ℚ.

To prove this, define `w_q(n)` as the sum of `n / q^k` (natural-number division) over 1 ≤ k ≤ n; the terms with `q^k > n` vanish.

`Σ_{k≥1} ⌊n/q^k⌋` counts the pairs (l, k) with 1 ≤ l ≤ n, k ≥ 1 and `q^k | l`, which is `Σ_{l≤n} v_q(l)`.

Hence `w_q(n + 1) − w_q(n) = v_q(n + 1)`, `w_q(n) = 0 iff n < q`, and `w_q(q) = 1`.

Superadditivity `w_q(m) + w_q(n) ≤ w_q(m + n)` termwise from ⌊x⌋ + ⌊y⌋ ≤ ⌊x + y⌋.

For q = p prime this is Mathlib's Legendre formula `(padicValNat_factorial)`.

**Checks.**

- `w_2(4) = 3` and `w_3(10) = 4`.
- `w_4(4) = 1`.
- `w_q(n) = 0` for every n < q, and `w_q(0) = 0`.
- `w_5(26) = 6 = padicValNat 5 26!`.
- `w_4(8) = 2`, whereas padicValNat 2 8! = 7: for a prime power `q = p^f` with f ≥ 2, `w_q(n)` is not the p-adic valuation of n!.
- `w_2(4) = 3 = v_2(24)`, `w_4(4) = 1`, `w_3(10) = 3 + 1 = 4`.
- `w_q(n) = 0` for n < q.

*Needs:* Mathlib `padicValNat_factorial`; Mathlib `Nat.factorization_factorial`.

<a id="layer-3-topic-14"></a>

### 3.14 The ideals `Π_q(D)`: product of the primes of norm q

Let D be a Dedekind domain that is not a field, with finite residue fields. For an integer q ≥ 2, `Π_q(D)` is the product of 𝔪.asIdeal over 𝔪 in HeightOneSpectrum D with N(𝔪) = q; these are precisely the nonzero maximal ideals. It is the unit ideal D when no such ideal has norm q (for example when q is not a prime power). Only finitely many such ideals have a given norm, so the product is finite.

D a Dedekind domain, not a field, with finite residue fields. The pigeonhole argument of [The local formula for the characteristic ideals of a Dedekind domain](#layer-3-topic-60) gives finiteness of the ideals of each norm.

The supporting API comprises:

- `polyaIdeal`: `Π_q(D)` : Ideal D, the product indexed by 𝔪 in HeightOneSpectrum D of absolute norm q.
- `PolyaIdeal.count_polyaIdeal`: For 𝔪 in HeightOneSpectrum D, its exponent in `Π_q(D)` is 1 if N(𝔪) = q and 0 otherwise.
- `PolyaIdeal.eq_top_iff`: `Π_q(D) = ⊤ iff` no maximal ideal of D has norm q.
- `PolyaIdeal.eq_top_of_not_isPrimePow`: If q is not a prime power, `Π_q(D) = ⊤`.
- `PolyaIdeal.isCoprime`: `Π_q(D)` and `Π_{q′}(D)` are coprime for q ≠ q′.
- `polyaIdeal_pow_ramificationIdxIn`: For K/ℚ Galois and p with residue degree f and ramification index e: `Π_{p^f}(𝓞_K)^e = p𝓞_K`, and `Π_{p^j}(𝓞_K) = ⊤` for j ≠ f.
- `PolyaIdeal.ne_bot`: Under these hypotheses `Π_q(D) ≠ ⊥`, so its class in the class group is defined.

(Amandine Leriche, [Pólya fields, Pólya groups and Pólya extensions: a question of capitulation](#reference-leriche-polya-2011), Section 2, Notation before Proposition 2.2, p. 239.) Defines `Π_q(K)` as the product of the maximal ideals of `𝓞_K` of norm q, equal to `𝓞_K` when q is not a norm.

(Paul-Jean Cahen and Jean-Luc Chabert, [What You Should Know About Integer-Valued Polynomials](#reference-cahen-chabert-intvalued-2016), Section 6, Pólya groups and Pólya fields, printed pp. 332–333.) The same products, as generators of the Pólya group (citing the book, Proposition II.3.9).

(Jean-Luc Chabert, [Integer-Valued Polynomials: Looking for Regular Bases (a Survey)](#reference-chabert-regularbases-survey), Section 5.4, after Definition 6, p. 13.) The same definition for a Dedekind domain D.

To prove this, take the finite product of 𝔪.asIdeal over the elements of HeightOneSpectrum D of norm q.

Its exponent at 𝔪 is 1 if N(𝔪) = q and 0 otherwise; hence `Π_q` and `Π_{q′}` are coprime for q ≠ q′.

If q is not a prime power, no residue field has q elements and `Π_q(D) = D`.

Galois case ([Ostrowski's theorem: the Pólya group of a Galois number field](#layer-3-topic-65)): `Π_{p^f}(𝓞_K)^e = p𝓞_K`, where e and f are the common ramification index and residue degree of p.

**Checks.**

- `Π_p(ℤ) = Ideal.span {p}` for p prime, and `Π_4(ℤ) = ⊤`.
- In ℤ[i]: `Π_2 = (1 + i)`, `Π_5 = (5)`, `Π_9 = (3)` and `Π_3 = ⊤`.
- `Π_6(D) = ⊤` for every D, since 6 is not a prime power.
- The field D=𝔽₂ is excluded: an all-maximal-ideal product at q=2 would contain (0), whose powers cannot have the asserted additive finite exponent.
- For K = ℚ(√−5): `Π_2(𝓞_K) = (2, 1 + √−5)` is not principal although its square `2𝓞_K` is; `Π_q` is not the extension of an ideal of ℤ.
- `Π_p(ℤ) = pℤ` and `Π_4(ℤ) = ℤ`.
