### 5.16a A lower bound for the class number times the regulator from a truncated Euler product

Let `κ_K = NumberField.dedekindZeta_residue K = 2^(r_1) (2π)^(r_2) h_K R_K / (w_K √Δ_K)` be the residue of `ζ_K` at 1, n = [K:ℚ], `ψ_K = TauCeti.primePsi K Set.univ` and `ψ = Chebyshev.psi`, and for T ≥ 2 let `S_K(T) = Σ_(2 ≤ m ≤ T) (Λ_K(m) − Λ(m)) / (m log m)`, where `Λ_K(m)` is the sum of log N(P) over the prime powers `P^k` of norm m (Tau Ceti `TauCeti.primeVonMangoldtCoeff K Set.univ`) and Λ is Mathlib's `ArithmeticFunction.vonMangoldt`. (i) Under DedekindERH K, every x ≥ 100 satisfies `|ψ_K(x) − x| ≤ √x ((log x/(2π) + 2) log Δ_K + (log² x/(8π) + 2) n)`; for K = ℚ, under RiemannHypothesis, this bounds `|ψ(x) − x|`. (ii) Under DedekindERH K and RiemannHypothesis, for every T ≥ 100, `|log κ_K − S_K(T)| ≤ ε_K(T)`, where `ε_K(T)` is the explicit bound that partial summation of (i), for K and for ℚ, gives for the tail beyond T of the series `Σ_m (Λ_K(m) − Λ(m)) / (m log m)`; `ε_K(T) → 0` as T → ∞. (iii) If `|log κ_K − S| ≤ ε` for real numbers S and ε, then `h* = w_K √Δ_K / (2^(r_1) (2π)^(r_2)) · exp(S − ε)` satisfies `h* ≤ h_K R_K ≤ h* · exp(2ε)`.

With `S = S_K(T)` and `ε = ε_K(T)`, the lower bound of (iii) is the specified `h*` of [The class-number–regulator completeness criterion](#layer-5-topic-16), and the interval of (iii) gives the a and η of §5.22. Equivalently `S_K(T) = Σ 1/(k N(P)^k) − Σ 1/(k p^k)`, the first sum over the prime powers `P^k` of norm at most T and the second over the rational prime powers `p^k ≤ T`: a truncation of the logarithm of the Euler product of `ζ_K/ζ`. Clauses (i) and (ii) carry DedekindERH K (AnalyticNumberTheoryPartI §2.42), which has no carrier at the pins, so they are README targets; RiemannHypothesis is Mathlib's. Clause (iii) has a Lean signature.

The supporting API comprises:

- `abs_primePsi_sub_le_of_dedekindERH`: clause (i).
- `abs_log_dedekindZeta_residue_sub_le_of_dedekindERH`: clause (ii).
- `classNumber_mul_regulator_bounds_of_abs_log_residue_sub_le`: clause (iii).

(Loïc Grenié and Giuseppe Molteni, [Explicit versions of the prime ideal theorem for Dedekind zeta functions under GRH](#reference-grenie-molteni-2016), Corollary 1.2 and inequality (1.5), p. 3, deduced from Theorem 1.1, p. 2, by choosing its height parameter; the hypothesis `ζ_K(s) ≠ 0` for Re s > 1/2 is stated in Section 1, p. 2, and the case K = ℚ is covered in the proof of Corollary 1.2, p. 13.) Clause (i) is Corollary 1.2.

(Eric Bach, [Improved approximations for Euler products](#reference-bach-euler-products-1995), cited by title; no theorem number is verified.) Under the Riemann hypothesis for `ζ_K` the source approximates `log κ_K = log (ζ_K/ζ)(1)` by weighted averages of log A(x + i), where A(x) is the product of `(1 − 1/N(P))^(−1)` over the primes with N(P) < x and of (1 − 1/p) over the rational primes p < x, with error `O(log Δ_K / (√x log x))`. Clause (ii) is the unweighted truncation, with the explicit constants of (i).

(Jean-François Biasse and Claus Fieker, [Subexponential class group and unit group computation in large degree number fields](#reference-biasse-fieker-classgroup-2014), Section 4.3, printed p. 398.) The source writes `hR = (|μ| √|Δ| / (2^(r_1) (2π)^(r_2))) · lim_(s→1) (s − 1) ζ_K(s)` and certifies with a bound `h*` satisfying `h* ≤ hR < 2h*`, obtained from the Euler product under GRH; clause (iii) reads that formula as an interval.

To prove this, for (i) Grenié and Molteni insert Re ρ = 1/2 into the truncated explicit formula for `ψ_K`, bound the sums over zeros with an explicit zero count for `ζ_K`, and choose the truncation height; these analytic inputs are those of the conditional route of AnalyticNumberTheoryPartI §2.49, made explicit.

For (ii), for real σ > 1 the Euler products of `ζ_K` (Tau Ceti `TauCeti.log_dedekindZeta_re_eq_tsum_neg_log_one_sub`) and of ζ give `log ζ_K(σ) − log ζ(σ) = Σ_m (Λ_K(m) − Λ(m)) m^(−σ) / log m`. As σ → 1⁺ the left side tends to `log κ_K` (Mathlib `NumberField.tendsto_sub_one_mul_dedekindZeta_nhdsGT` and `riemannZeta_residue_one`), and by Abel's theorem for Dirichlet series the right side tends to the series at 1. The tail of that series beyond T is bounded by partial summation of the Grenié–Molteni bound applied to `ψ_K − ψ` (Mathlib `sum_mul_eq_sub_integral_mul`).

Clause (iii) is Mathlib `NumberField.dedekindZeta_residue_def` solved for `h_K R_K`.

**Checks.**

- K = ℚ(i), x = 10⁴: `ψ_K(x) ≈ 10041.9`, so `|ψ_K(x) − x| ≈ 41.9`, well inside the bound of (i), about 1555.5; for ℚ, `|ψ(10⁴) − 10⁴| ≈ 13.4` against about 537.5.
- K = ℚ(i): `S_K(10⁴) ≈ −0.24117`, against `log κ_K = log(π/4) ≈ −0.24156`.
- K = ℚ: `Λ_K = Λ`, so `S_K(T) = 0` for every T, and `κ_ℚ = 1`; (ii) holds with any ε ≥ 0, and (iii) gives `h* = exp(−ε) ≤ 1 = h_ℚ R_ℚ`.
- The truncated sum alone gives no lower bound: for ℚ(i), `(4/π) exp(S_K(10⁴)) ≈ 1.0004 > h_K R_K = 1`. The error term of (ii) is what makes `h*` a lower bound.

### 5.17 The negative Pell equation and units of norm −1

Let d > 1 be squarefree with d ≢ 1 (mod 4) and K = ℚ(√d). The equation x² − dy² = −1 has an integer solution if and only if `𝓞_K` has a unit of norm −1; in that case the norm-one units have index 2, and the least positive solution `x_1 + y_1√d` generates `𝓞_K^×` modulo ±1.

d > 1 squarefree, d ≢ 1 (mod 4).

(Keith Conrad, [Pell's equation, I](#reference-conrad-pell-one-2025), Theorem 7.5, p. 12.) The Pell-side statement; the result transports it to the units of `𝓞_K`.

To prove this, under the isomorphism `ℤ√d ≅ 𝓞_K` ([The ring ℤ√d inside the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)](#layer-5-topic-6)), x + y√d has norm x² − dy²; an element of norm −1 is a unit `(Zsqrtd.norm_eq_one_iff)`.

Conversely a unit of norm −1 of `𝓞_K = ℤ[√d]` is x + y√d with x² − dy² = −1.

The index statement is [Pell solutions are the units of norm one](#layer-5-topic-14) with the norm surjective onto {±1}.

The last clause, that the least positive solution generates the units modulo ±1, is [Classification of the solutions of x² − dy² = ±1 when the negative equation is solvable](#layer-4-topic-47) read through the identification of ℤ[√d] with `𝓞_K` ([The ring ℤ√d inside the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)](#layer-5-topic-6)); nothing is re-proved here.

**Checks.**

- d = 2: 1² − 2·1² = −1, the unit 1 + √2 of norm −1.
- d = 3: x² ≡ −1 (mod 3) has no solution, so no unit of norm −1; the fundamental unit 2 + √3 has norm 1.
- d = 10: 3² − 10·1² = −1.

### 5.18 The class group of ℚ(√−14) is cyclic of order 4

For K = ℚ(√−14), Cl(K) ≅ ℤ/4ℤ.

K = ℚ(θ), θ² = −14.

(Keith Conrad, [Class group calculations by Minkowski bound](#reference-conrad-classgroups-2026), Example 2.3, p. 2.) The target is Example 2.3, rewritten as a relation-matrix computation.

To prove this, `m_K = (2/π)√56 ≈ 4.76`, so Cl(K) is generated by the primes of norm ≤ 4, which lie over 2 and 3 ([The class group is generated by the primes of norm at most the Minkowski bound](#layer-5-topic-1)).

`𝓞_K = ℤ[θ]` since −14 ≡ 2 (mod 4); by [Dedekind–Kummer at every prime for a monogenic presentation](#monogenic-prime-factorisation-input), X² + 14 ≡ X² (mod 2) and ≡ (X − 1)(X + 1) (mod 3), so `(2) = p_2²` and `(3) = p_3 p_3′`, and `p_3′ ∼ p_3^{−1}`.

Relations: `p_2² = (2)`; (2 + θ) has norm 18 = 2·3² and is not divisible by 3, so `(2 + θ) = p_2 p_3²` for the suitably named `p_3`. The relation lattice of `(p_2, p_3)` contains the columns (2, 0) and (1, 2).

Completeness: `p_2` is not principal (a² + 14b² = 2 has no solution), so `[p_2]` has order 2; `[p_3]² = [p_2]^{−1} ≠ 1`, so `[p_3]` has order 4 and generates. Hence Λ is spanned by (2, 0), (1, 2), of index 4 = h.

The Smith form of the matrix with columns (2, 0), (1, 2) is diag(1, 4) ([Smith normal form of a rectangular integer matrix](#layer-3-topic-40)); [The class group from a complete relation matrix](#layer-5-topic-10) gives Cl(K) ≅ ℤ/4.

**Checks.**

- h = 4 = |det| of the relation matrix.
- The class group is cyclic, unlike ℚ(√−30) of the same class number.
- The generator is the class of a prime of norm 3.

K = ℚ(θ), θ² = −30.

### 5.20 Arithmetic invariants of ideal, relation and unit presentations

For a number field K, basis, ideal, relation and unit data with the explicit comparisons below are interpreted by the comparison theorems of this layer as follows. (1) A family b of n elements of `𝓞_K` with a comparison `disc(b) = d_K` (or disc(b) squarefree) is an integral basis ([The discriminant of a basis of a sublattice of `𝓞_K`](#layer-5-topic-5)). (2) A matrix specified to be in Hermite normal form with an `𝓞_K`-stable column lattice is the Hermite matrix of a unique ideal, of norm the product of its pivots ([Which Hermite matrices are the matrices of ideals](#layer-5-topic-13), [The norm of an ideal is the product of its Hermite pivots](#layer-5-topic-12)). (3) A family of prime ideals containing all primes of norm `≤ M_K` with a relation matrix whose columns span the relation lattice (the completeness hypothesis, which clause (4)'s inequality can establish) determines `Cl(K) ≅ ⊕ ℤ/d_i` by the Smith form ([The class group from a complete relation matrix](#layer-5-topic-10)); without the completeness comparison it determines only a multiple of `h_K` ([Found relations bound the class number from above](#layer-5-topic-11)). (4) Let A be as in (3) but only a square matrix of nonzero determinant whose columns are relations. A unit family u with IsMaxRank and a specified bound `h* ≤ h_K R_K` with |det A| R(u) < 2h* generates `𝓞_K^×` together with `μ_K`, and then the columns of A span the relation lattice ([The class-number–regulator completeness criterion](#layer-5-topic-16)).

Each clause is an intrinsic implication from its stated discriminant, lattice or index hypotheses.

(Jean-François Biasse and Claus Fieker, [Subexponential class group and unit group computation in large degree number fields](#reference-biasse-fieker-classgroup-2014), Section 4.3, printed p. 400.) The completeness step of a class group and unit computation; the result lists which intrinsic invariant each specified output determines.

To prove this, each clause applies its named Layer 5 comparison theorem to data satisfying the explicitly stated hypotheses. Together these theorems identify the intrinsic invariants from the stated hypotheses.

A rigorous analytic bound h* with its error control enters only through `h* <= h_K R_K`. These implications depend only on the arithmetic hypotheses.

**Checks.**

- The worked examples ℚ(√−14) and ℚ(√−30) are instances of clause (3) with the explicit complete relation lattices.
- A relation matrix of determinant 8 for ℚ(√−14) (h = 4) is an output without completeness comparison: clause (3) yields only 4 | 8.
- For ℚ(√5) the unit (1 + √5)/2 with any specified `L > R_K/2` is an instance of clause (4) with the class group trivial.

### 5.21 Negative Pell and norm-minus-one units for every squarefree radicand

Under the quadratic presentation hypotheses, there exist integers x,y with x²-dy²=-1 iff there is a unit u of the full ring `O_K` with `N_K/Q(u)=-1`. The direction from an integral solution to a unit of norm −1 is the current Tau Ceti library's `NumberField.exists_norm_eq_neg_one_of_sq_sub_mul_sq_eq_neg_one`; the converse is the new content. This removes the mod-four condition by combining [The negative Pell equation and units of norm −1 when d ≡ 1 (mod 4)](#layer-5-topic-15) and [The negative Pell equation and units of norm −1](#layer-5-topic-17).

d>1 is a squarefree integer; K is a number field with θ in `O_K`. `minpoly_Z(θ)=X²-d` and Q[θ]=K; these hypotheses specify the quadratic presentation.

(Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano, [On Stevenhagen’s conjecture](#reference-koymans-pagano-2022-v1), Introduction, p. 1, equation (1.1), and p. 2, first paragraph (definition of D⁻).) Koymans and Pagano define D⁻ by integral solubility of the negative Pell equation (1.1) and then compare it with class-group and unit conditions in ℚ(√d) (pp. 2–4). Those comparisons need this passage between integral solutions and units of the full ring of integers, which the paper leaves implicit; the result combines those two order-to-unit comparisons.

To prove this, use the order-to-unit embedding of [The ring ℤ√d inside the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)](#layer-5-topic-6) for the forward implication.

If d is not 1 modulo 4, `O_K=Z[θ]`, and read the inverse coordinates and norm from [The ring ℤ√d inside the ring of integers of ℚ(√d)](#layer-5-topic-6).

If d is 1 modulo 4, invoke the half-coordinate unit comparison: d=1 modulo 8 puts any unit in Z[θ]; d=5 modulo 8 puts its cube there. The odd power preserves norm minus one.

The condition d>1 excludes the degree-one radicand, where quadratic norm transport would be false.

**Checks.**

- d=2 gives (1,1); d=3 is obstructed modulo 3.
- For d=5, ((1+θ)/2)³=2+θ; for d=13, ((3+θ)/2)³=18+5θ.
- For d=17, the negative unit 4+θ is already in Z[θ]; d=1 is excluded.

### 5.22 Class-number and regulator completeness from rigorous intervals

Let φ:`Z^N→Additive Cl(K)` be surjective; let A be a square integer matrix with nonzero determinant and `φ(A_col_j)=0` for all j. Let u be a unit family of size rank K satisfying IsMaxRank. Write h=classNumber K, R=regulator K and `R_u=regOfFamily u`. Suppose ε,η≥0, `|Rhat-R_u|≤ε`, |a-hR|≤η, and |det A|·(Rhat+ε)<2(a-η). Then range A=ker φ, the subgroup generated by u and torsion is all units, |det A|=h, and `R_u=R`. The interval inequalities are explicit hypotheses; no GRH assumption occurs.

φ surjective; nonzero determinant; every column is a genuine relation. Maximal-rank units; rigorously valid error intervals; strict inequality.

(Jean-François Biasse and Claus Fieker, [Subexponential class group and unit group computation in large degree number fields](#reference-biasse-fieker-classgroup-2014), Section 4.3, printed pp. 398 and 400, the test h* ≤ h′R′ < 2h*, Lemma 4.4 and Proposition 4.5.) Biasse–Fieker establish a tentative class number and regulator by the test h* ≤ h′R′ < 2h* against a bound h* with h* ≤ hR < 2h* (obtained under GRH, p. 398), computing R′ from fixed-point logarithms (p. 400). This result is the soundness half with explicit two-sided error intervals and without GRH; only `R_u ≤ Rhat+ε` and a−η ≤ hR are used. Their explicit precision in Proposition 4.5 undercounts the determinant loss ; the result takes ε as a hypothesis and does not depend on it.

To prove this, [Found relations bound the class number from above](#layer-5-topic-11) gives |det A|=h·i, where i=[ker φ:range A] is a positive integer.

Pinned regulator positivity and `regOfFamily_div_regulator` give `R_u=R·j`, where j is the positive index of the subgroup generated by units and torsion.

The interval hypotheses imply `R_u≤Rhat+ε` and a-η≤hR. Hence `hR·ij=|det A|R_u<2hR`. Positivity of hR implies ij<2.

Positive integers i,j therefore both equal one. Apply relative-index-one and index-one to obtain completeness, and substitute back for the numerical equalities.

[A rigorous determinant enclosure from entrywise errors](#layer-5-topic-9) supplies ε when Rhat is an absolute determinant of a rigorous weighted log table. The bound involving η is a separate hypothesis.

**Checks.**

- An index-two relation lattice or an index-two unit family makes the left product at least 2hR and cannot pass.
- Equality at the threshold two is rejected; rounding below two without a rigorous ε is rejected.
- Rank zero uses the empty determinant one and the torsion subgroup as the full unit group; N=0 is allowed only when φ is surjective onto the trivial class group.

### 5.23 Negative Pell and the narrow principal square-root class

Under the quadratic presentation hypotheses, x²-dy²=-1 has an integral solution iff mkPrincipal(θ)=1 in Cl⁺(K). Here θ is read as a unit of the field K, not as an integral unit; θ≠0 by the pinned `coe_gen_ne_zero`. The current Tau Ceti library, identifies the narrow class of any element of negative norm with that of `(θ) (NumberField.mkPrincipal_eq_mkPrincipal_gen_of_norm_neg)`; the target is the criterion for this class to be trivial.

d>1 is a squarefree integer; K is a number field with θ in `O_K`. `minpoly_Z(θ)=X²-d` and Q[θ]=K; these hypotheses specify the quadratic presentation.

(Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano, [On Stevenhagen’s conjecture](#reference-koymans-pagano-2022-v1), Introduction, p. 4, running text after the reflection principle (1.3).) Koymans and Pagano state, without proof, that negative Pell solubility is equivalent to the ideal (√d) being trivial in the narrow class group, which is why they must compute the Artin pairing with d. The target proves it from the pinned positivity lemmas and the all-radicand comparison.

To prove this, (⇐) The all-radicand comparison turns an integral solution into a unit u of `O_K` with N(u) = −1. Since θ ≠ 0, the pinned `exists_unit_isTotallyPositive_smul_of_norm_eq_neg_one` gives a unit v with v·θ totally positive, and the pinned `mkPrincipal_eq_one_iff` makes the narrow class of (θ) trivial.

`(⇒) mkPrincipal_eq_one_iff` turns triviality into a unit w with w·θ totally positive. As d > 0, the pinned `norm_eq_neg_one_of_isTotallyPositive_smul_gen` gives N(w) = −1: the two real embeddings send θ to the two roots ±√d, so w has opposite signs there, and a unit norm is ±1. The all-radicand comparison returns an integral solution.

Replacing θ by −θ changes neither the principal ideal nor its narrow class, so the statement does not depend on the chosen square root.

Under the quadratic presentation hypotheses, x²-dy²=-1 has an integral solution iff the natural map q:Cl⁺(K)→Cl(K) restricts bijectively from Cl⁺(K)[2∞] to Cl(K)[2∞]. ### 5.25 The Galois action on the full quadratic unit group

Under the quadratic presentation hypotheses, there exist s in Z/2 and an additive equivalence F:`Additive(O_Kˣ)→Z×Z/2` with F(-1)=(0,1), `F(σu)=τ_s(F(u))` for every unit u, and s=1 iff negative Pell is integrally soluble. Here σ is the pinned ring-of-integers quadratic conjugation. Consequently the soluble case has the Galois module `τ_1` described by Koymans and Pagano (Introduction, p. 3), while the insoluble case has `τ_0`. Equivalently, negative Pell is soluble iff an additive equivalence carrying -1 to (0,1) intertwines conjugation with `τ_1`.

d>1 is a squarefree integer; K is a number field with θ in `O_K`. `minpoly_Z(θ)=X²-d` and Q[θ]=K; these hypotheses specify the quadratic presentation.

(Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano, [On Stevenhagen’s conjecture](#reference-koymans-pagano-2022-v1), Introduction, p. 3, second paragraph (the remark after Theorem 1.1 on the unit Galois module).) Koymans and Pagano remark that the Galois module structure of the unit group of a real quadratic field is determined by the solubility of the negative Pell equation, and name the soluble case: ℤ ⊕ ℤ/2ℤ with (1,0) sent to (−1,1) and (0,1) fixed. The insoluble alternative `τ_0` and the coordinate statement are derived here from the Dirichlet decomposition and the norm identity; the paper gives no proof.

To prove this, the real quadratic presentation gives two real places, no complex places, and unit rank one. Evaluate a torsion unit at a real embedding: a real root of unity is ±1, and the embedding is injective; hence the torsion is exactly {±1}.

Apply the pinned Dirichlet product equivalence, reindex its single free coordinate and identify the torsion coordinate with Z/2. This gives a generator ε and unique expressions `ε^a(-1)^b`.

The pinned identity `εσ(ε)=±1 (mul_ringOfIntegersQuadraticConj_unit_eq_one_or_neg_one)`, read as the field norm through `norm_eq_intCast_iff_mul_ringOfIntegersQuadraticConj_eq_intCast`, gives `εσε=N(ε)=(-1)^s` for exactly one s. Thus `σε=ε^(-1)(-1)^s`, while σ(-1)=-1; multiplying these formulas gives `τ_s` on all coordinates.

Since N(-1)=1 in degree two, a norm-minus-one unit exists exactly when s=1. Use the all-radicand negative Pell comparison.

For the converse characterization by `τ_1`, take the inverse image of (1,0). Its sum with its conjugate is the inverse image of (0,1), namely -1. The conjugation norm formula then gives a unit of norm -1, and the order bridge gives negative Pell. Thus an abstract action comparison is not inferred merely from one choice of normal form.

Changing ε to its inverse or to -ε leaves its norm sign unchanged; the coordinate equivalence is existential and requires no canonical choice.

- For d=3, ε=2+θ has norm +1 and the parameter is zero.
- For d=5 use ε=(1+θ)/2 in the full ring; choosing only the Pell order generator would miss this full-unit coordinate.
- The torsion coordinate is fixed for every d.

## Layer 6: special algebraic numbers and Mahler measure

Build the conjugate geometry of Pisot and Salem numbers and the analytic inputs for the Smyth, Dobrowolski and Dimitrov bounds. The potential-theory objects have explicit compactness, normalisation and continuation hypotheses.

Polynomial Mahler measure uses Mathlib's `Polynomial.mahlerMeasure` and `Polynomial.logMahlerMeasure`. For a nonzero p ∈ ℂ[X], write its roots as a multiset, with each root repeated according to its algebraic multiplicity. Then `M(p) = ‖lc(p)‖ · ∏_{z ∈ p.roots} max(1, ‖z‖)`, and `log M(p) = log ‖lc(p)‖ + ∑_{z ∈ p.roots} log(max(1, ‖z‖))`; both operations retain multiplicities. For integer polynomials apply these same definitions after mapping coefficients to ℂ. At the zero polynomial Mathlib sets M(0) = 0 and logMahlerMeasure(0) = 0; the identity M(p) = exp(logMahlerMeasure(p)) requires p ≠ 0. The algebraic-number measure remains that of the primitive minimal polynomial supplied by DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), §1, formulas (1)–(2), printed p. 322.) The degree-indexed factorization counts roots with multiplicity. Mathlib's `Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_eq_leadingCoeff_mul_prod_roots` and `Polynomial.logMahlerMeasure_eq_log_leadingCoeff_add_sum_log_roots` express the product and sum using `Multiset.map`.

**Checks.**

- p = (X − 2)² has root multiset {2, 2}, M(p) = 4 and logMahlerMeasure(p) = 2 log 2.
- M(pq) = M(p)M(q) for all complex polynomials p, q (`Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_mul`), including p = q = X − 2. For pq ≠ 0 the logarithmic measures add; the nonzero hypothesis is necessary when one factor is zero and the other has nonzero logarithmic measure.
- The zero polynomial has both measures zero, whereas the constant polynomial 1 has multiplicative measure 1 and logarithmic measure 0. Thus exponentiating the zero polynomial's logarithmic measure does not give its multiplicative measure.

### 6.1 Pisot numbers

A Pisot number is a real number θ that is an algebraic integer (integral over ℤ), satisfies θ > 1, and all of whose other complex conjugates lie in the open unit disc: every complex root z ≠ θ of the minimal polynomial minpoly ℤ θ has |z| < 1. The conjugates are the complex roots of minpoly ℤ θ (Mathlib's aroots of the minimal polynomial over ℤ, which for an algebraic integer is the monic minimal polynomial over ℚ by Gauss's lemma). Convention (pinned): degree one is allowed, so the Pisot numbers of degree one are exactly the integers n ≥ 2; the inequality θ > 1 is strict, so 1 is not a Pisot number.

θ real; the definition is a predicate on ℝ, not on an abstract number field. Strict inequalities: θ > 1 and |z| < 1 for every other conjugate z. A conjugate on the unit circle makes θ a Salem number ([Salem numbers](#layer-6-topic-2)) or neither, never a Pisot number. Integrality is part of the definition: 3/2 has no other conjugate but is not a Pisot number.

The supporting API comprises:

- `IsPisot`: IsPisot θ :⟺ θ integral over ℤ, 1 < θ, and |z| < 1 for every complex root z ≠ θ of minpoly ℤ θ.
- `IsPisot.isIntegral`: IsPisot θ → θ is an algebraic integer.
- `IsPisot.one_lt`: IsPisot θ → 1 < θ.
- `IsPisot.norm_lt_one`: IsPisot θ, z a complex root of minpoly ℤ θ, z ≠ θ → |z| < 1.
- `IsPisot.eq_of_one_le_norm`: IsPisot θ, z a complex root of minpoly ℤ θ with |z| ≥ 1 → z = θ: θ is the only conjugate outside the open unit disc.
- `isPisot_iff_minpoly_rat`: IsPisot θ ⟺ θ integral over ℤ, 1 < θ and every complex root z ≠ θ of minpoly ℚ θ has |z| < 1 (the definition read with Mathlib's minimal polynomial over ℚ).
- `isPisot_natCast_iff`: For n ∈ ℕ: IsPisot n ⟺ n ≥ 2.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 1, p. 5 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the definition; the source's condition that the number exceed 1 presupposes a real number.

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 1, Definition 3 and the Example, p. 1.) Same definition; the Example (the golden ratio) is the first Check below.

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 2, Proposition 5, p. 1.) The pinned degree-one convention (`isPisot_natCast_iff`).

To prove this, define IsPisot θ as the conjunction of IsIntegral ℤ θ, 1 < θ and the modulus condition on the roots of minpoly ℤ θ in ℂ other than θ.

Projections isIntegral, `one_lt`, `norm_lt_one` are the three conjuncts.

`eq_of_one_le_norm`: a root z with |z| ≥ 1 cannot be ≠ θ by the modulus condition.

`isPisot_iff_minpoly_rat`: for θ integral over ℤ, minpoly ℤ θ maps to `minpoly ℚ θ (minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions')`, so the two root multisets in ℂ agree.

`isPisot_natCast_iff`: minpoly ℤ n = X − n has the single root n, so the modulus condition is vacuous and IsPisot n ⟺ n > 1 ⟺ n ≥ 2.

**Checks.**

- IsPisot φ for the golden ratio φ = Real.goldenRatio.
- IsPisot 2: a degree-one Pisot number.
- ¬ IsPisot 1: a definition with 1 ≤ θ would accept it.
- ¬ IsPisot (3/2): a definition without integrality would accept it (it has no other conjugate).
- ¬ IsPisot √2: its conjugate −√2 has modulus > 1; a definition asking only for θ > 1 and integrality would accept it.
- Mathlib's Mahler measure of minpoly ℤ φ = X² − X − 1 mapped to ℂ[X] equals φ.
- The golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 is a Pisot number (its conjugate −1/φ has modulus 0.618…).
- 2 is a Pisot number; 1, 3/2 and √2 are not.
- M(φ) = φ, agreeing with Mathlib's Polynomial.mahlerMeasure of X² − X − 1.

*Needs:* Mathlib `IsIntegral`; Mathlib `minpoly.monic`; Mathlib `Polynomial.aroots`; Mathlib `Polynomial.mem_aroots`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions'`.

### 6.2 Salem numbers

A Salem number is a real number τ that is an algebraic integer, satisfies τ > 1, all of whose other complex conjugates lie in the closed unit disc (every complex root z ≠ τ of minpoly ℤ τ has |z| ≤ 1), and at least one of whose conjugates lies on the unit circle (some complex root z of minpoly ℤ τ has |z| = 1). This is Salem's form of the definition; by Salem's lemma ([Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24)) it is equivalent to the form 'degree at least 4, conjugate to τ⁻¹, all conjugates other than `τ^{±1}` of modulus 1'. Convention (pinned): the reciprocal quadratic units (3 + √5)/2, … (sometimes called quadratic Salem numbers) are not Salem numbers.

τ real, τ > 1 strictly. The existence of a conjugate on the circle is what excludes Pisot numbers; without it the definition would contain every Pisot number. No degree bound is imposed: degree ≥ 4 is a consequence ([Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24)).

The supporting API comprises:

- `IsSalem`: IsSalem τ :⟺ τ integral over ℤ, 1 < τ, |z| ≤ 1 for every complex root z ≠ τ of minpoly ℤ τ, and some complex root has |z| = 1.
- `IsSalem.isIntegral`: IsSalem τ → τ is an algebraic integer.
- `IsSalem.one_lt`: IsSalem τ → 1 < τ.
- `IsSalem.norm_le_one`: IsSalem τ, z a complex root of minpoly ℤ τ, z ≠ τ → |z| ≤ 1.
- `IsSalem.exists_norm_eq_one`: IsSalem τ → some complex root of minpoly ℤ τ has modulus 1.
- `IsSalem.not_isPisot`: IsSalem τ → ¬ IsPisot τ: the two classes are disjoint.
- `IsSalem.isConjRoot_inv`: IsSalem τ → τ and τ⁻¹ are conjugate over ℚ (IsConjRoot ℚ τ τ⁻¹).
- `IsSalem.four_le_natDegree`: IsSalem τ → deg τ ≥ 4.
- `IsSalem.even_natDegree`: IsSalem τ → deg τ is even.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Lemma 1, p. 2 (arXiv v3).) The hypotheses of Lemma 1 are taken as the definition (the source calls it the usual definition); the source's own definition becomes [Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 1, p. 1.) The equivalent form, `IsSalem.isConjRoot_inv` and `IsSalem.four_le_natDegree`.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 8.1, printed p. 335.) Third equivalent description used for the Mahler measure computation M(τ) = τ.

To prove this, define IsSalem τ as the conjunction of IsIntegral ℤ τ, 1 < τ, |z| ≤ 1 for every complex root z ≠ τ of minpoly ℤ τ, and the existence of a complex root z with |z| = 1.

Projections are the four conjuncts.

`not_isPisot`: a root z with |z| = 1 is ≠ τ (as τ > 1), so the Pisot condition |z| < 1 fails for it.

`isConjRoot_inv`, `four_le_natDegree`, `even_natDegree`: read off from [Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24) (τ⁻¹ is a conjugate; the conjugates other than `τ^{±1}` lie on the circle, are non-real and come in complex-conjugate pairs, so the degree is 2 + an even number ≥ 2).

**Checks.**

- The largest real root 2.1537… of X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1 is a Salem number.
- ¬ IsSalem 2: a degree-one algebraic integer has no conjugate on the circle.
- ¬ IsSalem ((3 + √5)/2): a 'reciprocal of degree ≥ 2' definition would accept this quadratic unit.
- ¬ IsSalem φ: φ is a Pisot number, with no conjugate on the circle.
- Mathlib's Mahler measure of X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1 mapped to ℂ[X] equals its largest real root.
- The largest real root 2.1537… of X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1 is a Salem number (Smyth's example).
- Lehmer's number τ₁₀ = 1.17628… is a Salem number ([Lehmer's number is a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-59)).
- 2, φ and (3 + √5)/2 are not Salem numbers.

### 6.3 Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials

Let α ≠ 0 be an algebraic integer in a field of characteristic 0, with minimal polynomial P = minpoly ℤ α of degree d, and let `P* = X^d P(1/X)` (Mathlib's Polynomial.reverse). Then α is conjugate to α⁻¹ over ℚ (IsConjRoot ℚ α α⁻¹) iff P* = P or P* = −P. In that case P(0) = ±1, so α is a unit.

α ≠ 0, so P(0) ≠ 0 and deg P* = deg P. Sign convention: P* = −P occurs exactly for P = X − 1 (a reciprocal polynomial with the minus sign is divisible by X − 1, and P is irreducible).

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, printed p. 327.) The polynomial side, with both signs.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, printed p. 327.) The implication (⇒); the result adds the converse and the sign analysis.

To prove this, (⇒) If α⁻¹ is a root of P then α is a root of `P* (Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_mul_pow)`; P is irreducible, so P ∣ P* in ℚ[X]; both have degree d, so P* = c P with c = leading coefficient of `P* = P(0) (Polynomial.coeff_zero_reverse, reverse_leadingCoeff)`.

Comparing constant terms: the constant term of P* is the leading coefficient 1 of P, so 1 = c·P(0) = P(0)²; hence P(0) = ±1 and P* = ±P.

(⇐) If P* = ±P then P*(α) = 0 gives `P(α⁻¹) = 0 (Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_eq_zero_iff)`; P is irreducible and monic, so P = minpoly ℤ α⁻¹ and minpoly ℚ α = minpoly ℚ α⁻¹ (Gauss's lemma, `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions'`).

**Checks.**

- α = 1: P = X − 1, P* = −P, and 1 is conjugate to 1⁻¹.
- α = 2: P = X − 2, P* = 1 − 2X ≠ ±P, and 2 is not conjugate to 1/2.
- Lehmer's polynomial L satisfies L* = L; X³ − X − 1 has reverse −X³ − X² + 1 ≠ ±(X³ − X − 1).

*Needs:* Mathlib `IsConjRoot`; Mathlib `Polynomial.reverse`; Mathlib `Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_mul_pow`; Mathlib `Polynomial.eval₂_reverse_eq_zero_iff`; Mathlib `Polynomial.coeff_zero_reverse`; Mathlib `Polynomial.reverse_leadingCoeff`; Mathlib `minpoly.irreducible`; Mathlib `minpoly.dvd`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions'`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_dvd`.

τ algebraic integer, so M(τ) is the Mahler measure of the monic minpoly ℤ τ.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 8.1, printed p. 335.) M(τ) = τ read off from formula (2).

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, printed p. 328.) The Pisot case M(θ) = θ.

### 6.5 Lehmer's number τ₁₀

Lehmer's number τ₁₀ = 1.1762808182… is the largest real root of Lehmer's polynomial L = X¹⁰ + X⁹ − X⁷ − X⁶ − X⁵ − X⁴ − X³ + X + 1. As a declaration: the supremum of the set of real roots of L (which is {τ₁₀⁻¹, τ₁₀}).

L has exactly two real roots, τ₁₀ ∈ (1.17628, 1.17629) and τ₁₀⁻¹ = 0.85013…, and eight roots on the unit circle.

The supporting API comprises:

- `lehmerNumber`: τ₁₀ := the supremum of the real roots of L.
- `lehmerNumber_isRoot`: L(τ₁₀) = 0.
- `one_lt_lehmerNumber`: 1 < τ₁₀.
- `lehmerNumber_mem_Ioo`: 1.17628 < τ₁₀ < 1.17629.
- `eq_lehmerNumber_of_isRoot`: x ∈ ℝ, x > 1, L(x) = 0 → x = τ₁₀.
- `inv_lehmerNumber_isRoot`: L(τ₁₀⁻¹) = 0 (L is reciprocal).
- `lehmerNumber_add_inv_isRoot`: τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ is a root of y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3.
- `mahlerMeasure_lehmerPolynomial`: Mathlib's Mahler measure of L mapped to ℂ[X] equals τ₁₀.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 2, printed pp. 323-324.) The polynomial and the numerical value M(L) = τ₁₀.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 2, p. 5 (arXiv v3).) The name τ₁₀.

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Example 2.16, printed p. 7.) The root configuration; the result proves it by the sign changes of Q.

To prove this, define τ₁₀ := sup {x ∈ ℝ : L(x) = 0}.

L is reciprocal (reverse L = L), so L(x) = x⁵ Q(x + 1/x) with Q(y) = y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3.

Q takes the values −8389/100000, 3/32, −1, 13/32, 103/32, −1, −1, 333411/100000 at −19/10, −3/2, −1, −1/2, 1/2, 1, 2, 21/10, so it changes sign in each of (−19/10, −3/2), (−3/2, −1), (−1, −1/2), (1/2, 1) and (2, 21/10) (no change on (−1/2, 1/2) or (1, 2)); hence its five roots are real: four in (−2, 2) and one, α₁₀ = 2.0264…, in (2, 21/10).

A root y ∈ (−2, 2) of Q gives two roots of L on the unit circle; α₁₀ gives the two real roots `τ₁₀^{±1}` (solutions of x² − α₁₀x + 1 = 0); these are the ten roots of L.

The real roots of L are therefore τ₁₀ > 1 and τ₁₀⁻¹ < 1, so the supremum is τ₁₀; its enclosure follows from sign evaluations of L at 1.17628 and 1.17629.

**Checks.**

- τ₁₀ < θ₀: a Salem number below the smallest Pisot number.
- 2 < τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ < 2.03.
- τ₁₀ is not a Pisot number (a definition as the root of maximal modulus would not distinguish).
- The other real root τ₁₀⁻¹ of L lies in (0, 1).
- τ₁₀ ∈ (1.17628, 1.17629); τ₁₀ < θ₀; M(L) = τ₁₀.

### 6.6 Mahler measure versus house

Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d with r > 0 conjugates of modulus > 1. Then `M(α)^{1/d} ≤ M(α)^{1/r} ≤ ⌈α⌉ ≤ M(α)`.

α integral over ℤ, so M(α) = ∏ max(1, |αᵢ|) over its conjugates. r > 0 (if r = 0 then M(α) = 1 and the middle term is undefined).

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 3, (6), printed p. 324.) Exactly the statement (for algebraic integers, the survey's standing context in Section 3).

Each of the r factors is ≤ ⌈α⌉, so `M(α) ≤ ⌈α⌉^r`.

⌈α⌉ > 1 is one of the factors and the others are ≥ 1, so ⌈α⌉ ≤ M(α).

M(α) ≥ 1 and r ≤ d give `M(α)^{1/d} ≤ M(α)^{1/r}`.

For α in a number field K, ⌈α⌉ = NumberField.house α (TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2).

### 6.7 Algebraic numbers with M(α) < 2 are units

If α is a nonzero algebraic number with M(α) < 2, then α and α⁻¹ are algebraic integers.

M(α) is the Mahler measure of the primitive minimal polynomial (TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §§0.1–0.2), equal to `absMulHeight₁(α)^{deg α}`.

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Lemma 2.9, printed p. 6.) Exactly the statement; the proof uses Lemma 2.8 and Corollary 2.6.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 3, printed p. 324.) Same statement in passing.

To prove this, the leading coefficient a₀ of the primitive minimal polynomial `F_α` satisfies a₀ ≤ M(α) < 2 (`leadingCoeff_le_mahlerMeasure` of TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2), so a₀ = 1: `F_α ∈ ℤ[X]` is monic and vanishes at α (`aeval_primitiveMinpoly` of TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.1), hence α is an algebraic integer (equivalently `isIntegral_leadingCoeff_primitiveMinpoly_smul` with a₀ = 1).

N(α) = ± the product of the conjugates is a nonzero rational integer with |N(α)| ≤ M(α) < 2, so N(α) = ±1.

`α⁻¹ = ±∏_{i ≥ 2} αᵢ` is a product of algebraic integers (Berrevoets Lemma 2.8).

### 6.10 If `α^k` and `α^l` are conjugate (k ≠ l) then α is 0 or a root of unity

k, l ≥ 1 distinct.

With N the order of σ: `α^{k^N} = α^{l^N}`, `k^N ≠ l^N`, so α = 0 or `α^{|k^N − l^N|} = 1`.

(Alternative: `h(α^k) = k h(α)` and conjugates have equal height, so (k − l)h(α) = 0 and Kronecker applies.)

### 6.11 Reduction when a power of α has smaller degree

Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d with M(α) > 1, and suppose deg(αⁿ) < d for some n ≥ 1. Then there is an algebraic integer β with deg β < d and 1 < M(β) ≤ M(α).

α algebraic integer (the source states the lemma for algebraic numbers, but its computation of M(β) is valid for algebraic integers only).

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Lemma 4.7 and its proof, printed pp. 16-17.) Corrected statement for the integral application with the essential M(α)>1 hypothesis; the source omits that hypothesis.

To prove this, let f be the monic minimal polynomial of α over ℚ(αⁿ), of degree r = [ℚ(α) : ℚ(αⁿ)] ≥ 2, and β = f(0) ∈ ℚ(αⁿ), an algebraic integer with deg β ≤ deg αⁿ < d.

f divides Xⁿ − αⁿ = ∏(X − ζᵏα), so `β = ±ζᵐ α^r` for an n-th root of unity ζ; hence `|σ(β)| = |σ(α)|^r` for every embedding σ of ℚ(α).

Each conjugate of β occurs [ℚ(α) : ℚ(β)] ≥ r times among the σ(β), so `M(β) = (∏_σ max(1, |σ(α)|))^{r/[ℚ(α):ℚ(β)]} ≤ M(α)`.

M(α) > 1 gives some |σ(α)| > 1, so |σ(β)| > 1 and M(β) > 1.

### 6.12 Dobrowolski's auxiliary polynomial

Let α be an algebraic integer of degree d, and N, M positive integers with M ≥ 3, N ≥ 10 and dM < N/2. Then there is a nonzero F ∈ ℤ[X] of degree ≤ N with `f_α^M ∣ F` (α is a zero of multiplicity ≥ M) and `max_i |F_i| ≤ N^{2dM²/N} M(α)^{2M}`.

α algebraic integer; `M(α) = ∏ max(1, |σ_k(α)|)`.

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Lemma 4.8, printed p. 17.) Exactly the statement, with the bound `max |Fi| ≤ N^{2dM²/N}M(α)^{2M} (16)`; the displayed system (17) has the misprint `F_k` for `F_j` .

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Lemma 3.2, printed p. 11.) The product-form Siegel lemma used in the proof below.

To prove this, the conditions `F^{(i)}(α)/i! = Σ_j C(j, i) F_j α^{j−i} = 0` for 0 ≤ i ≤ M − 1 are M linear equations over ℚ(α) in the N + 1 integer unknowns `F_0`, …, `F_N`, with algebraic-integer coefficients `a_ij = C(j, i)α^{j−i}` (the row i has the entry `a_ii = 1 ≠ 0`).

Siegel's lemma over ℚ(α) in product form (Berrevoets, Lemma 3.2) gives a nonzero integer solution with `max |F_j| ≤ ((2√2(N+1))^{dM} ∏_k ∏_i max_j |σ_k(a_ij)|)^{1/(N+1−dM)}`. The supplier is TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §2.8, `siegelRelativeKernelBasis`, applied with F = ℚ(α) over K = ℚ: an algebraic-integer row `a_i` has H₂,`proj(a_i)^d ≤ ∏_k √(N+1)·max_j |σ_k(a_ij)|`, and a primitive integer vector has absolute height equal to its sup norm, so the same bound holds with the smaller constant √(N+1) in place of 2√2(N+1). The house-form integer Siegel estimate of that roadmap's §0.3 does not suffice: it would give `house(α)^{2dM}` in place of `M(α)^{2M}`.

`max_j |C(j,i) σ_k(α)^{j−i}| ≤ N^i max(1, |σ_k α|)^N`, and `∏_k ∏_{i<M}` gives `N^{dM²/2} M(α)^{MN}`.

`2√2(N + 1) ≤ N^{M/2} (N ≥ 10, M ≥ 3)` and N − dM ≥ N/2 give the bound `N^{2dM²/N} M(α)^{2M}`.

The vanishing of F, F′, …, `F^{(M−1)}` at α gives `f_α^M ∣ F` in ℚ[X], hence in ℤ[X] as `f_α` is monic.

**Checks.**

- α = φ (d = 2, M(φ) = φ), M = 3, N = 13 (dM = 6 < 13/2): F = (X² − X − 1)³ = X⁶ − 3X⁵ + 5X³ − 3X − 1 is divisible by `f_φ³`, has degree 6 ≤ 13 and largest coefficient `5 ≤ 13^{36/13}·φ⁶ ≈ 2.18·10⁴`.
- The bound is not automatic for obvious multiples: for α = τ₁₀, M = 20, N = 4000 it is `4000²·M(τ₁₀)^{40} ≈ 1.058·10¹⁰`, but `(Φ₆L)^{20}` has largest coefficient ≈ 1.47·10¹² ; the lemma's F comes from Siegel's lemma, not from a product of the minimal polynomial with small factors.

### 6.13 The polynomial `P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m)`

For a commutative ring R, a monic P ∈ R[X] of degree n and m ∈ ℕ, `P_m` is the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by `x^m` on the free R-module R[x]/(P) of rank n (basis 1, x, …, `x^{n−1}`, AdjoinRoot.powerBasis'). If P = ∏(X − αᵢ) over a field containing the roots, then `P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m)`; in particular `P_m ∈ ℤ[X]` for P ∈ ℤ[X] monic.

P monic (so R[x]/(P) is free of rank deg P); m ≥ 0 arbitrary.

The supporting API comprises:

- `rootPowPoly`: `P_m :=` charpoly of multiplication by `x^m` on R[x]/(P), for P monic.
- `rootPowPoly_monic`: `P_m` is monic (R nontrivial).
- `natDegree_rootPowPoly`: `deg P_m = deg P`.
- `rootPowPoly_one`: `P_1 = P`.
- `rootPowPoly_zero`: `P_0 = (X − 1)^{deg P}`.
- `map_rootPowPoly`: For f : R →+* S: `(P.map f)_m = (P_m)`.map f.
- `rootPowPoly_eq_prod_roots`: Over a field in which P splits: `P_m = ∏` over the roots a of P (with multiplicity) of `(X − a^m)`.
- `rootPowPoly_rootPowPoly`: `(P_m)_k = P_{mk}`.
- `rootPowPoly_eq_minpoly_pow`: For L/K finite and α ∈ L: `(minpoly K α)_m = (minpoly K α^m)^{[K(α):K(α^m)]}`.
- `rootPowPoly_two_comp_X_sq`: `P_2(X²) = (−1)^{deg P} P(X) P(−X)` (Graeffe's root squaring).
- `rootPowPoly_two_cyclotomic`: For every N: `(Φ_N)_2 = Φ_N` when N is odd, `Φ_{N/2}` when N ≡ 2 (mod 4), and `Φ_{N/2}²` when 4 ∣ N (both sides are 1 at N = 0). Over ℂ, squaring maps the primitive N-th roots of unity bijectively onto the primitive N-th (N odd) or N/2-th (N ≡ 2 mod 4) roots, and two-to-one onto the primitive N/2-th roots when 4 ∣ N; apply `rootPowPoly_eq_prod_roots`.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Lemma 2.1, pp. 3-4 (arXiv v1).) Exactly the object; the characteristic-polynomial construction is the intrinsic form that makes `P_m ∈ ℤ[X]` a definition rather than a claim.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Proof of Theorem 1, p. 16 (arXiv v1).) Source for `rootPowPoly_eq_minpoly_pow` at m = 2.

To prove this, define `P_m :=` charpoly of Algebra.leftMulMatrix of `x^m` in the power basis of AdjoinRoot P.

The power-basis matrix of the quotient generator is the companion matrix of P (with the chosen row/column convention). Apply [The companion matrix of a polynomial](#layer-2-topic-46) for its characteristic polynomial. `Matrix.charpoly_monic` gives monicity and degree n, including n=0; hence `P_1=P` and `P_0=(X-1)^n`.

Base change: the power basis and the matrix commute with ring homomorphisms, so `(P.map f)_m = (P_m)`.map f.

Over a field where P splits, the matrix of x is triangularisable with diagonal αᵢ, so that of `x^m` has diagonal `αᵢ^m`: `P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m)` (equivalently, the eigenvalues of a power are the powers of the eigenvalues).

For arbitrary commutative coefficient rings, first prove the iteration identity for the universal monic degree-n polynomial over `Z[c_0...,c_(n-1)]`. Embed this domain in the splitting field of its fraction field and use the root product formula there. Injectivity brings the identity back to the universal coefficient ring. Characteristic polynomial coefficients are polynomial expressions in the matrix entries, so base change along `c_i -> P.coeff i` specializes the identity to R, including rings with zero divisors and repeated roots. The embedding Z -> C alone would establish only integer-coefficient instances.

For P = minpoly K α (L/K finite): K[x]/(P) ≅ K(α) with x ↦ α (IntermediateField.adjoinRootEquivAdjoin), so `P_m` is the characteristic polynomial of multiplication by `α^m` on K(α). In the product of a `K(α^m)`-basis of K(α) with the power basis of `K(α^m)` over K this matrix is block diagonal with `[K(α):K(α^m)]` copies of the matrix of `α^m` on `K(α^m)`, whose characteristic polynomial is `minpoly K α^m (charpoly_leftMulMatrix, Matrix.BlockTriangular.charpoly)`. Hence `P_m = (minpoly K α^m)^{[K(α):K(α^m)]}` in every characteristic; counting distinct conjugates would need K(α)/K separable.

Graeffe relation: `P_2(X²) = (−1)^n P(X)P(−X)`.

**Checks.**

- `(X − a)_m = X − a^m` in ℤ[X].
- `(X² − 2)_2 = (X − 2)²`.
- `(Φ₃)_2 = Φ₃` (an odd-level cyclotomic polynomial is fixed by squaring its roots).
- `1_m = 1` (degree 0).
- For P = X² + 1: `P_2 = (X + 1)²`, which differs from P(X²) = X⁴ + 1 (the tempting definition by substitution).
- Over ZMod 4, `(X^2-2)_2 = X^2`; the root-power construction applies over a nonreduced ring as well as over fields.
- `(X − a)_m = X − a^m`; `(X² − 2)_2 = (X − 2)²`; `(Φ₃)_2 = Φ₃`.

*Needs:* Mathlib `AdjoinRoot.powerBasis'`; Mathlib `Algebra.leftMulMatrix`; Mathlib `Matrix.charpoly`; Mathlib `Matrix.charpoly_monic`; Mathlib `charpoly_leftMulMatrix`; Mathlib `Polynomial.Splits.eq_prod_roots_of_monic`; Mathlib `IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank`; [The companion matrix of a polynomial](#layer-2-topic-46); Mathlib `IntermediateField.adjoinRootEquivAdjoin`; Mathlib `Matrix.BlockTriangular.charpoly`.

### 6.14 √(1 + 4Y) has integer coefficients

There is T ∈ ℤ⟦Y⟧ with constant term 1 and T² = 1 + 4Y; explicitly `T = 1 + 2Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k C_k Y^{k+1}` with `C_k` the Catalan numbers, equivalently `T = Σ_k C(1/2, k) 4^k Y^k`.

Power series over ℤ.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Section 2, (3), p. 4 (arXiv v1).) Exactly the statement; the Catalan form is the proof of integrality.

To prove this, with `c(x) = Σ C_k x^k`, the Catalan recurrence `(catalan_succ)` is c = 1 + x c² in ℤ⟦x⟧.

T = 1 − 2x c(x) at x = −Y; T² = 1 − 4x c + 4x²c² = 1 − 4x(c − x c²) = 1 − 4x = 1 + 4Y.

**Checks.**

- T = 1 + 2Y − 2Y² + 4Y³ − 10Y⁴ + …

*Needs:* Mathlib `catalan`; Mathlib `catalan_succ`; Mathlib `PowerSeries.constantCoeff`; Mathlib `PowerSeries.X`.

### 6.15 h(αⁿ) = n·h(α) for the absolute Weil height

Consume HeightsAndUnits §1.3's scalar power law, with DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2's field comparison: for every α in a characteristic-zero field and n∈N, Habs(αⁿ)=Habs(α)ⁿ and h(αⁿ)=n h(α). Both laws use Mathlib's absolute scalar heights; this section has no separate homogeneity declaration.

No algebraicity hypothesis is needed for these laws. For transcendental α and n≥1, αⁿ is transcendental, so the multiplicative values are 1 and the logarithmic values are 0. At n=0 the identities include α=0 and 0⁰=1. The algebraic case is the supplier's field-independent transport of `Height.mulHeight₁_pow`, followed by logarithms.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 12, printed pp.338–339; Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), proof of Lemma2.3, p.5, arXiv v1.) The scalar law supplies the canonical-height comparison for the power map.

- h(φ⁵)=5 h(φ)=(5/2)log φ.
- n=0, including α=0: Habs(α⁰)=1 and h(α⁰)=0.
- A transcendental α and positive n have h(αⁿ)=h(α)=0.

Consume HeightsAndUnits §1.3's `absMulHeight₁_eq_one_iff` and its logarithmic corollary: for α algebraic over Q in a characteristic-zero field, h(α)=0 iff α=0 or α is a root of unity. ### 6.17 Real coefficient Schur series

A real coefficient sequence e : ℕ → ℝ is a real Schur series when there exists f : ℂ → ℂ holomorphic on |z|<1 such that `Σ e_j z^j` converges to f(z) at every point of that disc and |f(z)|≤1 there. The function is uniquely determined on the disc; no boundary extension is required. The formal series is PowerSeries.mk e.

The disc is open. Real coefficients are part of the object, rather than a reality assumption on f at every complex point.

The supporting API comprises:

- `RealSchurSeries.function_unique`: Two holomorphic witnesses with the specified HasSum expansion agree throughout the open unit disc.
- `RealSchurSeries.conj`: For a witness f, f(conj z)=conj(f(z)) on the disc.
- `RealSchurSeries.constant`: The constant sequence `e_0=c`, `e_j=0` for j>0 is Schur exactly when |c|≤1.
- `RealSchurSeries.mul`: The coefficient convolution of two real Schur series is a real Schur series.
- `RealSchurSeries.coeff_zero_eq`: Its constant coefficient is f(0), and its formal coefficients are exactly PowerSeries.coeff j (PowerSeries.mk e).

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §2 lemma, pp. 170–171.) The coefficient estimates apply to real-coefficient bounded holomorphic functions; this definition removes the unnecessary neighbourhood-of-the-closed-disc restriction.

To prove this, use HasSum for the coefficient expansion and DifferentiableOn for holomorphy; uniqueness of sums makes the associated function independent of its witness.

Conjugating the expansion gives f(conj z)=conj(f(z)); a function holomorphic on the open disc is the sum of its Taylor series at every point of the `disc (Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball)`, which gives the coefficient sequence of a witness; polynomial and rational examples also follow from the Cauchy power series on smaller closed discs.

**Checks.**

- Both constant series 1 and −1 are Schur.
- For k≥1, the coefficient sequence of `z^k` is Schur, with `e_0=0` and `e_k=1`.
- The constant series 3/2 is not Schur.
- (1/2+z)/(1+z/2) is Schur and has coefficients `e_0=1/2`, `e_1=3/4`, `e_2=−3/8`.
- The closed bound permits constant functions ±1, while every nonconstant witness maps into the open disc.

*Needs:* Mathlib `PowerSeries.mk`; Mathlib `DifferentiableOn.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall`; Mathlib `Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball`.

### 6.18 Finite Fekete diameters and transfinite diameter

For a compact K⊆ℂ and n≥2, `δ_n(K)=sup_(z∈K^n) (∏_(0≤i<j<n)|z_i−z_j|)^(2/(n(n−1)))`. Set `δ_n(∅)=0`, `δ_0=δ_1=0`. Define `d(K)=inf_(n≥2) δ_n(K)`. This d is the transfinite diameter, with the usual length normalization for logarithmic capacity. Only compact sets receive mathematical assertions.

K compact for the API. The total real-valued formula on other sets has no specified meaning. Repeated tuple entries are permitted; a collision gives product zero. The infimum excludes indices 0 and 1.

The supporting API comprises:

- `feketeDiameter_nonneg`: `δ_n(K)≥0` and d(K)≥0 for compact K.
- `feketeDiameter_attained`: For nonempty compact K and n≥2, a tuple in `K^n` attains `δ_n(K)`.
- `feketeDiameter_mono`: Compact K⊆L implies `δ_n(K)≤δ_n(L)` and d(K)≤d(L).
- `transfiniteDiameter_affine`: d(aK+b)=|a|d(K), including a=0; `δ_n` has the same rule for n≥2.
- `transfiniteDiameter_finite`: A finite set has d=0; `δ_n=0` once n exceeds its cardinality.
- `finiteFeketeDiameter_two`: For nonempty compact K, the two-point Fekete diameter δ₂(K) equals the metric diameter of K; the limiting diameter is identified with the Chebyshev limit by the key theorem below.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), §1.1, p. 1; 1.4.1–1.4.4, p. 2.) The pairwise-distance supremum defines the finite diameter; its limit is monotone under inclusion and scales like length.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), (1.1), p. 167; Lemma 1.1, p. 168; (1.4) and the remarks after it, p. 169; Theorem 1.9, (1.14), p. 172.) `δ_n` is the maximum of the normalized pairwise-distance product; Lemma 1.1 makes it nonincreasing, its limit is the transfinite diameter (monotone under inclusion, scaling like length, zero on finite sets), and Theorem 1.9 identifies that limit with logarithmic capacity.

To prove this, for nonempty K, continuity on compact `K^n` gives a maximizing Fekete tuple and a finite nonnegative supremum. Define the empty-set values explicitly.

Use the nonnegative real power with exponent 2/(n(n−1)). The monotonicity and limit are separate theorem targets, rather than assumptions in the definition.

**Checks.**

- For K={0,2}, `δ_2=2`, `δ_3=0`, and d=0.
- For K={7}, every `δ_n` with n≥2 and d are zero.
- For the closed radius-2 disc, `δ_2=4` and d=2.
- d([−1,1])=1/2 and d([0,1])=1/4, rather than the ordinary segment diameter.
- `δ_2` is the ordinary diameter, while d is typically smaller.

*Needs:* Mathlib `IsCompact.exists_isMaxOn`.

### 6.19 Monic Chebyshev norms on a compact set

For compact K⊆ℂ, let `‖p‖_K=sup_(z∈K)|p(z)|`, with empty-set value 0. For n∈ℕ let `t_n(K)=inf{‖p‖_K : p∈ℂ[X], p monic of degree n}`. For nonempty K, `t_0(K)=1`. For n≥1, set `T_n(K)=t_n(K)^(1/n)`. Minimizers need not be chosen canonically or claimed unique.

K compact; degree means natDegree together with monicity.

The supporting API comprises:

- `compactPolynomialNorm_eval_le`: For z∈K, `|p(z)|≤‖p‖_K`.
- `compactPolynomialNorm_mul_le`: `‖pq‖_K≤‖p‖_K‖q‖_K`.
- `chebyshevNorm_attained`: For compact K and every n, some monic degree-n polynomial attains `t_n(K)`.
- `chebyshevNorm_submultiplicative`: `t_(n+m)(K)≤t_n(K)t_m(K)`.
- `chebyshevNorm_mono`: K⊆L implies `t_n(K)≤t_n(L)`.
- `chebyshevNorm_affine`: For a≠0, `t_n(aK+b)=|a|^n t_n(K)`.
- `compactPolynomialNorm_eq_continuousMap_norm`: For compact K, the evaluation restriction z↦p(z) is a ContinuousMap K ℂ, and `‖p‖_K` equals its existing continuous-map norm, including empty K. No second general function sup norm is specified.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), §1.2–1.3, pp. 1–2.) The monic minimax norm supplies the same limiting constant as the finite-diameter construction.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), polynomial extremal problem, `t_n(E)` and (1.18), p. 175; Theorem 1.18, pp. 176–178.) Monic minimax norms `t_n(E)`, their submultiplicativity and the limit of `t_n^(1/n)` as an infimum; Theorem 1.18 relates them to Fekete points. Saff assumes E infinite for the uniqueness of the minimizer, which this result does not claim.

To prove this, bound the evaluation norm by compactness. The class of monic degree-n polynomials is nonempty, so its nonnegative norm infimum is finite.

For existence of a minimizer, if K has at most n points use its annihilating polynomial with a monic padding factor. Otherwise evaluation at n+1 distinct points bounds the coefficients of a norm-bounded minimizing sequence by Vandermonde inversion; take a convergent subsequence.

**Checks.**

- `t_0({0})=1`, whereas `t_n({0})=0` for every n≥1.
- For a radius-R closed disc with R>0, `t_n=R^n`.
- For [−1,1], `t_1=1` and `t_2=1/2`, attained by X and X²−1/2.
- For nonempty compact K and constant p=c, both `‖p‖_K` and the existing continuous-map norm of its restriction equal |c|; on ∅ both are 0.
- At degree zero the monic polynomial is 1, so its norm on nonempty K is 1 even if K is a singleton.

### 6.20 Conformal radius using the existing normalized map

For a proper simply connected open Ω⊆ℂ and p∈Ω, take any existing TauCeti.IsNormalizedRiemannMapOn φ Ω p and define cr(Ω,p)=1/|φ′(p)|>0. The pinned existence and on-domain uniqueness theorems make this independent of φ. Outside the eligible pointed-domain class use value 0. No second normalized-map predicate or Riemann-map construction is introduced.

Ω is nonempty, open, simply connected and proper; p is a specified point of Ω. Derivative positivity means its imaginary part is zero and its real part is strictly positive.

The supporting API comprises:

- `conformalRadius_pos`: cr(Ω,p)>0 on an eligible pointed domain.
- `conformalRadius_independent`: The reciprocal derivative norm is independent of the existing normalized-map witness, by the pinned IsNormalizedRiemannMapOn.eqOn theorem.
- `conformalRadius_deriv`: cr(Ω,p)=1/|φ′(p)| for any biholomorphism φ with φ(p)=0, even before fixing its phase.
- `conformalRadius_mono`: If Ω⊆Ω′ are eligible domains containing p, cr(Ω,p)≤cr(Ω′,p).
- `conformalRadius_affine`: cr(aΩ+b,ap+b)=|a|cr(Ω,p) for a≠0.
- `conformalRadius_exhaustion`: If `Ω_j` increase to Ω and all are eligible with `p∈Ω_j`, then `cr(Ω_j,p)→cr(Ω,p)`. This follows by placing the inverse image of every closed radius-q disc, q<1, inside one `Ω_j`.

(V. N. Dubinin, [On the change in harmonic measure under symmetrization](#reference-dubinin-1985), §1, corollary and normalized slit maps, pp. 270–271.) The slit-domain comparison is expressed through the derivative of a disc map normalized at zero.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), §3, Theorem 3.5, p. 185.) Exterior logarithmic capacity is determined by the derivative normalization of a conformal map at infinity.

To prove this, use the pinned `exists_isNormalizedRiemannMapOn`; its derivative is a positive real number. On-domain uniqueness from IsNormalizedRiemannMapOn.eqOn implies equality of derivatives at p and hence equality of the reciprocal moduli.

For Ω⊆Ω′ with normalized maps φ on Ω and ψ on Ω′ at p, the composition ψ∘φ⁻¹ is a holomorphic self-map of the unit disc fixing 0; the inverse is holomorphic by DifferentiableOn.invFunOn. Its derivative at 0 is ψ′(p)/φ′(p), so Schwarz’s derivative bound at 0 gives |ψ′(p)|≤|φ′(p)|, that is, cr(Ω,p)≤cr(Ω′,p).

The affine coordinate change z↦az+b gives cr(aΩ+b,ap+b)=|a|cr(Ω,p) for a≠0. For an increasing open exhaustion, the inverse image of a closed radius-q disc is compact; it lies in one exhausting domain and gives the lower bound q·cr(Ω,p).

**Checks.**

- cr(ball(b,R),b)=R for R>0, using (z−b)/R.
- For Re z>0 at p=1, cr=2, using (z−1)/(z+1).
- For ℂ∖(−∞,0] at p=1, cr=4, using (√z−1)/(√z+1) with the principal square root.
- On the unit disc, cr at p is 1−|p|²; it is not identically 1 for all base points.
- Normalization is at the specified base point; an arbitrary Riemann map derivative does not define a conformal radius.

### 6.21 The shifted leading Hankel determinant

For a sequence a:ℕ→R over a commutative ring and n∈ℕ, `H_n(a)` is the n×n matrix with entry `a_(i+j+1)`, 0≤i,j<n, and `D_n(a)=det H_n(a)`. In particular D₀=1. The coefficient a₀ does not enter these determinants.

The +1 shift corresponds to the Laurent coefficient extracted by `∮G(z)z^k dz`; use this convention throughout.

The supporting API comprises:

- `shiftedHankelDet_zero`: D₀(a)=1.
- `shiftedHankelDet_one`: D₁(a)=a₁.
- `shiftedHankelDet_two`: D₂(a)=a₁a₃−a₂².
- `shiftedHankelDet_map`: A ring homomorphism φ sends `D_n(a)` to `D_n(φ∘a)`.
- `shiftedHankelDet_integer`: For integer a, its complex determinant is the integer cast of `D_n(a)`; hence a nonzero determinant has complex norm at least 1.
- `shiftedHankelDet_monic_basis`: Replacing powers `X^i` in both rows and columns by monic degree-i polynomials leaves the determinant of the moment matrix unchanged.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), §4, Hankel determinant in the proof of Theorem 4, pp. 13–14.) The matrix uses the coefficient shift `a_(i+j+1)`.

(Aitor Iribar López, [The Carlson-Pólya theorem on rational functions](#reference-iribar-kronecker), §2, Theorem 1 and proof, pp. 2–3.) Kronecker’s criterion is written for the unshifted sequence; apply it to the tail `a_(j+1)`.

To prove this, use Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R and the existing determinant. Ring-hom compatibility follows from determinant naturality.

A tail recurrence makes sufficiently many columns dependent, while the exact converse needs eventual vanishing of every leading determinant, as in Kronecker’s criterion.

**Checks.**

- D₀=1, not zero.
- For `a_j=2^j`, D₁=2 and D₂=0.
- For a₀=7, a₁=2, a₂=3, a₃=5, D₂=1; changing a₀ has no effect.
- For a₁=0, a₂=1, a₃=0, D₁=0 but D₂=−1. One vanishing determinant is insufficient.
- A single zero leading determinant does not establish rationality.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Matrix.det`; Mathlib `Matrix.det_apply`; Mathlib `RingHom.map_det`.

<a id="layer-6-topic-22"></a>

### 6.22 The classification of Pisot and Salem numbers by conjugate moduli

Let τ be a real algebraic integer with τ > 1, and let `r_>` and `r_=` be the numbers of complex roots of minpoly ℤ τ (counted in the multiset of roots) of modulus > 1 and of modulus = 1. Then (a) τ is a Pisot number `iff r_> = 1` and `r_= = 0`; (b) τ is a Salem number `iff r_> = 1` and `r_= ≥ 1`. In particular every real algebraic integer τ > 1 whose other conjugates lie in the closed unit disc is exactly one of Pisot or Salem, and τ is neither `iff r_> ≥ 2`. In case (b) the number of roots of modulus < 1 is 1 and `r_= = deg τ − 2 ≥ 2` ([Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24)).

τ real, integral over ℤ, τ > 1; τ itself is always one of the `r_>` roots, so `r_> ≥ 1`. The counts refer to the minimal polynomial; for a non-minimal polynomial P with root τ the criterion form is [A root criterion for Pisot numbers](#layer-6-topic-23).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 1, p. 5, and Lemma 1, p. 2 (arXiv v3).) Together with Lemma 1's hypotheses (closed disc, at least one on the circle) this is the dichotomy (a)/(b).

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 8.1, printed p. 335.) `r_> = 1` for Salem numbers.

To prove this, τ is a root of minpoly ℤ τ of modulus > 1, and the roots are simple (separability in characteristic 0), so `r_> ≥ 1` with equality iff every root z ≠ τ has |z| ≤ 1.

(a) IsPisot τ ⟺ every root z ≠ τ has |z| < 1 ⟺ (`r_> = 1` and no root of modulus 1), since |τ| > 1.

(b) IsSalem τ ⟺ every root z ≠ τ has |z| ≤ 1 and some root has modulus `1 ⟺ r_> = 1` and `r_= ≥ 1`.

Exclusivity and exhaustion follow from (a) and (b) as `r_= = 0` or `r_= ≥ 1`.

**Checks.**

- φ: `r_> = 1`, `r_= = 0` (Pisot). Lehmer's number: `r_> = 1`, `r_= = 8` (Salem).
- 1 + √3 (conjugate 1 − √3 = −0.73): Pisot. 3 + √2 (conjugate 3 − √2 = 1.59): `r_> = 2`, neither Pisot nor Salem.

*Needs:* [Pisot numbers](#layer-6-topic-1); [Salem numbers](#layer-6-topic-2); Mathlib `Polynomial.aroots`; Mathlib `Polynomial.mem_aroots`; Mathlib `minpoly.irreducible`.

<a id="layer-6-topic-23"></a>

### 6.23 A root criterion for Pisot numbers

Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic and θ > 1 a real root of P such that every complex root of P other than one copy of θ (the multiset of complex roots of P with one occurrence of θ removed) has modulus < 1. Then θ is a Pisot number. No irreducibility of P is needed.

P monic with integer coefficients; θ real, θ > 1, P(θ) = 0. If θ were a multiple root of P the hypothesis would put θ itself inside the unit disc, which is false; so the hypothesis forces θ to be a simple root.

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 1, Definitions 1–3, p. 1; Section 2, Proposition 6, p. 2.) The source defines Pisot numbers through the irreducible monic minimal polynomial and shows rational Pisot numbers are integers (Prop 6); the criterion from a reducible monic multiple is not in the source, it is the result's own routine Gauss-lemma extension.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 3.2, p. 9 (arXiv v3).) Section 3.2 (p. 9) establishes a Salem number from a possibly reducible monic reciprocal integer polynomial by locating the irreducible factor carrying `τ^{±1}`; the result is the simpler Pisot analogue, needing no reciprocity and no factor identification.

To prove this, θ is integral over ℤ (root of the monic P).

minpoly ℤ θ divides P in ℤ[X] (Gauss: minpoly ℤ θ is primitive and minpoly ℚ θ ∣ P in ℚ[X]); hence the complex roots of minpoly ℤ θ form a sub-multiset of those of P.

A root z ≠ θ of minpoly ℤ θ is therefore a root of P different from θ, hence in the multiset with one copy of θ removed, so |z| < 1.

**Checks.**

- X² − X − 1 establishes φ; X³ − X − 1 establishes θ₀ (its complex roots have |z|² = 1/θ₀ < 1 since the product of the three roots is 1); (X² − X − 1)(X² + X + 1) does not satisfy the hypothesis (the roots of X² + X + 1 have modulus 1), although φ is Pisot.
- P = (X − 2)(X² + 1): the hypothesis fails (the roots ±i have modulus 1), so the lemma does not apply although 2 is Pisot; the criterion is sufficient, not necessary.

*Needs:* [Pisot numbers](#layer-6-topic-1); Mathlib `minpoly.dvd`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_eq_field_fractions'`; Mathlib `Polynomial.mem_aroots`; Mathlib `IsIntegral`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_dvd`.

<a id="layer-6-topic-24"></a>

### 6.24 Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number

A real number τ is a Salem number iff τ is an algebraic integer, τ > 1, deg τ ≥ 4, τ is conjugate to τ⁻¹, and every complex conjugate z of τ other than τ and τ⁻¹ has |z| = 1. Consequently τ⁻¹ is the only conjugate of τ in the open unit disc, the conjugates on the circle are non-real and occur in pairs z, z̄ = z⁻¹, and deg τ is even.

τ real; conjugates are the complex roots of minpoly ℤ τ.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Lemma 1 and its proof, p. 2 (arXiv v3).) The implication (⇒) except the degree bound, which the proof does not address .

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 1, p. 1.) The right-hand side of the equivalence.

To prove this, (⇐) The conditions give |z| ≤ 1 for z ≠ τ (τ⁻¹ < 1 and the others have modulus 1), and deg τ ≥ 4 provides a conjugate other than `τ^{±1}`, which has modulus 1.

(⇒) Let τ′ be a conjugate on |z| = 1. It is not ±1 (otherwise minpoly ℤ τ = X ∓ 1 and τ = ±1), so it is non-real and τ̄′ = τ′⁻¹ is also a conjugate (the minimal polynomial has real coefficients).

Hence the minimal polynomial P of τ and its reverse P* share the root τ′⁻¹; by irreducibility P ∣ P*, so the roots of P are closed under z ↦ z⁻¹ ([Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3)); in particular τ⁻¹ is a conjugate: IsConjRoot ℚ τ τ⁻¹. (Source: apply a Galois automorphism mapping τ′⁻¹ to any conjugate τ₁.)

τ is the only conjugate of modulus > 1, so by the pairing τ⁻¹ is the only one of modulus < 1, and all others have modulus 1.

Degree: τ, τ⁻¹, τ′ and τ̄′ are four distinct roots (`τ^{±1}` real ≠ ±1, τ′ non-real); the circle roots come in pairs z ≠ z̄, so deg τ = 2 + 2k with k ≥ 1.

**Checks.**

- For Lehmer's number: deg 10, conjugates τ₁₀, τ₁₀⁻¹ and eight on the unit circle.
- For the quartic example 2.1537…: conjugates τ, τ⁻¹ = 0.4643… and 0.19098 ± 0.98159i of modulus 1.

*Needs:* [Salem numbers](#layer-6-topic-2); [Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3); Mathlib `IsConjRoot`; Mathlib `minpoly.irreducible`; Mathlib `minpoly.dvd`; Mathlib `Polynomial.mem_aroots`; Mathlib `minpoly.isIntegrallyClosed_dvd`.

### 6.25 Powers of a Salem number

If τ is a Salem number of degree d and n ≥ 1, then τⁿ is a Salem number of degree d.

n ≥ 1 (τ⁰ = 1 is not Salem).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Lemma 2 and its proof, p. 2 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement (ℕ = {1, 2, …} in the source).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proof of Lemma 2, p. 2.) The degree-preservation step.

To prove this, the conjugates of τⁿ are the n-th powers of the conjugates of τ (a ℚ-embedding of ℚ(τ) sends τⁿ to σ(τ)ⁿ).

The degree of τⁿ is d unless two conjugates satisfy τ₁ⁿ = τ₂ⁿ with τ₁ ≠ τ₂; applying a Galois automorphism mapping τ₁ ↦ τ gives τⁿ = τ₃ⁿ with τ₃ ≠ τ a conjugate, impossible since |τⁿ| > 1 ≥ |τ₃ⁿ|.

τⁿ > 1 is an algebraic integer; its other conjugates σ(τ)ⁿ have modulus ≤ 1, and a conjugate on the circle stays on the circle.

**Checks.**

- τ₁₀² is a Salem number of degree 10; the quartic example's square is a Salem number of degree 4.

### 6.26 Powers of a Pisot number

If θ is a Pisot number and n ≥ 1, then θⁿ is a Pisot number.

n ≥ 1.

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 2, Proposition 7, p. 2.) Exactly the statement; the result supplies the step excluding σ(θ)ⁿ = θⁿ.

To prove this, the conjugates of θⁿ are among the n-th powers σ(θ)ⁿ of the conjugates of θ.

A conjugate σ(θ)ⁿ equal to θⁿ with σ(θ) ≠ θ is impossible (|σ(θ)ⁿ| < 1 < θⁿ); so every conjugate of θⁿ other than θⁿ is σ(θ)ⁿ with σ(θ) ≠ θ, of modulus < 1.

θⁿ > 1 is an algebraic integer.

**Checks.**

- φ² = φ + 1 = 2.618… is a Pisot number (minimal polynomial X² − 3X + 1); θ₀³ = θ₀ + 1 is Pisot.

### 6.27 λτⁿ is close to integers for a Salem number τ

For every Salem number τ and every ε > 0 there is a real λ > 0 such that ‖λτⁿ‖ < ε for all n ∈ ℕ, where ‖x‖ = |x − round x| is the distance to the nearest integer. λ can be taken to be an algebraic integer of ℚ(τ).

n ranges over all of ℕ, including 0.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proposition 4, p. 4 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proof of Proposition 4, pp. 4-5.) The trace step; the lattice step is Minkowski's theorem .

To prove this, let K = ℚ(τ), d = [K : ℚ]. By Minkowski's convex body theorem in the Minkowski space of `K (NumberField.mixedEmbedding.exists_ne_zero_mem_ringOfIntegers_lt)` there is a nonzero `λ ∈ 𝓞_K` with |w(λ)| < ε′ at every infinite place w except the real place of τ, where the bound is chosen large enough.

Replacing λ by −λ, its value at τ's real embedding is positive (it is nonzero since λ ≠ 0).

`σₙ = Tr_{K/ℚ}(λτⁿ) = Σ` over the embeddings of λ(τᵢ)τᵢⁿ is an integer (`Algebra.isIntegral_trace`, ℤ integrally closed).

All terms but λτⁿ have modulus < ε′ (the other conjugates of τ have modulus ≤ 1), so |σₙ − λτⁿ| < (d − 1)ε′ ≤ ε for ε′ = ε/(d − 1).

**Checks.**

- For τ₁₀ and ε = 1/10 some `λ ∈ 𝓞_{ℚ(τ₁₀)}` works (the source applies the same lattice argument to the order ℤ[τ₁₀], so λ can be taken there); with λ = 1 the statement fails (τⁿ mod 1 is dense in (0, 1), Salem's Theorem V, quoted in Smyth's Section 3.4).

*Needs:* [Salem numbers](#layer-6-topic-2); Mathlib `NumberField.mixedEmbedding.exists_ne_zero_mem_ringOfIntegers_lt`; Mathlib `Algebra.isIntegral_trace`; Mathlib `IsIntegrallyClosed.isIntegral_iff`; Mathlib `trace_eq_sum_embeddings`.

### 6.28 Reciprocal Pisot numbers are quadratic units

If θ is a Pisot number conjugate to θ⁻¹, then minpoly ℤ θ = X² − aX + 1 for an integer a ≥ 3; so θ = (a + √(a² − 4))/2 ≥ (3 + √5)/2.

θ Pisot and IsConjRoot ℚ θ θ⁻¹.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 4, p. 12 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement, with the misprint n ≥ 3 corrected to a ≥ 3 .

To prove this, the conjugates are closed under z ↦ z⁻¹ ([Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3)). A conjugate z ≠ θ has |z| < 1, so z⁻¹ has modulus > 1 and equals θ: z = θ⁻¹.

So the conjugates are θ, θ⁻¹ (distinct, θ > 1): minpoly ℤ θ = X² − aX + 1 with a = θ + θ⁻¹ ∈ ℤ and constant term θθ⁻¹ = 1.

a = θ + θ⁻¹ > 2 (θ ≠ 1), so a ≥ 3.

**Checks.**

- a = 3: θ = (3 + √5)/2 = φ².

### 6.29 Mahler measure of a unit versus the houses of α and α⁻¹

Let α ≠ 0 be an algebraic unit (α and α⁻¹ algebraic integers) of degree d. Then M(α) = M(α⁻¹) and `M(α) ≤ max(⌈α⌉, ⌈α⁻¹⌉)^{d/2}`.

α a unit; α ≠ 0.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 3, printed p. 324.) Exactly the statement.

To prove this, the conjugates of α⁻¹ are the αᵢ⁻¹ and ∏|αᵢ| = |N(α)| = 1, so `M(α⁻¹) = ∏_{|αᵢ| < 1} |αᵢ|⁻¹ = ∏_{|αᵢ| > 1} |αᵢ| = M(α)`.

M(α)² = M(α)M(α⁻¹) is a product of at most d factors |αᵢ| (|αᵢ| > 1) and |αᵢ|⁻¹ (|αᵢ| < 1), each at most max(⌈α⌉, ⌈α⁻¹⌉).

**Checks.**

- α = φ: `M = φ ≤ max(φ, φ)^{1} = φ` (equality).

### 6.30 ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + h(α)

For a nonzero algebraic integer α of degree d, `⌈α⌉ ≥ M(α)^{1/d} = exp(h(α)) ≥ 1 + h(α)`, where h(α) = log M(α)/d is the absolute logarithmic Weil height (Mathlib's NumberField.absLogHeight₁). Consequently any lower bound M(α) ≥ c₀ > 1 gives ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + log(c₀)/d.

α ≠ 0 (for α = 0, ⌈α⌉ = 0 < 1).

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 3, (9), printed p. 325.) Exactly the statement.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 1, (5), printed p. 323.) The normalisation h = log M/d, which TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2 identifies with Mathlib's absLogHeight₁.

To prove this, if some conjugate has modulus > 1 use [Mahler measure versus house](#layer-6-topic-6); otherwise M(α) = 1 and `⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 (NumberField.one_le_house_of_isIntegral)`.

`M(α)^{1/d} = absMulHeight₁ α` (TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2), so `M(α)^{1/d} = exp(h(α))`.

`exp(t) ≥ 1 + t (Real.add_one_le_exp)`.

### 6.31 Smyth's rational function F = P(0)P/P* has integer coefficients

Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic with P(0) = ±1 and `P* = X^d P(1/X)` its reverse (so P*(0) = 1). Then F = P(0)·P/P* has a Maclaurin expansion with integer coefficients, F(0) = 1, and F is constant iff P is reciprocal (P* = ±P).

P monic, P(0) = ±1. (If |P(0)| ≥ 2 then M(P) ≥ |P(0)| ≥ 2 and Smyth's bound is immediate.)

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, printed p. 328.) Exactly the statement (the survey takes P monic, the minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer; the unit hypothesis P(0) = ±1 is the case that matters, see the hypotheses).

To prove this, p*(0) = 1 is a unit of ℤ, so P* is invertible in ℤ⟦X⟧ and F = P(0)·P·(P*)⁻¹ ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧.

F(0) = P(0)·P(0)/1 = P(0)² = 1.

If F = c is constant then c = F(0) = 1 and P(0)P = P*, so P* = ±P; conversely P* = ±P = P(0)P (compare constant terms) gives F = 1.

**Checks.**

- P = X³ − X − 1: F = −(X³ − X − 1)/(1 − X² − X³) = 1 + X + … is nonconstant.
- P = L (Lehmer): F = 1.

### 6.35 Arnold–Smyth congruence P₄ ≡ P₂ (mod 4)

For every monic P ∈ ℤ[X], P₄ − P₂ ∈ 4ℤ[X].

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Lemma 2.1, (2), and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v1).) The Arnold-Smyth congruence. The source calls its subset-product construction a symmetric-power argument; the proof here specifies products indexed by k-element subsets, that is the exterior-power polynomial.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Proof of Lemma 2.1, p. 4.) The first step (e₁⁴ ≡ e₁² and 2e₂² ≡ −2e₂ mod 4).

To prove this, coefficient of `X^{n−1}`: s₂ = e₁² − 2e₂ and s₄ = e₁⁴ + 2e₂² − 4(e₁²e₂ − e₁e₃ + e₄) (Newton), so s₄ − s₂ ≡ e₁²(e₁² − 1) + 2e₂(e₂ + 1) ≡ 0 (mod 4) for integers eᵢ (e₁²(e₁² − 1) ≡ 0 mod 4 in both parities, e₂(e₂ + 1) is even).

Coefficient of `X^{n−k}`: it is `± e_k(α₁^m, …, α_n^m) = ± s_m(β)` for the k-fold products `β = α_{i₁}⋯α_{i_k}`, the roots of the k-th exterior-power (subset-product) polynomial `∏_I(X − α_I) ∈ ℤ[X]` (fundamental theorem of symmetric polynomials); apply the first step to that polynomial.

Hence every coefficient of P₄ − P₂ is divisible by 4.

Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic irreducible of degree n > 1 with P₂ not a perfect square. Then the following are equivalent: `(i) P = Φ_N` for N > 0 with 4 ∤ N; (ii) P₂ = P₄; (iii) P₂P₄ is a perfect square in ℤ[X]; (iv) P₂P₄ is a square in ℚ(X) (the function √(P₂P₄) is rational).

The source odd-level condition is false: P=Φ₆ has P₂=P₄=Φ₃ and P₂ is not a square. Under the standing nonsquare hypothesis the correct cyclotomic levels have 4 ∤ N. This includes odd N and twice an odd N.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Lemma 2.3, p. 5 (arXiv v1).) The equivalence after correcting (i) to cyclotomic of level N with 4∤N; Φ₆ disproves the printed odd-level restriction. (ii) ⇒ (iii) ⇒ (iv): P₂P₄ = P₂².

(iv) ⇒ (iii): a monic integer polynomial that is a square in ℚ(X) is the square of a monic polynomial in ℚ[X], which has integer coefficients (Gauss).

(iii) ⇒ (i): P₂ is irreducible and squarefree, so its roots occur in P₄. Hence α² and α⁴ are conjugate; [If `α^k` and `α^l` are conjugate (k ≠ l) then α is 0 or a root of unity](#layer-6-topic-10) gives α a root of unity, since α≠0. Thus `P=Φ_N` for N>0.
