### 6.38 Schur’s first and doubled-index coefficient conditions

If e is a real Schur series, `c=e_0` and k≥1, then `|e_k|≤1−c²`. If |c|<1, also `−(1−c²)+e_k²/(1+c) ≤ e_(2k) ≤ (1−c²)−e_k²/(1−c)`. For c=±1 all coefficients of positive index vanish; the fractional inequalities are not stated there.

e real Schur; k≥1. The doubled-index inequalities require |c|<1.

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §2 lemma (1)–(2), pp. 170–171.) The lemma bounds every positive coefficient and relates the kth and doubled-index coefficients. The Schur-transform proof here also applies without a boundary extension.

To prove this, average the witness over kth-root rotations. The resulting bounded function has expansion `h(w)=c+e_k w+e_(2k)w²+⋯`; existence on the disc follows from the rotation-invariant series.

For |c|<1, h is not a unimodular constant, so the maximum principle `(Complex.eqOn_of_isPreconnected_of_isMaxOn_norm)` gives |h|<1 on the disc. Apply the disc automorphism to h and divide by w: s(w)=(h(w)−c)/(w(1−c h(w))). Schwarz’s lemma in difference-quotient form (`Complex.norm_dslope_le_div_of_mapsTo_ball`, for the automorphism image of h, which vanishes at 0) makes s a map into the closed disc. Its first two coefficients are `e_k/(1−c²)` and `e_(2k)/(1−c²)+c e_k²/(1−c²)²`.

Schwarz–Pick at zero bounds the derivative of s. A boundary value |s(0)|=1 forces s constant by the maximum principle, giving the same non-strict bounds. Rearrange to the two displayed inequalities. Treat c=±1 by the maximum principle on the original witness.

**Checks.**

- For `(c+z^k)/(1+c z^k)`, the upper doubled-index bound is attained: `e_k=1−c²` and `e_(2k)=−c(1−c²)`.
- For −1<c<1 both denominators are positive; no multiplication by an unknown-sign denominator is used.

### 6.42 Dirichlet capacity for radial slit condensers

For closed disjoint plates E₀,E₁⊆ℂ, with E₁ compact, positive separation, and G=ℂ∖(E₀∪E₁) bounded with finitely many analytic boundary arcs, define `Cap_D(E₀,E₁)=inf_u ∫_G |∇u|² dA`. The energy is the nonnegative extended integral of the squared real derivative norm; the infimum of an empty admissible class is +∞. The norm of the real Fréchet derivative ℂ→ℝ equals the Euclidean gradient norm.

### 6.43 An exterior Laurent continuation

For a:ℕ→ℂ and compact nonempty K⊆ℂ, an exterior Laurent development is a function G:ℂ→ℂ holomorphic on ℂ∖K, together with R>0 such that K⊆closedBall(0,R) and, whenever |z|>R, `HasSum(Σ_j a_j z^(−j),G(z))`. Equivalently the summand is `a_j(z⁻¹)^j`. Values of G on K are irrelevant.

Only a convergent germ at infinity is claimed; arbitrary formal series are not silently treated as analytic functions. Connectedness of ℂ∖K is not required for the formal rationality conclusion. If the conclusion also identifies G with the rational function everywhere off K, require connectedness.

The supporting API comprises:

- `exteriorContinuation_enlarge_radius`: Any larger positive radius containing K is a valid convergence radius.
- `exteriorContinuation_enlarge_set`: If K⊆L are compact, restrict the same witness to ℂ∖L and enlarge its radius.
- `exteriorContinuation_unique`: For connected ℂ∖K, two witnesses for the same coefficients agree off K.
- `exteriorContinuation_coeff`: The coefficient of `z^(−j)` is PowerSeries.coeff j (PowerSeries.mk a).
- `exteriorContinuation_moment`: For a finite smooth contour cycle enclosing K with total index 1 and lying off K, `a_(k+1)=(2πi)⁻¹∮G(z)z^k dz` for every k≥0.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), §4, Theorem 4 and Corollary 5, pp. 13–15.) A convergent integer Laurent germ extends as a single-valued holomorphic function outside a small-diameter compact set.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), §3.1, Théorème, p. 12.) The extension assumption is imposed on the germ, not merely on an unrelated holomorphic function. Bertrandias also asks for a simply connected complement; this definition needs no connectedness.

To prove this, store an unbundled holomorphic witness and an exterior convergence radius. The radius can be enlarged, and the excluded compact set can be enlarged, without changing the germ.

On a connected complement the identity theorem makes the witness unique there. The formal series at infinity is PowerSeries.mk a in the variable w=1/z.

**Checks.**

- G(z)=1/(z−2), K={2}, a₀=0 and `a_j=2^(j−1)` for j≥1 give a development and a rational formal series.
- G(z)=sqrt(1−1/z) on the complement of [0,1] has the normalized branch at infinity but coefficients a₁=−1/2, so it fails integer integrality.
- G(z)=exp z is holomorphic outside {0} but has no convergent series in nonpositive powers at infinity; holomorphy alone is insufficient.
- G=7 and a₀=7, `a_j=0` for j>0 work for every nonempty compact K.
- A0 may be nonzero. It is a constant term and has no effect on the shifted Hankel rationality criterion.

*Needs:* [The shifted leading Hankel determinant](#layer-6-topic-21); Mathlib `PowerSeries.mk`; Mathlib `DifferentiableOn.hasFPowerSeriesOnBall`.

<a id="layer-6-topic-44"></a>

### 6.44 Kronecker’s eventual Hankel vanishing criterion

For a sequence a over a field k, PowerSeries.mk a is rational in the sense of [The rationality predicate for a formal power series](#layer-2-topic-26) if and only if there exists N such that `D_n(a)=0` for all n≥N. The denominator may be normalized to have constant term 1; no degree bound on the numerator is assumed.

k is a field; no characteristic-zero hypothesis is needed for this algebraic criterion.

(Aitor Iribar López, [The Carlson-Pólya theorem on rational functions](#reference-iribar-kronecker), §2, Theorem 1 and proof, pp. 2–3.) Eventual vanishing of all leading Hankel determinants characterizes rational formal series. The proof is used with corrections to its signs, indices and recurrence.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), §2.1, p. 6, and §3.1, proof, p. 12.) Bertrandias calls `det(u_(h+k))` the Kronecker determinant (§2.1) and concludes rationality from its eventual vanishing (§3.1) without restating the criterion; the theorem of §2.1 is the non-archimedean growth bound, not this criterion.

To prove this, rationality gives a linear recurrence for the coefficients after the numerator degree. For large n its shifted moment matrix has dependent columns, and `D_n=0`.

Conversely apply the source criterion to the tail `b_j=a_(j+1)`. If all its leading determinants vanish, its first nonzero coefficient would give a nonzero anti-diagonal determinant, so the tail is zero. Otherwise take r maximal with a nonzero r×r leading determinant. Solve the unique r-term recurrence from its invertible block.

If the first subsequent recurrence failure is at the index controlled by d≥0, a block determinant factors as `det(A_r)` times a nonzero anti-diagonal block of size d+1, with sign `(−1)^((d+1)d/2)`. This contradicts maximality. The recurrence is therefore valid from a finite index onward. Multiply the series by its recurrence polynomial to get a polynomial (coefficients of the coerced polynomial by `Polynomial.coeff_coe`); adding a₀ does not change rationality.

**Checks.**

- The +1 shift discards only the constant coefficient. A zero determinant at one size does not satisfy the eventual condition.

*Needs:* [The shifted leading Hankel determinant](#layer-6-topic-21); [The rationality predicate for a formal power series](#layer-2-topic-26); Mathlib `Matrix.det`; Mathlib `Polynomial.coeff_coe`.

### 6.45 The minimal polynomial of a Salem number is reciprocal

If τ is a Salem number with minimal polynomial P = minpoly ℤ τ of degree d, then `X^d P(1/X) = P`, i.e. Polynomial.reverse P = P (the plus sign).

τ a Salem number.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 1, p. 1 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement; the source's 'zdeg P P(z−1) = P(z)' fixes the plus sign.

To prove this, τ is conjugate to τ⁻¹ ([Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24)), so reverse P = ±P ([Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3)).

The sign is + : reverse P = −P forces P = X − 1 (P(1) = 0 from P*(1) = P(1) = −P(1) and irreducibility), but deg P ≥ 4.

Equivalently: `P(0) = (−1)^d ∏` roots = (+1)·τ·τ⁻¹·∏ z z̄ = 1 with d even.

**Checks.**

- reverse L = L for Lehmer's polynomial; reverse (X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1) = X⁴ − 3X³ + 3X² − 3X + 1.

*Needs:* [Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24); [Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3); Mathlib `Polynomial.reverse`.

### 6.46 Salem numbers through their traces τ + τ⁻¹

Let τ > 1 be real and α = τ + τ⁻¹. Then τ is a Salem number iff α is an irrational algebraic integer all of whose conjugates other than α are real and lie in (−2, 2). In that case ℚ(α) is a totally real subfield of index 2 in ℚ(τ), α > 2, and deg τ = 2 deg α. Equivalently (Salem): a number field K is ℚ(τ) for a Salem number τ iff K has a totally real subfield ℚ(α) of index 2 with K = ℚ(τ), τ + τ⁻¹ = α, α > 2 an irrational algebraic integer with all other conjugates in (−2, 2).

τ > 1 real (so α > 2 automatically). Irrationality of α is essential: α = 3 gives the quadratic unit (3 + √5)/2, which is not a Salem number.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proposition 3(i), p. 2 (arXiv v3).) The field form; the result's element form is what the proof on p. 3 establishes.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proof of Proposition 3(i), p. 3.) Step (⇐).

To prove this, (⇒) Every conjugate of α is τ₁ + τ₁⁻¹ for a conjugate τ₁ of τ; `τ₁ = τ^{±1}` gives α, and |τ₁| = 1 gives τ₁ + τ̄₁ = 2 Re τ₁ ∈ (−2, 2) (τ₁ ≠ ±1). α is an algebraic integer. α is irrational since some conjugate of τ lies on the circle and yields a conjugate of α different from α. τ² − ατ + 1 = 0 gives [ℚ(τ) : ℚ(α)] ≤ 2, and ℚ(α) ≠ ℚ(τ) because every conjugate of α is real while τ has a non-real conjugate (a circle conjugate other than ±1); so the index is 2.

(⇐) τ is a root of X² − αX + 1, monic over ℤ[α], so τ is an algebraic integer. Every conjugate τ₁ of τ satisfies τ₁ + τ₁⁻¹ = α₁ for a conjugate α₁ of α: α₁ = α gives `τ₁ = τ^{±1}`; α₁ ∈ (−2, 2) gives |τ₁| = 1 (the roots of X² − α₁X + 1 are non-real of product 1). Every conjugate α₁ of α arises from some τ₁, and α is irrational, so some α₁ ∈ (−2, 2) exists and gives a conjugate of τ on the circle.

**Checks.**

- Lehmer: α = τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ = 2.0264… is the root > 2 of y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3, whose other roots −1.887, −1.469, −0.585, 0.914 lie in (−2, 2).
- Quartic example: α = (3 + √5)/2 with conjugate (3 − √5)/2 = 0.382 ∈ (−2, 2).

### 6.47 Powers of a Pisot number are near integers

If θ is a Pisot number then ‖θⁿ‖ = |θⁿ − round(θⁿ)| → 0 as n → ∞; more precisely |θⁿ − Tr(θⁿ)| ≤ (d − 1)ρⁿ with d = deg θ, ρ < 1 the largest modulus of a conjugate other than θ, and Tr(θⁿ) ∈ ℤ.

θ a Pisot number; for d = 1 the statement is trivial (θⁿ ∈ ℤ).

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 3, Theorem 8 and its proof, p. 2.) Exactly the statement; the proof's power-sum argument is the result's (with the index misprint corrected).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proof of Proposition 4, p. 5 (arXiv v3).) The same trace argument (there with λ and a Salem number).

To prove this, sₙ = Σ over the complex roots z of minpoly ℤ θ of zⁿ is a rational integer: [Power sums of roots: `s_{np} ≡ s_n (mod p)`](#layer-6-topic-32) (power sums of the roots of a monic integer polynomial are integers); alternatively it is `Tr_{ℚ(θ)/ℚ}(θⁿ)` by mathlib `trace_eq_sum_embeddings` with `Algebra.isIntegral_trace`.

`|sₙ − θⁿ| ≤ Σ_{z ≠ θ} |z|ⁿ ≤ (d − 1)ρⁿ → 0`.

For n large, (d − 1)ρⁿ < 1/2, so round(θⁿ) = sₙ and ‖θⁿ‖ = |θⁿ − sₙ|.

**Checks.**

- φⁿ + (−1/φ)ⁿ = Lₙ (Lucas numbers), so `‖φⁿ‖ = φ^{−n}` for n ≥ 2.
- θ₀¹⁰⁰ is within 2·(0.8689)¹⁰⁰ < 2·10⁻⁶ of the integer Tr(θ₀¹⁰⁰).

### 6.48 The smallest Pisot number θ₀

θ₀ = 1.3247179572… is the unique real root of X³ − X − 1 (the plastic number). As a declaration: the supremum of the set of real roots of x³ − x − 1, which is a singleton.

X³ − X − 1 has exactly one real root (its discriminant −23 is negative).

The supporting API comprises:

- `plasticNumber`: θ₀ := the supremum of the real roots of x³ − x − 1 (a singleton).
- `plasticNumber_cube`: θ₀³ = θ₀ + 1.
- `eq_plasticNumber_of_cube`: x ∈ ℝ, x³ = x + 1 → x = θ₀ (the real root is unique).
- `plasticNumber_mem_Ioo`: 1.3247 < θ₀ < 1.3248.
- `minpoly_plasticNumber`: minpoly ℤ θ₀ = X³ − X − 1.
- `isPisot_plasticNumber`: θ₀ is a Pisot number.
- `plasticNumber_not_isConjRoot_inv`: θ₀ is not conjugate to θ₀⁻¹ (it is nonreciprocal).
- `mahlerMeasure_plasticNumber`: Mathlib's Mahler measure of X³ − X − 1 mapped to ℂ[X] equals θ₀.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, (15), printed p. 328.) The definition (the real root of z³ − z − 1) and `plasticNumber_not_isConjRoot_inv`.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 3.1, p. 7 (arXiv v3).) θ₀ as a Pisot number, and the comparison τ₁₀ < θ₀ of the Checks of [Lehmer's number τ₁₀](#layer-6-topic-5).

To prove this, define θ₀ := sup {x ∈ ℝ : x³ − x − 1 = 0}.

Uniqueness: x ↦ x³ − x − 1 has local extrema at ±1/√3 with negative values, so exactly one real zero, in (1.3247, 1.3248) by evaluation and the intermediate value theorem.

minpoly ℤ θ₀ = X³ − X − 1: the polynomial has no rational root (±1 are not roots), hence is irreducible (degree 3).

θ₀ is Pisot: the two complex roots z, z̄ have |z|² = 1/θ₀ < 1 since the product of the roots is 1 ([A root criterion for Pisot numbers](#layer-6-topic-23)).

θ₀ is nonreciprocal: the reverse −X³ − X² + 1 is not ±(X³ − X − 1) ([Reciprocal algebraic integers and reciprocal minimal polynomials](#layer-6-topic-3)).

**Checks.**

- θ₀ < φ.
- φ < θ₀² (used by Smyth's trinomial argument).
- −θ₀ is the real root of X³ − X + 1 and is negative: the misprinted polynomial X³ − X + 1 does not define θ₀.
- θ₀ is irrational, so it is not one of the degree-one Pisot numbers.
- θ₀ ∈ (1.3247, 1.3248); θ₀ < φ < θ₀²; M(X³ − X − 1) = θ₀.

### 6.49 Dobrowolski's house bound ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²)

Let α be a nonzero algebraic integer of degree d that is not a root of unity. Then ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²), e = exp(1). Equivalently: if ⌈α⌉ ≤ 1 + 1/(4ed²) then α = 0 or α is a root of unity.

α algebraic integer; the bound is for the house (maximal modulus of a conjugate).

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Theorem 2.17, printed p. 8.) Exactly the statement (due to Dobrowolski 1978, the source's [4]).

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Proof of Theorem 2.17, printed p. 10.) The key step.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 7.1, printed pp. 333-334.) The survey quotes Dobrowolski's original constant; the result proves the source's 1/(4ed²).

To prove this, choose a prime p with 2ed < p ≤ 4ed (Bertrand, `Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul` with n = ⌊2ed⌋).

Suppose ⌈α⌉ ≤ 1 + 1/(4ed²). For 1 ≤ n ≤ d: `|s_{np}| ≤ d⌈α⌉^{np} ≤ d(1 + 1/(4ed²))^{4ed²} ≤ de` and `|sₙ| ≤ de (1 + t ≤ eᵗ, Real.add_one_le_exp)`, so `|s_{np} − sₙ| ≤ 2de < p`.

With `s_{np} ≡ sₙ (mod p)` ([Power sums of roots: `s_{np} ≡ s_n (mod p)`](#layer-6-topic-32)) this forces `s_{np} = sₙ` for n = 1, …, d.

So the multisets `{αᵢ^p}` and {αᵢ} have the same first d power sums and are equal ([Power sums determine a multiset in characteristic zero](#layer-6-topic-9)): `α^p` is a conjugate of α.

p ≠ 1, so α = 0 or a root of unity ([If `α^k` and `α^l` are conjugate (k ≠ l) then α is 0 or a root of unity](#layer-6-topic-10)), a contradiction.

**Checks.**

- d = 2: every quadratic non-torsion algebraic integer has ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(16e) = 1.0230; e.g. ⌈φ⌉ = 1.618.
- Lehmer's number (d = 10): 1.176 > 1 + 1/(400e) = 1.00092.

### 6.50 Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)

Let Q ∈ ℤ[X] with Q(0) = 1 and Q a square modulo 4 (Q = U² + 4V with U, V ∈ ℤ[X]). Then there is S ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧ with S(0) = 1 and S² = Q. In particular, for P ∈ ℤ[X] monic with `P* = X^n P(1/X)`, √(P₂*·P₄*) ∈ 1 + Xℤ⟦X⟧.

Q(0) = 1.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Proposition 2.2 and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v1).) Exactly the statement.

To prove this, from Q(0)=U(0)²+4V(0)=1, U(0) is odd; it need not equal ±1 (U=3,V=−2,Q=1 is a counterexample). Put k=(1−U(0))/2, U′=U+2k and V′=V−kU−k². Then Q=U′²+4V′, U′(0)=1 and V′(0)=0. Use U′,V′ in the following steps.

U′ is a unit of ℤ⟦X⟧ because U′(0)=1. Put Y=V′/(U′)², whose constant term is zero, and substitute Y into the integral series T of [√(1 + 4Y) has integer coefficients](#layer-6-topic-14). Define S=U′·T(Y).

The substitution identity gives S²=(U′)²(1+4V′/(U′)²)=Q; its constant term is U′(0)·T(0)=1.

For P monic: (P₂P₄)* = P₂*P₄* has constant term 1 and is ≡ (P₂*)² (mod 4) by [Arnold–Smyth congruence P₄ ≡ P₂ (mod 4)](#layer-6-topic-35) (reversal commutes with reduction mod 4).

**Checks.**

- Q = 1 − 4X = 1² + 4(−X) (Catalan): S = 1 − 2X − 2X² − 4X³ − ….
- Q = 1 − 6X + X² = (1 − X)² + 4(−X) (large Schröder numbers): S ∈ ℤ⟦X⟧.

### 6.51 Smyth’s bounded holomorphic quotient

Let P∈ℤ[X] be monic, P(0)=±1, with no complex root on the unit circle. Put Q=P.reverse and A=M(P). There are real-coefficient finite Blaschke products f,g, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc, with f(0)=g(0)=c=A⁻¹>0 and Q(z)f(z)=P(0)P(z)g(z). On points where Q and g are nonzero, f/g=P(0)P/Q. If P is irreducible and nonreciprocal, that quotient is nonconstant and not a polynomial.

P(0)=±1 excludes zero roots; no roots on the unit circle is explicit. Irreducibility and nonreciprocity are used only for the final non-polynomial assertion.

The supporting API comprises:

- `smythFactorization_schur`: The Taylor coefficients of f and g are real Schur series.
- `smythFactorization_constant`: Their common constant coefficient is M(P)⁻¹.
- `smythFactorization_boundary`: Both products have modulus 1 on the unit circle.
- `smythFactorization_coeff_mul`: For the integral formal expansion F of P(0)P/Q, the real-coefficient identity F·g=f holds coefficient by coefficient.
- `smythFactorization_nonpolynomial`: If P is irreducible and P.reverse≠±P, F is not the coercion of any polynomial.

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §3, pp. 171–172, root-product quotient and (3).) The two bounded root products have the same positive constant, the inverse Mahler measure.

(C. J. Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), §5.1, published pp. 328–329.) Smyth’s own outline: `F=P(0)P(z)/(z^dP(1/z))` has integer Maclaurin coefficients, is nonconstant for nonreciprocal P, and is a quotient f/g of two functions bounded by 1 on the disc with f(0)=g(0)=M(P)⁻¹, whose coefficients obey Schur’s conditions.

To prove this, use `b_α` for roots α of P inside the disc to form f, and `b_(α⁻¹)` for roots α of P outside the disc to form g, with multiplicities. Work with the scalar formula (z−α)/(1−conj(α)z) of the pinned disc factor: for |α|<1 its denominator does not vanish on |z|<1/|α|, so `hasDerivAt_unitDiscMoebiusFormula` gives holomorphy on a neighbourhood of the closed disc, and `Complex.hasSum_taylorSeries_on_ball` gives the Taylor coefficients of the products.

The inside-root product and the inverse outside-root product both have absolute value A⁻¹ because the total root product has modulus 1. Conjugation-stability makes the products real-coefficient; choose real signs to make both constants positive.

Compare the two rational functions by their zeros and poles and their value at zero. In the irreducible nonreciprocal case P and Q are coprime and have equal degree, so their nonconstant quotient is not polynomial.

**Checks.**

- For P=X³−X−1, c=θ₀⁻¹ for both products.
- For P=X²−3X+1, f=g and F=1; this is permitted by the construction but excluded by the nonreciprocal theorem.
- P=X−2 is outside the unit-constant hypothesis; the assertion `c_f=c_g=1/2` would be false for its inside-root product.
- Keep the cross-multiplied identity; dividing at a zero of g is not permitted.

### 6.52 The first two nonzero integral quotient coefficients

Let f,g have real Schur coefficient sequences u,v with `u_0=v_0=c`, 3/4≤c<1, and F∈ℤ⟦z⟧ satisfy `F_0=1` and Fg=f. Suppose F is not a polynomial. Let 0<k<l be its first two nonzero positive indices, with coefficients `a_k`,`a_l`. Then `|a_k|=|a_l|=1`, `|u_k|+|v_k|=c`, and c/2≤1−c². Coefficient coupling gives `u_k−v_k=a_k c`, `u_(k+i)−v_(k+i)=a_k v_i` for 0<i<l−k, and `u_l−v_l=a_k v_(l−k)+a_l c`.

F non-polynomial ensures two positive nonzero coefficients exist; it is stronger than merely nonconstant. All equalities are formal coefficient equalities and require no division at a zero of g.

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §3, (3)–(5), p. 172.) The integer quotient coefficients and the Schur bounds force the two first nonzero coefficients to be signs and the kth coefficients to have opposite signs.

To prove this, choose the first two nonzero indices using well-ordering and the non-polynomial hypothesis; apply the pinned finite coefficient convolution to Fg=f.

The Schur coefficient bound gives `|a_k|c≤2(1−c²)`. Since c≥3/4, the integer `|a_k|` cannot be ≥2.

Because 1−c²<c, `u_k` and `v_k` have opposite signs, giving the absolute-value sum. At index l, `|a_l|c≤3(1−c²)<2c`, which rules out `|a_l|≥2`.

The larger of `|u_k|` and `|v_k|` is at least c/2, giving the weak quadratic condition.

**Checks.**

- The k<l<2k branch gives `u_(l−k)=v_(l−k)`; the long-gap branch uses the doubled-index coupling instead.

### 6.53 Transfinite diameter under a monic polynomial inverse image

If K⊆ℂ is nonempty compact and P∈ℂ[X] is monic of degree m≥1, then P⁻¹(K) is nonempty compact and `d(P⁻¹(K))=d(K)^(1/m)`. In particular `d({z: |P(z)|≤r^m})=r` for r≥0.

P monic and m≥1; inverse image means P(z)∈K, an existential membership condition.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), 1.4.5 and its Application, p. 2.) The monic degree-m inverse-image law raises the diameter to the power 1/m; its set-membership quantifier is misprinted and is corrected here.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), exercise after Theorem 1.18, p. 178.) The lemniscate case: a set {|P|≤Rⁿ} with P monic of degree n has capacity R.

To prove this, a positive-degree polynomial is proper and surjective on ℂ, so its inverse image is compact and nonempty.

Pull back a monic degree-n Chebyshev polynomial on K to obtain `t_(mn)(P⁻¹K)≤t_n(K)`.

For a monic degree-j Q on P⁻¹K, form its polynomial norm `N_Q(y)=∏_(P(z)=y)Q(z)`, with root multiplicities. The resultant construction (`resultant_eq_prod_eval`, applied to P−y, which splits over ℂ) gives a monic polynomial in y of degree j after its harmless sign normalization, and `|N_Q(y)|≤‖Q‖_(P⁻¹K)^m`. Hence `t_j(K)≤t_j(P⁻¹K)^m`.

Apply the Fekete–Chebyshev limit to both inequalities. This proof uses a determinant norm, rather than assuming an unspecified equilibrium measure.

**Checks.**

- For `P=X^m` and `K=[0,R^m]`, the regular m-spike hedgehog has `d=R·4^(−1/m)`.
- For P=X² and K={1}, the inverse image is {−1,1} with d=0; finite Fekete diameter `δ_2` need not be zero.

### 6.54 Dirichlet conformal invariance and the annulus formula

For the radial slit condenser class, `Cap_D` is invariant under eligible conformal changes of coordinates. For round plates E₀={|z|≥R}, E₁={|z|≤r}, 0<r<R, `Cap_D=2π/log(R/r)`. Plate monotonicity holds with the direction stated in the definition.

Coordinate maps are biholomorphisms of the open condenser domains with continuous corresponding boundary values; the composed tests remain in the prescribed class.

(V. N. Dubinin, [On the change in harmonic measure under symmetrization](#reference-dubinin-1985), §1, Dirichlet integral characterization, pp. 269–270.) The proof uses capacity invariance and comparison of test-function energies.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), Example 5.1, (5.3), p. 193.) The logarithmic annulus denominator confirms the normalization after multiplication by 2π.

To prove this, for a holomorphic conformal map the derivative multiplies real lengths by |φ′| and area by |φ′|². The chain rule and the holomorphic change of variables (`TauCeti.lintegral_image_eq_lintegral_enorm_deriv_sq_mul`, area factor ‖φ′‖²) cancel the factors in the nonnegative Dirichlet integral; apply both map directions.

For an annulus, the admissible radial function log(R/|z|)/log(R/r) has energy 2π/log(R/r). On each radial line, the endpoint value difference is 1; weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives radial energy at least 1/log(R/r). Integrate angles and discard the nonnegative angular contribution.

The larger-plate admissible class is a subset of the smaller-plate class, and gradients vanish in the plate regions. This proves monotonicity.

**Checks.**

- Any formula log(R/r)/(2π) would be the reciprocal capacity and fails the thin-annulus check.

### 6.55 Dubinin’s finite rotational desymmetrization

For n≥1 distinct ray directions `θ_j` and 0<r<1, let `D(r;θ)=ball(0,1)∖⋃_j{t exp(iθ_j):r≤t<1}`. Let D*(r,n) use equally spaced directions 2πj/n. There is a finite partition into angular pieces with rotations about 0 sending the regular slit configuration to the prescribed one. On identified cut boundaries, the inverse images differ by elements of the dihedral symmetry group of the regular configuration. Consequently every dihedrally invariant admissible test function on D* transfers to a continuous admissible test function on D with the same Dirichlet energy and unchanged circular inner and outer plate values.

Distinct directions and positive slit tip radius; repeated rays are collapsed before applying this construction. A partition of the plane into closed angular pieces has disjoint interiors; energy is computed on those interiors, and finite cuts have area zero.

The supporting API comprises:

- `desymmetrization_partition`: The angular pieces cover the plane and have pairwise disjoint interiors, both before and after rotation.
- `desymmetrization_boundary_match`: On each common cut, the two inverse images are related by an element of the regular configuration’s dihedral group.
- `desymmetrization_transfer`: A dihedrally invariant admissible function transfers by the inverse rotations and agrees on all cuts.
- `desymmetrization_energy`: The transferred nonnegative Dirichlet integral equals the original integral.
- `desymmetrization_capacity_le`: Averaging first over the dihedral group and then transferring gives `Cap_D(D,ε)≤Cap_D(D*,ε)` for 0<ε<r.

(V. N. Dubinin, [On the change in harmonic measure under symmetrization](#reference-dubinin-1985), §1, Lemmas 1–2 and Theorem 1 proof, pp. 268–270.) A finite angular partition, its boundary matching, and the transferred symmetric test function give the desymmetrization capacity inequality.

To prove this, use the angle-subdivision construction in Dubinin Lemma 1: move sectors by rotations, split a sector at every mismatch, and match cut rays by the dihedral reflections. The unmatched angular pieces decrease in this finite subdivision argument.

Define the transferred function on each rotated piece by composing the original function with the inverse rotation. Dihedral invariance gives equal values on common cuts. Lemma 2 supplies local Lipschitz regularity across them; finite C1 cuts are transported to finite C1 cuts.

Rotations have area Jacobian 1 and preserve the gradient norm, so the sum of piece energies is unchanged. Rotations preserve the concentric plate circles and send the regular slits to the prescribed slit plate.

**Checks.**

- For n=1, a single global rotation transfers the slit domain and preserves capacity.
- For equally spaced directions the identity partition works and the capacities agree.
- For two distinct but non-antipodal rays the construction must still cover both domains and match cuts; a single global rotation cannot supply it.
- Every piece rotation fixes the radius-ε inner plate; moving that plate independently violates the construction.
- Boundary matching is a mathematical condition, not an assertion that arbitrary independently rotated sectors automatically produce a continuous function.

*Needs:* [Dirichlet capacity for radial slit condensers](#layer-6-topic-42).

### 6.56 Transfinite diameter and the inverted exterior radius

Let K be a nontrivial finite radial hedgehog and b>0. Put `U_b={0}∪{b/z:z∈ℂ∖K}`. Then `U_b` is a proper simply connected open domain containing 0 and `d(K)=b/cr(U_b,0)`. Equivalently the normalized exterior map Ψ:ℂ∖K→{|w|>1} has Ψ(z)=γz+O(1) at infinity with γ=1/d(K)>0.

Nontrivial means K contains a nonzero endpoint; the singleton hedgehog has d=0 and its inverted domain is the entire plane, which has no disc Riemann map.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), §3, Theorem 3.5 and Example 3.6, p. 185; §1, Theorem 1.9, pp. 172–173.) The leading coefficient of the exterior conformal map is the reciprocal capacity (Φ(z)=z/c+⋯, c=cap E, in (3.3)), and capacity equals the transfinite diameter. The displayed proof uses the already specified Chebyshev characterization instead of adding a general energy-minimization theory.

To prove this, the inverted domain is the plane with finitely many outward rays deleted, hence is open and star-convex at 0. Use the pinned contractibility and Riemann-mapping results. Compose its normalized map φ with the inversion to obtain Ψ(z)=1/φ(b/z); since φ(w)=φ′(0)w+O(w²), Ψ(z)=z/(bφ′(0))+O(1), so `γ=1/(bφ′(0))=cr(U_b,0)/b`.

For r>1 the level curve `Γ_r=Ψ⁻¹({|w|=r})` encloses K. The polynomial part `Q_n` of γ⁻ⁿΨⁿ is monic of degree n. Its Cauchy integral over one level curve (homologyCauchyTheorem), with different level curves compared through the cycle form of Cauchy’s theorem, gives `‖Q_n‖_K≤C_r(r/γ)^n`. The Chebyshev limit gives d(K)≤1/γ as r decreases to 1.

For every monic degree-n p, p/Ψⁿ is holomorphic on the exterior, including infinity, and tends to γ⁻ⁿ there. The maximum principle on the exterior of `Γ_r`, applied after the inversion w=1/z to a bounded domain `(Complex.norm_le_of_forall_mem_frontier_norm_le)`, yields `γ⁻ⁿ≤r⁻ⁿ‖p‖_(Γ_r)`. The curves approach K as r decreases to 1, yielding `‖p‖_K≥γ⁻ⁿ`. Take the Chebyshev limit for the reverse inequality.

**Checks.**

- For [0,a], the exterior radius relation gives d=|a|/4. The scale b is retained explicitly; taking b=R in the hedgehog comparison avoids a reciprocal-scale error.

### 6.57 The square-root branch outside a hedgehog

For a nonempty finite endpoint family `β_i∈ℂ`, put K=K(β) and `Q(w)=∏_i(1−β_i w)`. There is a unique complex formal series S with S(0)=1 and S²=Q. Off K define `G(z)=∏_i exp((1/2)log(1−β_i/z))`, using the principal log. Then G is holomorphic off K, G(z)²=Q(1/z), G tends to 1 at infinity, and G is an exterior Laurent development of the coefficients of S.

0∈K, so z⁻¹ is well-defined at every point of the holomorphy domain. Zero and repeated `β_i` are allowed. This statement produces a complex series; integer coefficients must be supplied separately by [Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)](#layer-6-topic-50).

The supporting API comprises:

- `hedgehogSqrt_square`: `G(z)²=∏_i(1−β_i/z)` for z∉K.
- `hedgehogSqrt_holomorphic`: G is holomorphic on ℂ∖K.
- `hedgehogSqrt_at_infinity`: G tends to 1 as |z| tends to infinity.
- `hedgehogSqrt_coeff_unique`: The formal square equation and constant coefficient 1 uniquely determine S.
- `hedgehogSqrt_continuation`: The convergent Laurent germ of G has exactly the coefficients of that formal S.
- `hedgehogSqrt_integer_import`: When the normalized square equation is supplied by the integer-series construction of [Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)](#layer-6-topic-50), the complex coefficients equal its integer casts.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), §4, proof of Theorem 1, p. 15.) The cuts join 0 to the roots of P₂ and P₄, making the normalized square root single-valued outside their hedgehog.

To prove this, if `z∉[0,β_i]`, then `1−β_i/z` avoids the nonpositive real ray. Indeed a nonpositive real value would make z a real multiple `tβ_i` with 0<t≤1. Thus each principal-log factor is holomorphic outside K (DifferentiableAt.clog), and exp(log u)=u gives its square.

For |z| larger than every `|β_i|` the usual normalized analytic square root has a convergent expansion at infinity. The coefficient recursion `2s_m=q_m−Σ_(0<j<m)s_js_(m−j)` uniquely specifies S over ℂ. Hence the analytic branch and the formal normalized square root have identical coefficients.

Multiply finitely many factors. Every factor tends to 1 at infinity; this fixes the sign of the square root.

**Checks.**

- For β=1, G(2)=sqrt(1/2)>0 and G(−1)=sqrt 2>0.
- With all `β_i=0`, K={0}, Q=1 and G=1.
- For endpoints 1,1 the normalized branch is G(z)=1−1/z, not its negative.
- For one β=1 there is no global single-valued holomorphic square root on ℂ∖{0,1}; a loop around the simple branch point changes its sign.
- No free choice of signs on separate factors is allowed: the value at infinity is 1.

### 6.58 Salem numbers inside ℚ(τ)

Let τ and τ′ be Salem numbers with τ′ ∈ ℚ(τ). Then ℚ(τ′) = ℚ(τ), and if τ′ > τ then τ′/τ is a Salem number (in ℚ(τ)).

Both τ, τ′ Salem; the statement uses that a Salem number has a non-real conjugate (it fails for the quadratic units, which have none).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proposition 3(ii), p. 3 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement; the proof on pp. 3-4 is the result's proof steps.

To prove this, write τ′ = p(α) + τ q(α) with p, q ∈ ℚ[X], α = τ + τ⁻¹ ([Salem numbers through their traces τ + τ⁻¹](#layer-6-topic-46): [ℚ(τ) : ℚ(α)] = 2).

If k = [ℚ(τ) : ℚ(τ′)] > 1, then k of the values p(αᵢ) + τᵢ q(αᵢ) over the conjugates τᵢ equal τ′ and k equal τ′⁻¹, so one of them with τᵢ non-real is real, forcing q(αᵢ) = 0, hence q(α) = 0 and τ′ = p(α) totally real, a contradiction. So ℚ(τ′) = ℚ(τ).

Let σ be the embedding of ℚ(τ) with σ(τ) = τ⁻¹ (an automorphism, as τ⁻¹ ∈ ℚ(τ)); it fixes α, so σ(τ′) = p(α) + τ⁻¹q(α) is real. The real conjugates of the Salem number τ′ are τ′ and τ′⁻¹ only. σ(τ′) = τ′ would give σ = id on ℚ(τ′) = ℚ(τ), contradicting σ(τ) = τ⁻¹ ≠ τ. So σ(τ′) = τ′⁻¹ and τ′/τ is conjugate to its inverse.

The only conjugate of τ′τ⁻¹ outside the closed disc is τ′τ⁻¹ itself (a conjugate τ′₁τ₁⁻¹ outside needs τ′₁ = τ′, then τ₁ = τ, or τ₁ = τ⁻¹, then τ′₁ = τ′⁻¹ and the value is ττ′⁻¹ < 1); with the pairing, all other conjugates lie on the circle: τ′/τ is a Salem number ([Salem's lemma: the conjugates of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-24)). Some conjugate lies on the circle: an embedding sending τ to a point of the circle (deg τ ≥ 4) cannot send τ′ to `τ′^{±1}`, so it sends τ′ to a circle point, and the quotient has modulus 1.

**Checks.**

- τ₁₀² ∈ ℚ(τ₁₀) generates ℚ(τ₁₀) and τ₁₀²/τ₁₀ = τ₁₀ is Salem.

### 6.59 Lehmer's number is a Salem number

τ₁₀ is a Salem number and its minimal polynomial is L = X¹⁰ + X⁹ − X⁷ − X⁶ − X⁵ − X⁴ − X³ + X + 1; in particular deg τ₁₀ = 10 and M(τ₁₀) = τ₁₀.

No numerical root finding: the criterion is the table of values of Q(y) = y⁵ + y⁴ − 5y³ − 5y² + 4y + 3 at −19/10, −3/2, −1, −1/2, 1/2, 1, 2, 21/10, which shows sign changes in (−19/10, −3/2), (−3/2, −1), (−1, −1/2), (1/2, 1) and (2, 21/10).

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Section 2, p. 5 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 8.1, printed p. 335.) Same statement, with the Mahler measure.

To prove this, α₁₀ = τ₁₀ + τ₁₀⁻¹ is a root of the monic integer polynomial Q (`lehmerNumber_add_inv_isRoot`); the other four roots of Q lie in (−2, 2) by the sign changes, so every other conjugate of α₁₀ (a root of minpoly ℤ α₁₀, which divides Q) is real in (−2, 2).

α₁₀ ∈ (2, 21/10) is not an integer, hence irrational (an algebraic integer that is rational is an integer).

τ₁₀ is a Salem number by [Salem numbers through their traces τ + τ⁻¹](#layer-6-topic-46).

minpoly ℤ α₁₀ = Q: Q has no rational root (the candidates ±1, ±3 are not roots) and no quadratic factor over ℤ (Q mod 2 = y⁵ + y⁴ + y³ + y² + 1 has no root in 𝔽₂ and is not divisible by y² + y + 1, the only irreducible quadratic over 𝔽₂), so deg α₁₀ = 5; deg τ₁₀ = 2 deg α₁₀ = 10 ([Salem numbers through their traces τ + τ⁻¹](#layer-6-topic-46)), and minpoly ℤ τ₁₀ divides the degree-10 monic L, so they are equal.

**Checks.**

- deg τ₁₀ = 10, and L is irreducible over ℚ.

### 6.60 Dobrowolski's lower bound for the Mahler measure

Let α be a nonzero algebraic number of degree d ≥ 2 that is not a root of unity. Then M(α) ≥ 1 + (1/11700)·(log log d / log d)³. Here M(α) is the Mahler measure of the primitive minimal polynomial (TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §§0.1–0.2), equal to `absMulHeight₁(α)^d`; equivalently d·h(α) ≥ log(1 + (1/11700)(log log d/log d)³).

d ≥ 2 (for d = 2 the right-hand side is below 1, since log log 2 < 0, and the statement is immediate). The constant 1/11700 is the one Berrevoets proves; Dobrowolski's own constant 1/1200 and Voutier's 1/4 (Smyth's survey, (11) and Section 4.2) are stronger and are not targets of this result.

(O. B. Berrevoets, [On Lehmer's problem (bachelor thesis, supervisor J.-H. Evertse)](#reference-berrevoets-lehmer-2016), Theorem 4.1, printed p. 15.) The constant and statement agree. The proof sketch supplies degree padding, the N+1 correction in the sum bound, and an independent calculation with the rounded M that still yields 1/11700; it does not assert a proof of the remaining supplier inputs.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 4.2, (11), printed p. 326.) The stronger original constant is 1/1200.

To prove this, non-integral α: the leading coefficient a₀ ≥ 2 of the primitive minimal polynomial gives M(α) ≥ 2 (`leadingCoeff_le_mahlerMeasure` of TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.2) . Assume α integral.

d ≤ 20: M(α) ≥ ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²) ≥ 1 + 1/(4e·400) > 1 + (1/11700)(1/e)³ ≥ the bound, since log log x/log x ≤ 1/e ([Dobrowolski's house bound ⌈α⌉ > 1 + 1/(4ed²)](#layer-6-topic-49), [Mahler measure versus house](#layer-6-topic-6)).

If deg αⁿ < d for some n, pass to β of [Reduction when a power of α has smaller degree](#layer-6-topic-11) and use strong induction on d: for deg β ≥ 21 the bound is non-increasing in the degree (log log x/log x decreases for `x ≥ e^e`), for 2 ≤ deg β ≤ 20 use the previous step, for deg β = 1 M(β) = |β| ≥ 2 . Assume deg αⁿ = d for all n ≥ 1.

d ≥ 21: M := ⌈7 log d/log log d⌉ (≥ 20), N := dM². [Dobrowolski's auxiliary polynomial](#layer-6-topic-12) gives F; [A prime p with `F(α^p) ≠ 0` in a dyadic range](#layer-6-topic-34) gives a prime p ∈ (3M² log M², 6M² log M²] with `F(α^p) ≠ 0`. Replace F by `X^(N−natDegree F)·F` so its degree is exactly N before invoking [A prime p with `F(α^p) ≠ 0` in a dyadic range](#layer-6-topic-34). Since α≠0, this preserves the zero multiplicity, coefficient maximum, and nonvanishing at each `α^p`.

Upper bound: `|N(F(α^p))| ≤ ‖F‖^d M(α)^{pN}` (each `|F(σ_k α^p)| ≤ ‖F‖ max(1, |σ_k α|)^{pN}`).

Lower bound: `F = f_α^M g` with g ∈ ℤ[X], so `N(F(α^p)) = N(f_α(α^p))^M N(g(α^p))` is a nonzero integer divisible by `p^{dM}` ([`N(f_α(α^p))` is divisible by `p^d`](#layer-6-topic-33)).

Using `||F||_1 <= (N+1)*max_i|F_i|` gives `(2M+pM^2)log M`(alpha) >= M log p-log(N+1)-2 log N. Put u=log log d and L=log d/u. For d>=21, elementary differentiation shows (d-1)log log d/log d is increasing, while 7 log 21/log log 21<20; hence M=ceil(7L)<=d-1. Also L is increasing on this range and 7 log 21/log log 21>19, so M>=20. Since L>=e, M<=7L+1<=(7+1/e)L. It follows that `N+1<=d^3` and log(N+1)+2 log N<=9 log d. The inequality log u<=u/7+log 7-1 gives log M>=log 7+u-log u>=6u/7+1, and 9 log d<=(3/2)M log M. The prime range gives log p>2 log M and `p<=12M^2 log M`. The numerator is therefore >=(1/2)M log M, and `2M+pM^2<=13M^4 log M`. Thus log M(alpha)`>=1/(26M^3) >=(u/log d)^3/[26(7+1/e)^3]>(u/log d)^3/11700`, because e>2 and `26*(15/2)^3=10968.75<11700`. ### 6.61 The cubic condition in Smyth’s long-gap case

Under the preceding Schur-pair assumptions, except that F need not be non-polynomial, write `F=Σa_m z^m`, let k be the first positive index with `a_k≠0`, and suppose `|a_k|=1` and `a_m=0` for every m with k<m≤2k. Then c³+c²≤1. If the second nonzero index equals 2k, replacing F by F⁻¹ and interchanging the Schur pair produces the same case after ruling out a coefficient of magnitude 2.

3/4≤c<1; `|a_k|=1` at the first nonzero positive index k; `a_m=0` for k<m≤2k. The computation uses no coefficient beyond index 2k, so it also applies to the inverse series F⁻¹ in the swap, which may be a polynomial.

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §5, (6)–(7) and the final minimization, pp. 174–175.) The doubled-index coefficient restrictions give the cubic condition after a one-variable minimization.

To prove this, put S=1−c². For `a_k=1` write `x=u_k≥0` and `v_k=x−c≤0`; then c−S≤x≤S and `u_(2k)−v_(2k)=x−c`.

The lower Schur bound for `u_(2k)` and upper bound for `v_(2k)` give J(x)=x²/(1+c)+(c−x)²/(1−c)+(c−x)≤2S. For `a_k=−1` the same expression follows by replacing the positive-coefficient variable by its complementary value c−x.

J is decreasing on [c−S,S]: its derivative has numerator at most 3−5c²−2c<0 for c≥3/4. Thus J(S)≤2S. The identity J(S)−2S=(c³+c²−1)/(1−c) proves the conclusion.

When l=2k, the inverse quotient has coefficient `a_k²−a_(2k)=1−a_(2k)`. The value 2 contradicts the reduction bound at its second nonzero coefficient; the value 0 gives the normalized long-gap case. Do not swap a second time just to set `a_k=1`, since this would restore `a_(2k)=1`.

**Checks.**

- The exact endpoint identity uses 1−c>0.
- The sign `a_k=−1` is included; normalizing l>2k and then swapping again would invalidate the normalization.

### 6.62 The quartic condition in Smyth’s short-gap case

### 6.63 Integrality of the Mahler measure of a monic integer polynomial

For a monic P∈ℤ[X], M(P), regarded as a real algebraic number, is integral over ℤ. In the Schur reduction for an irreducible nonreciprocal P with M(P)≤4/3, the weak bound M(P)≥(1+√17)/4 is therefore strict.

(C. J. Smyth, [On the Product of the Conjugates outside the unit circle of an Algebraic Integer](#reference-smyth-1971), §3, p. 172, strictness after the first quadratic bound.) The first bound is strict because a Mahler measure is integral but the quadratic endpoint is not.

To prove this, every complex root α is integral, as is its complex conjugate because P has real coefficients. Thus |α|²=α·conj(α) is integral; integrality of a positive power implies integrality of |α| in ℂ. Reflect integrality along the injective map `ℝ→ℂ (isIntegral_algebraMap_iff)`.

The root-product formula expresses M(P) as a finite product of 1 and |α|, hence as an integral element.

The quadratic number (1+√17)/4 has irreducible primitive polynomial 2T²−T−2 and field trace 1/2; it is not integral. Use this exclusion after the weak coefficient bound.

**Checks.**

- The claim is for monic integer P; it is not asserted for arbitrary complex polynomials.

### 6.64 A regular lemniscate enclosing a compact set

Given nonempty compact K⊆ℂ and r>d(K), there exist m≥1, a monic degree-m P, and ρ with d(K)<ρ<r such that `‖P‖_K<ρ^m` and `L={z:|P(z)|≤ρ^m}` contains K in its interior. The level `ρ^m` avoids the absolute values of the nonzero critical values of P; ∂L is a finite union of smooth analytic closed curves, positively oriented with total winding number 1 about every point of L°. Also d(L)=ρ<r. For every j≥0 there is a monic degree-`j Q_j` and a constant C independent of j such that `‖Q_j‖_L≤Cρ^j`.

r>d(K)≥0 implies r>0. No positive-capacity assumption on K is imposed. The enclosure is not asserted to lie in an arbitrarily small Euclidean neighbourhood of K; holes may be filled.

The supporting API comprises:

- `lemniscateEnclosure_subset_interior`: K⊆L° follows from the strict polynomial-norm inequality.
- `lemniscateEnclosure_diameter`: d(L)=ρ<r.
- `lemniscateEnclosure_boundary`: The chosen regular boundary is a finite analytic cycle enclosing every point of K with index 1.
- `lemniscateEnclosure_monic_basis`: `Q_(qm+s)=P^q X^s` is monic of degree qm+s and obeys the common exponential bound.
- `lemniscateEnclosure_contour_bound`: For continuous G on ∂L there is B with `|(2πi)⁻¹∮_(∂L)GQ_iQ_j dz|≤Bρ^(i+j)`.

(Françoise Bertrandias, [Diamètre transfini dans un corps valué. Application au prolongement analytique](#reference-bertrandias-1964), 1.4.6, p. 2; §2.6, pp. 10–12.) 1.4.6 encloses a bounded set in a polynomial lemniscate of nearly the same diameter (its multiplicative form fails for diameter zero; the additive form is used here), and §2.6 uses such an enclosure and its Chebyshev polynomials in the non-archimedean determinant estimate. The additive formulation here includes capacity-zero sets.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), §4, proof of Theorem 4, pp. 13–14.) Chebyshev polynomials on a boundary enclosing the singularity set provide the n²-growth estimate.

(E. B. Saff, [Logarithmic Potential Theory with Applications to Approximation Theory](#reference-saff-2010), exercises after Theorem 1.18, p. 178.) Every compact set lies in a lemniscate of capacity below its own capacity plus ε, which is the additive form used here.

To prove this, choose a degree m with `t_m(K)^(1/m)<r` and a monic P attaining that norm. Choose ρ strictly between its norm root and r, and above d(K), avoiding finitely many critical-value radii.

Properness and regularity of the polynomial level set give the compact enclosure, the strict interior inclusion and its finite analytic boundary. Apply the monic inverse-image formula to the radius-`ρ^m disc`.

For j=qm+s, 0≤s<m, use `Q_j=P^q X^s`. On L its norm is at most `ρ^(mq) max_(z∈L)|z|^s`; take `C=max_(0≤s<m) max(1,max_(z∈L)|z|^s ρ^(−s))`.

**Checks.**

- For K={0}, P=X and ρ>0 give d(L)=ρ; no multiplicative bound (1+ε)d(K) can describe this enclosure.
- P=X² and ρ=1 give L=closedBall(0,1), d(L)=1 and `Q_j=X^j`.
- For K=closedBall(0,1), P=X and ρ=1, K is not contained in L°; the strict norm hypothesis is necessary.
- For K={0} and r>0, choose P=X and 0<ρ<r: a positive-capacity enclosure is needed even though d(K)=0.

### 6.65 The small-inner-disc capacity asymptotic

Let D be a bounded simply connected radial slit disc containing 0, and `c_D=cr(D,0)`. For 0<ε sufficiently small put `C_D(ε)=Cap_D(ℂ∖D,closedBall(0,ε))`. Then `2π/C_D(ε)=log(1/ε)+log(c_D)+o(1)` as ε→0+. In particular `C_D(ε)≤C_E(ε)` for all sufficiently small ε implies cr(D,0)≥cr(E,0).

D and E have the specified finite slit geometry and contain 0. Capacity is finite and positive for these separated plates.

(V. N. Dubinin, [On the change in harmonic measure under symmetrization](#reference-dubinin-1985), §1 corollary proof, pp. 270–271.) The corollary’s proof compares condensers bounded by conformal images of concentric circles, using Grötzsch’s lemma, and lets the inner radius tend to 0 (pp. 270–271); the asymptotic here packages that limit.

To prove this, use the normalized Riemann map φ with `φ′(0)=1/c_D`. Its image of the small inner disc is sandwiched between concentric discs of radii `ε/c_D·(1±o(1))`, from uniform differentiability and the inverse-map expansion.

Conformal invariance and plate monotonicity sandwich the capacity between the two explicit annulus capacities. Taking reciprocals yields the asserted asymptotic with the plus sign in front of `log(c_D)`.

For the comparison, take reciprocal capacities, subtract log(1/ε), and pass to the limit.

### 6.66 The Salem numbers of a field are the powers of one of them

If K = ℚ(τ) for a Salem number τ, there is a Salem number τ₁ ∈ K such that the Salem numbers in K are exactly the powers τ₁ⁿ, n ≥ 1.

K generated by a Salem number.

(Chris Smyth, [Seventy years of Salem numbers](#reference-smyth-salem-survey-2015), Proposition 3(iii) and its proof, p. 4 (arXiv v3).) Exactly the statement; the finiteness step is the source's remark that the minimal polynomials can take only finitely many values.

To prove this, the Salem numbers of K below τ are finitely many: they are algebraic integers of degree ≤ [K : ℚ] all of whose conjugates have modulus ≤ τ (Northcott for the house, TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §0.3, or Mathlib's `NumberField.Embeddings.finite_of_norm_le` in K). Let τ₁ be the smallest.

Powers of τ₁ are Salem numbers in K ([Powers of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-25)). (Equivalently: a Salem number τ′ ≤ τ has M(τ′) = τ′ ≤ τ and degree ≤ [K : ℚ], and `Polynomial.finite_mahlerMeasure_le` leaves finitely many minimal polynomials.)

For a Salem number τ′ ∈ K we have τ′ ≥ τ₁, so choose r ≥ 1 with `τ₁^r ≤ τ′ < τ₁^{r+1}`. By [Salem numbers inside ℚ(τ)](#layer-6-topic-58), ℚ(τ₁) = K, and `τ₁^r` is a Salem number of degree [K : ℚ] ([Powers of a Salem number](#layer-6-topic-25)), so `ℚ(τ₁^r) = K ∋ τ′`. If `τ₁^r < τ′`, [Salem numbers inside ℚ(τ)](#layer-6-topic-58) gives that `τ′τ₁^{−r}` is a Salem number in K, smaller than τ₁, a contradiction; so `τ′ = τ₁^r`.

**Checks.**

- For the quartic example τ = 2.1537…, the Salem numbers of ℚ(τ) are the τⁿ, n ≥ 1, τ being the smallest one (Smyth, p. 13); the reciprocal quadratic unit τ + τ⁻¹ = (3 + √5)/2 ∈ ℚ(τ) is not among them.

The determinant expansion has n! terms; in every term `Σ_i(i+σ(i))=n(n−1)`. This gives the stated bound (enlarge B if needed and use ρ<r). Take n²th roots; log(n!)/n² and log(B)/n tend to zero, then let r decrease to d(K).

### 6.72 Bertrandias’s integer Laurent rationality criterion

Let a:ℕ→ℤ, and suppose its complex coefficient casts have an exterior Laurent development outside a nonempty compact K⊆ℂ with d(K)<1. If ℂ∖K is connected, the development agrees there with that rational germ wherever its expression in 1/z is defined.

The archimedean small-diameter development condition forces the integer Hankel determinants to vanish. Bertrandias allows rational coefficients integral outside finitely many primes and assumes a simply connected complement; the integer case here needs no connectedness, since the lemniscate-contour estimate does not use it.

To prove this, choose d(K)<r<1. The analytic estimate gives `|D_n|≤n!B^n r^(n(n−1))`, which tends to zero because its logarithm has a negative quadratic leading term.

Each complex determinant is the cast of an integer determinant. For sufficiently large n its norm is below 1, so the integer determinant is zero. Transfer zero to ℚ and apply Kronecker’s criterion over ℚ.

On a connected complement, the identity theorem extends the equality of the rational germ and G away from poles and z=0; removable points are interpreted through G.

**Checks.**

- The criterion applies to K={2} of diameter 0 for G=1/(z−2), despite a finite pole. K=[0,1] has diameter 1/4, but the normalized square-root example is excluded by its noninteger coefficients.

### 6.73 Siegel's theorem: θ₀ is the smallest Pisot number

Every Pisot number θ satisfies θ ≥ θ₀; θ₀ itself is a Pisot number.

θ Pisot, of any degree.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 5.1, printed p. 328.) The statement (Siegel); the proof given here derives it from Smyth's theorem, as the survey's remark on the spectrum (p. 328) indicates.

(Varun Srivastava and Sanjay Gollapudi, [Pisot numbers (Euler Circle student paper)](#reference-srivastava-pisot-2018), Section 6, Theorem 12, p. 2.) Same statement (the source's polynomial x³ − x + 1 is a misprint).

To prove this, θ₀ is Pisot (`isPisot_plasticNumber` of [The smallest Pisot number θ₀](#layer-6-topic-48)).

If θ is conjugate to θ⁻¹ then θ ≥ (3 + √5)/2 > θ₀ ([Reciprocal Pisot numbers are quadratic units](#layer-6-topic-28)).

Otherwise θ is a nonzero nonreciprocal algebraic integer, so θ = M(θ) ≥ θ₀ by Smyth's theorem ([M(τ) = house(τ) = τ for Pisot and Salem numbers](#layer-6-topic-4), [Smyth's theorem: M(α) ≥ θ₀ for nonreciprocal α](#layer-6-topic-70)).

Degree one: θ = n ≥ 2 > θ₀ (covered by the previous step, n being nonreciprocal).

**Checks.**

- θ₀ < φ < 2 < (3 + √5)/2: the Pisot numbers φ, 2 and (3 + √5)/2 are all strictly larger than θ₀, while θ₀ itself is Pisot (equality holds only at θ = θ₀).

**Auxiliary proof target.** Minimality uses the nonreciprocal lower bound and therefore its short-gap multiplier obligation. Verifying that X³−X−1 defines the plastic Pisot number does not by itself prove minimality among Pisot numbers.

### 6.74 The capacity-to-rationality input of Dimitrov’s bound

For n≥1, endpoints β₁,…,`β_n`, and an integer formal series S with S(0)=1 and `S²=∏_i(1−β_i w)` after casting to ℂ, if `R=max_i|β_i|` satisfies `R^n<4`, then S is rational over ℚ. In the Schinzel–Zassenhaus argument of [Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture](#layer-6-topic-75) use `β=(α_i²,α_i⁴)`, n=2d: if the house H>1 obeys `H<2^(1/(4d))`, then R≤H⁴ and `R^(2d)<4`, so this theorem makes the normalized integral square root of [Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)](#layer-6-topic-50) rational.

The integer square-root hypothesis is explicit and supplied by [Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)](#layer-6-topic-50). The displayed house substitution concerns the unit case H>1 used in the degree induction of [Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture](#layer-6-topic-75).

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), §4, proof of Theorem 1, pp. 15–16, after Corollary 5.) The strict capacity bound makes the normalized integral square root rational; the algebraic part then forces cyclotomicity or a smaller-degree contradiction.

To prove this, the hedgehog square-root construction gives the exterior development of the integer coefficient casts. Dubinin’s bound and `R^n<4` imply d(K)<1. Apply Bertrandias’s rationality criterion.

For a rational square root S of a polynomial, every irreducible factor of that polynomial has even valuation. The normalized reciprocal root product therefore corresponds to a square product P₂P₄ in the algebraic argument of [Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture](#layer-6-topic-75): P₂*P₄* has degree 2d and constant term 1, so a polynomial S with S²=P₂*P₄* has degree d, and `X^dS(1/X)` squares to `X^(2d)P₂*P₄*(1/X)=P₂P₄`; the same reversal goes back.

This analytic result feeds the degree induction of [Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture](#layer-6-topic-75) and the corrected square-cyclotomic criterion of [When P₂P₄ is a square (Dimitrov Lemma 2.3)](#layer-6-topic-36); it is not a second Schinzel–Zassenhaus theorem.

**Checks.**

- For d=1 the threshold in the contradiction is `H<2^(1/4)`, and the estimate uses 2d segments, not d. A rational square-root branch does not alone prove cyclotomicity; the arithmetic induction of [Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture](#layer-6-topic-75) is required.

### 6.75 Dimitrov's theorem: the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture

Let P ∈ ℤ[X] be monic irreducible of degree n > 1 and not cyclotomic. Then P has a complex root of modulus at least `2^{1/(4n)} = 1 + log 2/(4n) + O(1/n²)`. Equivalently, a nonzero algebraic integer α of degree n > 1 that is not a root of unity has `⌈α⌉ ≥ 2^{1/(4n)}`.

Cyclotomic means `P = Φ_N` for some N, i.e. its roots are roots of unity. This settles the Schinzel–Zassenhaus conjecture ⌈α⌉ ≥ 1 + c/d (Smyth's (8)) with c = (log 2)/4 in every degree: `2^{1/(4n)} = exp(log 2/(4n)) > 1 + log 2/(4n) (Real.add_one_le_exp)`, and in degree 1 a nonzero integer other than ±1 has modulus ≥ 2.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Theorem 1, p. 1 (arXiv v1).) Exactly the statement.

(Vesselin Dimitrov, [A proof of the Schinzel-Zassenhaus conjecture on polynomials](#reference-dimitrov-2019), Proof of Theorem 1, pp. 15-16.) The analytic core, whose inputs (Theorem 3 of Dubinin, Corollary 5 of Bertrandias) are the required auxiliary target.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 3, (8), printed p. 325.) The conjecture that the theorem settles.

To prove this, suppose all roots have modulus `< 2^{1/(4n)}`. Reverse: P* = ∏(1 − αᵢX), P*(0) = 1; P₂*, P₄* are the reverses of P₂, P₄ ([The polynomial `P_m = ∏(X − αᵢ^m)`](#layer-6-topic-13)).

f(1/X) := √(P₂*(1/X) P₄*(1/X)) ∈ ℤ⟦1/X⟧ ([Square roots with integer coefficients (Dimitrov Proposition 2.2)](#layer-6-topic-50)).

f continues analytically to the complement of the hedgehog K = union of the segments [0, αᵢ²], [0, αᵢ⁴], whose transfinite diameter is `≤ (max|αᵢ|^{8n}/4)^{1/(2n)} < 1` by Dubinin's theorem ([Finite Fekete diameters and transfinite diameter](#layer-6-topic-18) and [Dubinin’s radial hedgehog bound](#layer-6-topic-71); the development is [The square-root branch outside a hedgehog](#layer-6-topic-57) and the rationality [Bertrandias’s integer Laurent rationality criterion](#layer-6-topic-72)).

By Bertrandias's rationality theorem (Pólya–Carlson type: an integer power series in 1/X analytic off a compact set of transfinite diameter < 1 is rational; gap) f is rational, so P₂P₄ is a square.

If P₂ is not a square, [When P₂P₄ is a square (Dimitrov Lemma 2.3)](#layer-6-topic-36) makes P cyclotomic, a contradiction.

If P₂ is a square, P₂ = Q² with Q = minpoly α₁², deg Q = n/2, roots αᵢ²; Q is not cyclotomic. If n/2 > 1, induction gives a root of Q of modulus `≥ 2^{1/(2n)}`, i.e. `|αᵢ| ≥ 2^{1/(4n)}`; if n/2 = 1, Q = X − b with |b| ≥ 2 and `|αᵢ| = √|b| ≥ 2^{1/8}` (the base case the source omits).

**Checks.**

- P = X² − X − 1: `max|α| = φ ≥ 2^{1/8} = 1.0905`.
- Lehmer's L (n = 10): `τ₁₀ = 1.1763 ≥ 2^{1/40} = 1.0175`.
- Cyclotomic `Φ_N` has all roots of modulus 1: the hypothesis cannot be dropped.

### 6.76 Totally positive trace ratios and auxiliary resultants

Define `IsTotallyPositiveAlgebraicInteger α` for α∈ℂ by integrality over ℤ and strict positivity of every complex conjugate, all of which must be real. For such α set `totallyPositiveTraceRatio α = trace(α)/degree(α)`; the degree is positive. Define `traceFiniteExceptionThreshold` as the supremum of the real λ such that, for every ε>0, only finitely many totally positive algebraic integers satisfy `trace(α)/degree(α)<λ-ε`. Use finiteness of elements, equivalently finiteness of minimal polynomials because each has finitely many roots. Require `traceRatio_conjugate`, `traceRatio_positive`, finiteness under bounded degree and bounded trace, and the downward-closed threshold property, together with nonemptiness and boundedness before applying the real supremum. This corrects the “least” direction in Smith’s introductory definition: every smaller λ also has the finite-exception property (Smith, §1, pp. 1–2). Historical formulations predicted threshold 2; Smith’s Theorem 1.1 contradicts that prediction, and its proof belongs to LogarithmicPotentialTheoryAndAlgebraicIntegers.

For a finite family of nonzero integer polynomials `Q_k`, positive real weights `a_k` and real λ, name `auxiliaryResultantTraceBound`: suppose `x≥λ+Σ a_k log|Q_k(x)|` for every positive real x at which all `Q_k(x)` are nonzero. If α is totally positive and its minimal polynomial P is coprime to every `Q_k` in ℚ[X], then `trace(α)≥λ*degree(α)`. The roots of P avoid every `Q_k`; the products of `Q_k` over those roots are nonzero integral resultants, of absolute value at least one. Sum the pointwise inequality and use positivity of the weights. A totalized `Real.log 0` must never substitute for the nonvanishing requirement (Smith, §1, (1.2) and resultant argument, pp. 2–3).

**Checks for positivity, ratio and threshold.**

- α=2 is totally positive, has degree one, trace two and ratio two; α=0 and α=−1 fail strict positivity.
- Both roots of `X²-3X+1` are positive; their trace ratio is 3/2. A finite-exception asymptotic bound must not be asserted for every individual α.
- Lowering λ preserves the finite-exception property. Taking its infimum or “least” value would therefore give the wrong direction; using α of arbitrarily large degree requires the actual bounded-degree finiteness interface.

**Checks for the auxiliary-resultant interface.**

- The empty auxiliary family gives the direct lower bound from `x≥λ` on positive x.
- A constant auxiliary polynomial 2 has resultant `2^degree(α)` and a nonnegative logarithmic contribution.
- With Q=P the resultant is zero and the coprimality hypothesis fails; this is the negative control against silently taking log zero.

*Needs:* the height and algebraic-degree interfaces of TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §§0.1–0.3; Mathlib minimal polynomials, conjugates, algebraic trace and polynomial resultants; the root multiplicity convention of Layer 3. The supremum and resultant comparison are README constructions and theorem targets.

<a id="layer-6-topic-77"></a>

### 6.77 Asymptotic Dobrowolski bounds and exceptional powering primes

State `asymptoticDobrowolskiBound`: there are absolute constants C≥1 and c≥1 such that each monic irreducible noncyclotomic D∈ℤ[X] with D(0)≠0 and degree m≥1 satisfies `M(D)≥exp(1/L(m))`, where `L(m)=2*(log m/log log m)^3` for m>C and `L(m)=c` for 1≤m≤C. Choose C large enough that both logarithms in the asymptotic expression are positive. The bounded-degree completion uses finiteness of bounded-Mahler-measure integer polynomials and the exclusion of zero and cyclotomic factors.

(Chris Smyth, [The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey](#reference-smyth-mahler-survey-2008), Section 4.2, printed p. 326.) Dobrowolski's asymptotic bound M(α) > 1 + (1 − ε)(log log d/log d)³ for d ≥ d₀(ε). With ε = 1/4 and log(1 + y) ≥ y − y²/2 it gives log M(D) ≥ (1/2)(log log m/log m)³ for large m, which is the form above. The explicit constant of [Dobrowolski's lower bound for the Mahler measure](#layer-6-topic-60) does not give this strength.

(Lior Bary-Soroker, Dimitris Koukoulopoulos and Gady Kozma, [Irreducibility of random polynomials: general measures](#reference-bskk-random-polynomials-2023), §7, p. 37 (arXiv v3).) The random-polynomial application, citing Dobrowolski. It states the stronger form with L(m) = (1/2)(log m/log log m)³. That form needs an asymptotic constant above 2, which Louboutin's 9/4 − ε supplies (Smyth's survey, same page). The application only uses that L(m) is a fixed multiple of (log m/log log m)³, so the weaker form stated here suffices.

**Auxiliary proof target.** The asymptotic constant 1 − ε is taken from the survey's statement. Its proof is Dobrowolski's (Acta Arithmetica 34 (1979), 391–401), and no source cited here gives that proof.

For nonzero algebraic α define `degreeDroppingPrimes α = {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ degree(α^p)<degree(α)}`. Require `degreeDroppingPrimes_mem_iff`, `degreeDroppingPrimes_finite` and `degreeDroppingPrimes_card_le`: for degree d≥1, the cardinality is at most `log d/log 2`. This counts exceptional primes; constructing one smaller-degree integer does not prove it (Dobrowolski, Lemma 3, used in Bary-Soroker–Koukoulopoulos–Kozma, §7, p. 37).

**Checks.**

- At d=1 there are no degree-dropping primes and the bound is zero.
- For α=√2, degree two, p=2 drops the degree to one and odd primes preserve it; the cardinal bound is exactly one.
- For a primitive eighth root of unity α, the degree is four and the exceptional set is {2}, so the cardinality is one, strictly below `log 4/log 2=2`. Roots of unity remain valid for the exceptional-prime estimate even though the Mahler lower bound excludes them.
- D=X and cyclotomic D are excluded from the Mahler bound, because their Mahler measure is one. The degree-zero polynomial 1 is also outside it; the piecewise bounded-degree clause prevents evaluating log log at m=1.

*Needs:* Layer 6 Mahler measure, conjugate-power and root-of-unity criteria; the algebraic-degree and bounded-height interfaces of TauCetiRoadmap.DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence §§0.1–0.3. The asymptotic strength and the prime-cardinality argument remain explicit proof obligations.

### Examples

The plastic polynomial X³−X−1 and Lehmer polynomial give the Pisot and Salem reference roots. Constant Schur series ±1 satisfy the closed norm bound, while 3/2 does not. A single radial segment fixes the capacity normalisation. Every computed value and negative control attached to a result above is part of its required interface.

## Layer 7: integral Galois modules and arithmetic orders

Connect tame ramification to integral normal bases, local freeness and stable arithmetic classes. Build the noncommutative order, idele, character determinant and Gauss-sum comparisons needed for the Fröhlich–Taylor equality.

<a id="layer-7-topic-0"></a>

### 7.0 Pseudobases and Steinitz classes of lattices over a Dedekind domain

Let A be a Dedekind domain with fraction field K, V an n-dimensional K-vector space and M ⊆ V an A-lattice: a finitely generated A-submodule spanning V (Mathlib's Submodule.IsLattice). (a) For every K-basis `y_1`, …, `y_n` of V there are `x_1`, …, `x_n ∈ M` and nonzero fractional ideals `𝔞_1`, …, `𝔞_n` of A with `M = 𝔞_1x_1 ⊕ ⋯ ⊕ 𝔞_nx_n` and `x_j ∈ Ky_1 + ⋯ + Ky_j` for every j (a pseudobasis). (b) The class `st(M) = [𝔞_1⋯𝔞_n] ∈ Cl(A)`, the Steinitz class, does not depend on the pseudobasis and depends only on the isomorphism class of M as an A-module; st(M ⊕ N) = st(M)·st(N), and st(M) = 1 for n = 0. (c) For n ≥ 1, dropping the triangularity condition, one may take `𝔞_1 = ⋯ = 𝔞_(n−1) = A`, so `M ≅ A^(n−1) ⊕ 𝔞` with [𝔞] = st(M); two lattices are isomorphic exactly when they have the same rank and the same Steinitz class. (d) For lattices M, N ⊆ V there is a common pseudobasis, `M = ⊕ 𝔞_ix_i` and `N = ⊕ 𝔟_ix_i`, with `𝔡_i = 𝔟_i𝔞_i^(−1)` satisfying `𝔡_1 | ⋯ | 𝔡_n`, and these invariant factors of N relative to M are unique. Consequently every A-lattice is a finitely generated projective A-module, and it is free exactly when its Steinitz class is trivial.

A is a Dedekind domain; n = 0 is allowed (empty pseudobasis). Fractional ideals are Mathlib's FractionalIdeal A⁰ K and the class group is Mathlib's ClassGroup A, not a narrow or ray class group. The isomorphism criterion in (c) uses the product identity I ⊕ J ≅ A ⊕ IJ, proved below without (c).

The supporting API comprises:

- `Lattice.exists_pseudobasis`: Part (a), for every K-basis of V.
- `Lattice.steinitzClass`: st(M) ∈ ClassGroup A for an A-lattice M.
- `Lattice.steinitzClass_congr`: Isomorphic lattices have the same Steinitz class.
- `Lattice.steinitzClass_prod`: st(M ⊕ N) = st(M)·st(N).
- `Lattice.nonempty_equiv_pi_prod_ideal`: For n ≥ 1, `M ≅ A^(n−1) ⊕ 𝔞` with [𝔞] = st(M).
- `Lattice.nonempty_equiv_iff`: M ≅ N exactly when rank M = rank N and st(M) = st(N).
- `Lattice.free_iff_steinitzClass_eq_one`: M is free exactly when st(M) = 1.
- `Lattice.exists_common_pseudobasis`: Part (d), with the divisibility chain and uniqueness of the invariant factors.

(John Voight, [Quaternion Algebras](#reference-voight-quaternion-2021), Theorem 9.3.6 with its proof, printed p. 138.) Part (a).

(John Voight, [Quaternion Algebras](#reference-voight-quaternion-2021), Theorem 9.3.9 and 9.3.10, printed p. 139.) Part (d), the definition of the Steinitz class with its well-definedness (left there as Exercise 9.7), and the decomposition with all coefficient ideals but one equal to A.

(Charles A. Weibel, [The K-book, Chapter I: Projective Modules and Vector Bundles](#reference-w-i), I§3, Propositions 3.4–3.5, pp. 17–18.) The classification of finitely generated projective modules over a Dedekind domain by rank and Steinitz class.

To prove this, (a) is induction on n: with `W = Ky_1 + ⋯ + Ky_(n−1)` and N = M ∩ W, the image of M in V/W ≅ K is a fractional ideal `𝔞_n`, which is projective, so `M ≅ N ⊕ 𝔞_nx_n`. For (b), two pseudobases differ by a matrix in `GL_n(K)` carrying one sum of ideals onto the other, so the products of the coefficient ideals differ by the principal ideal of its determinant. The product identity I ⊕ J ≅ A ⊕ IJ follows by replacing I and J by coprime representatives of their classes, so that I + J = A and I ∩ J = IJ, and splitting 0 → IJ → I ⊕ J → A → 0; applying it repeatedly gives (c). Part (d) is the elementary-divisor argument over the semilocal localisations, glued by the local–global correspondence of lattices.

**Checks.**

- A = ℤ: Cl(ℤ) = 1, so every lattice is free; in ℚ², M = 2ℤ ⊕ 3ℤ has the pseudobasis `e_1`, `e_2` with coefficient ideals (2), (3) and st(M) = 1.
- A = ℤ[√−5] and 𝔭 = (2, 1 + √−5): st(𝔭) = [𝔭] ≠ 1, so 𝔭 is not free, while st(𝔭 ⊕ 𝔭) = [𝔭]² = [(2)] = 1 and 𝔭 ⊕ 𝔭 ≅ A².
- The zero lattice (n = 0) has Steinitz class 1.
- Coefficient ideals themselves are not invariants: the lattice 2ℤ ⊆ ℚ has the pseudobases 2·1 with ideal ℤ and 1 with ideal 2ℤ; only their class is well defined.
- For M = ℤ² and N = ℤ ⊕ 6ℤ in ℚ², the invariant factors of N relative to M are (1), (6); the pair (2), (3) is not a divisibility chain.

*Needs:* Mathlib `Submodule.IsLattice`; Mathlib `FractionalIdeal`; Mathlib `ClassGroup`; Mathlib `Module.Projective`; Mathlib `IsDedekindDomain`.
