### 7.113 The root-number class in the kernel group

For tame L/F with group G define t(W) as the class of the finite-S sign homomorphism `W_G` in `D_H`, for S containing the primes dividing |G|. In the all-place presentation use `W_G` at finite places and the constant positive value 1 at infinite places. The finite numerator permits negative signs; the diagonal algebraic-unit denominator retains its positivity requirement.

The supporting API comprises:

- `RootNumberClass.representative`: The finite-S root-sign homomorphism defines t(W).
- `RootNumberClass.two_torsion`: 2t(W)=0 because `W_G²=1`.
- `RootNumberClass.no_symplectic`: If G has no symplectic irreducible, t(W)=0.
- `RootNumberClass.hom_comparison`: Under the kernel/Hom comparison t(W) is the specified positive-unit class, not the class of a negative infinite representative.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), §§1–2, Theorem1 and quotient(2.1), pp.41–44; Fröhlich (1976), Appendix II, p.430.) The symplectic sign homomorphism defines a canonical kernel-group class.

To prove this, [Tame symplectic root factors are equivariant signs](#layer-7-topic-111) gives the required equivariance and finite-unit condition. The [Positive unit homomorphisms and the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-99) equivalence transfers the finite representative to an all-place positive one. Enlarge S only through the canonical quotient comparison.

**Checks.**

- The trivial extension has t(W)=0.
- Every odd-order group has t(W)=0.
- Using the same negative symplectic sign at infinity fails the all-place positive numerator condition.
- Squaring any sign representative gives the constant-one homomorphism, hence the zero class.

*Needs:* [Tame symplectic root factors are equivariant signs](#layer-7-topic-111); [Positive unit homomorphisms and the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-99).

<a id="layer-7-topic-114"></a>

### 7.114 The tame integer-ring class lies in the maximal-order kernel

For tame L/F with finite Galois group G, `c=[O_L]−[F:Q][Z[G]]` lies in D(Z[G]). Choose `a∈O_L` generating a normal integral basis at every place of F above S={ℓ:ℓ divides |G|}, and let A be its embedding-product norm resolvend. In the S-place positive-unit quotient, `u=Det(A)·W_G·τ⁻¹` represents c. The associated all-place representative uses the archimedean positivity adjustment. This is kernel membership; equality c=t(W) needs the additional determinant theorems.

(Albrecht Fröhlich, [Arithmetic and Galois module structure for tame extensions](#reference-f76), Theorems10–11 and formula(9.4), pp.411–413; Taylor (1981), (2.2), p.44.) The local integral class is a positive unit Hom class, represented by the Gauss-corrected resolvent.

To prove this, the finite valuations cancel by [Tame norm resolvents and Gauss sums have equal finite valuations](#layer-7-topic-108) and the norm-resolvent class formula. At infinite places the symplectic determinant positivity is corrected by the normalized root signs and the infinite factors, using Fröhlich (1976), Theorem10. Apply [The Hom quotient is the actual maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-106).

**Checks.**

- G = {1}: `c = [O_F] − [F : ℚ][ℤ] = 0`.
- G abelian: there is no symplectic character, `W_G = 1`, and the representative is Det(A)·τ⁻¹.

*Needs:* [Absolute and relative norm resolvents](#layer-7-topic-100); [Tame norm resolvents and Gauss sums have equal finite valuations](#layer-7-topic-108); [Tame symplectic root factors are equivariant signs](#layer-7-topic-111); [The Hom quotient is the actual maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-106); [The Galois module class of the ring of integers](#layer-7-topic-110).

### 7.115 The Gauss logarithm lifts through the commutator ideal

**Target.** Fix distinct primes p and ℓ and a tame local extension with ℚ-ℓ-elementary group `Γ=C⋊P`, where C is cyclic of order prime to ℓ and P is an ℓ-group. Put `K=ℚ(ζ_p)` and `𝒜=𝒪_K⊗ℤ_ℓ`. For a character x of C of order n, pass to `Γ/ker x` and write C for its cyclic quotient, so x is faithful. Put `H=ker(P→Aut(C))`, `Δ=C×H`, `L=K(ζ_n)` and `B=𝒪_L⊗ℤ_ℓ`. Both K and L are unramified at ℓ. The factor of `𝒜[C]` belonging to x gives the crossed product of §7.86; its comparison with `B[H]` is the character-induction and coefficient comparison of Taylor (7.1)–(7.4). For every embedding σ of `K∩ℚ(ζ_n)` into ℚ̄, the comparison sends a character homomorphism h on the corresponding Δ-character summand to `χ↦h(x^σ·χ)`. The product over σ identifies both ambient Hom groups and integral determinant subgroups. Fix one such component, and write `f(χ)=τ_Δ*(x^σ·χ)`, with the Artin correction and additive character of §7.112.

Define the carrier before any integrality assertion. Let `U_ℓ` be the direct limit of `(𝒪_E⊗ℤ_ℓ)×` over finite number fields E in ℚ̄, and set `ℋ_L(H)=Hom_(Gal(ℚ̄/L))(R_H,U_ℓ)`: homomorphisms from the additive virtual-character group to multiplicative coefficient units, equivariant for the character and coefficient actions. The determinant subgroup `D_B(H)=Det(B[H]×)` embeds in this carrier by §7.28. For the Gauss factor, ℓ≠p gives unit values and §7.112 gives equivariance, so `f∈ℋ_L(H)` independently of determinant membership. All statements for B and its fraction algebra are interpreted componentwise over the places above ℓ.

Let `|H|=ℓ^m` and let F on `L(ζ_(ℓ^m))` restrict to arithmetic Frobenius at ℓ on L and fix `ζ_(ℓ^m)`. These requirements are compatible because L is unramified at ℓ; this particular scalar extension is part of the coefficient data. Character evaluation identifies the conjugacy-class algebra `(L⊗ℚ_ℓ)[Cl(H)]` with the equivariant additive character functions. Define `ℒ_char` on all of `ℋ_L(H)` by

    `χ(ℒ_char(h)) = log_ℓ(h(χ)^ℓ / h(ψ^ℓχ)^F)`,
    `ν_char(h) = ℒ_char(h)/ℓ`.

The ℓ-adic logarithm on algebraic coefficient units kills roots of unity. Construct this extension and prove `ℒ_char(Det u)=L(u)` on the augmentation units of §7.46, hence `ν_char(Det u)=ν(Det u)` in that section's normalized convention. Prove that `Det(1+rad(B[H]))` has finite index in `ℋ_L(H)`, and that `ker ν_char=ℋ_L(H)_tors`. In particular this is the torsion of the full character carrier; the equality with `Det(H)` in §7.73 applies only after restriction to its integral augmentation determinant subgroup.

Let I be the cyclic inertia subgroup of H, `A_H=ker(B[H]→B[Hᵃᵇ])`, and `Cl_I(H)` the H-conjugacy classes represented by elements of I. Prove `ℒ_char(f)∈ℓ B[Cl_I(H)]`. There is `T′∈B[I]×` whose determinant agrees with f on every linear character, and there is `z∈(1+A_H)∩B[I]×` with `ν_char(f/Det T′)=ν_char(Det z)`. Thus for `d=Det(zT′)` the exact pre-integrality conclusion is

    `q=f/d ∈ ℋ_L(H)_tors`,   q(λ)=1 for every linear character λ.

No integral-determinant membership of q is asserted here. Its triviality is the congruence theorem of §7.118.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), §4 (4.2)–(4.5), pp.50–51; §7 (7.1)–(7.4), pp.54–56, Propositions7.5–7.7 and (7.10), pp.57–59; §8 Proposition8.1, Corollary8.2 and Theorem5, pp.62–65.) Taylor extends the logarithm to the full unit-valued Hom group and leaves its torsion subgroup at (7.10). His unnormalized `ν_H` is `ℒ_char`, whereas §7.46 uses `ν=L/ℓ`.

To prove this, character idempotents and sufficiently small principal units give the finite-index determinant subgroup; extend its logarithm by division by the finite index in the characteristic-zero class algebra. The internal determinant kernel theorem, together with the scalar unit logarithm, then identifies the ambient kernel with ambient torsion, without identifying that torsion with group-element determinants. Use the weak Hasse–Davenport relation, equality up to roots of unity, for Taylor's inertia coefficient calculation. Fourier inversion lifts the abelian restriction. Saturation of the commutator class image and §7.73 lift the remaining integral logarithm with its inertia support; this use of §7.73 is entirely inside its determinant domain.

**Checks.**

- H abelian: `A_H=0`, `z=1`, and the abelian lift already gives `f=Det T′` on every character, so `q=1`.
- For `B=ℤ₂`, `H=C₂` and the nontrivial element s, `Det(s)` has zero `ν_char` and sign-character value −1. The ambient logarithm retains torsion.
- For `B=ℤ₂`, `H=Q₈`, the homomorphism with value 1 on all four linear irreducibles and −1 on the faithful degree-two irreducible has zero `ν_char` and trivial abelian restriction. It is outside `Det(H)`; the full rejection test is in §7.118.
- On integral augmentation determinants, `ℒ_char=ℓν` with §7.46's normalization; replacing the coefficient Frobenius by an action on character roots would change the comparison.

### 7.116 The diagonal tame norm-resolvent factor is a determinant unit

For tame L/F with group G, `choose a∈O_L` that is an integral normal generator at every place over S={ℓ:ℓ divides |G|}; let A be its embedding-product norm resolvend as in Taylor (2.2). For each ℓ∈S there is a finite Galois E/Q such that `(y′_ℓ)⁻¹Det(A)∏_(𝔭|ℓ)τ_(G,𝔭)⁻¹` belongs to `Det(∏_(𝔮|ℓ)(O_(E_𝔮)^P_𝔮[G])×)`, with `P_𝔮` the wild inertia subgroup of `Gal(E_𝔮/Q_ℓ)`. Here `y′_ℓ` is the product of Taylor's global correction factors from p.49: at primes ramified in the normal closure of L/Q these are transferred from `y_p⁻¹Det(c_p)`; at unramified rational primes both `y′_p` and the corresponding global `τ_p` are chosen as 1. This convention distinguishes y′ from the local y of §7.112. The coefficient ring is the ring fixed by wild inertia, hence a tame local coefficient extension; no unspecified inertia-norm modification is part of the statement.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Theorem2(a), p.45; §3, global correction after Theorem3, p.49; §11 (proof of Theorem2(a)), (11.1)–(11.10) and Proposition11.6, pp.75–78; Fröhlich (1976), Theorem6 and its Corollaries1–2, pp.396–399.) The diagonal factor of the integral embedding norm resolvend is a group-ring determinant over the wild-inertia fixed integer rings.

To prove this, pass to a tame extension that splits cyclic inertia and contains the required roots of unity. Compare the inertia eigenresolvents with residue Gauss sums; [Tame norm resolvents and Gauss sums have equal finite valuations](#layer-7-topic-108) gives unit coefficients. Unramified character twisting identifies the ratios on the cyclic inertia factors. Use the tame norm/base-change compatibility of Fröhlich (1976), Theorem6 to reassemble the induced module; Taylor §11 then identifies the resulting unit as an integral group-ring determinant. Fröhlich’s (1976) valuation proof supplies this valuation comparison; the additional 1980 local unit identities are specified separately below.

**Checks.**

- Take L=ℚ(ζ₃), F=ℚ, G=⟨σ⟩=C₂ and a=ζ₃. Then S={2}. Since 2 is unramified, Taylor's y′₂ and global τ₂ are 1. With δ=ζ₃−ζ₃², the diagonal factor Det(ζ₃+ζ₃²σ) has trivial/sign values (−1,δ).
- The regular determinant of ζ₃+ζ₃²σ is ζ₃²−ζ₃=−δ. Since δ²=−3, it is a 2-adic unit. Thus the element is in `O_{ℚ₂(ζ₃)}[C₂]×`; the coefficient extension is unramified at 2, so its wild inertia is trivial.
- Multiplication by −σ, an integral group-ring unit, gives u=(1+ζ₃)−ζ₃σ with character values (1,δ) and regular determinant δ. This also checks the normalization in which the trivial-character value is 1.

*Needs:* [Absolute and relative norm resolvents](#layer-7-topic-100); [Adjusted tame Gauss homomorphisms](#layer-7-topic-112); [Tame norm resolvents and Gauss sums have equal finite valuations](#layer-7-topic-108); [Local rational Brauer reduction for determinant quotients](#layer-7-topic-63); [Noether's theorem for local fields](#layer-7-topic-88).

### 7.117 Fröhlich: the Galois module class lies in the kernel group

Let M/N be a tame Galois extension of number fields with group Γ, and 𝔐 a maximal order of ℚΓ containing ℤΓ. Then `[𝓞_M]_ℤ ∈ D(ℤΓ) = ker(Cl(ℤΓ) → Cl(𝔐))`: `𝓞_M` becomes stably free over 𝔐.

M/N tame Galois; 𝔐 ⊇ ℤΓ maximal.

(M. J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich's conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Section 2 (printed p. 44).) Taylor states kernel membership; prove it through [The Hom quotient is the actual maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-106) and [The tame integer-ring class lies in the maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-114).

To prove this, fröhlich's proof (his paper J. reine angew. Math. 286 (1976) 380–440, Taylor's [F1], with Appendix 11.2 for the Hom-description; Taylor p. 44 states the membership without proof) runs through Fröhlich's Hom-description of Cl(ℤΓ) and the resolvend of a local normal integral basis generator; it is decomposed in [The Hom quotient is the actual maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-106) and [The tame integer-ring class lies in the maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-114), with the boundary the virtual-character local-constant laws below.

**Checks.**

- For Γ abelian, Cl(𝔐) is a product of ideal class groups of cyclotomic fields.

### 7.118 Taylor’s congruences detect the pre-integrality character torsion

**Target.** Use `B,L,H,I,F,f` and `d=Det(zT′)` from §7.115, with `zT′∈B[I]×`. The detection theorem is on the carrier `ℋ_L(H)`, with no assumption that f or `q=f/d` is an integral determinant. Its hypotheses are: q is torsion and trivial on linear characters; f and d are congruent to one modulo `𝔪_ℓ` on virtual characters vanishing on ℓ-regular elements; and for each irreducible `χ=Ind_Φ^H α`, with `I≤Φ` and α linear, both `f(χ)` and `d(χ)` lie in `(L(χ|I)⊗ℚ_ℓ)×`. Here `L(χ|I)` is generated by the values of the restricted character, not by all values of α. In particular the residue condition and `q(1)=1` imply `q(χ)≡1 mod 𝔪_ℓ` on every χ.

The further hypotheses are the four paired identities below, for f and for every `d_b=Det(b)`, `b∈B[I]×`. All congruences mean differences in the displayed coefficient ideal after passage to a common finite splitting extension. Write 𝒪 for the algebraic ℓ-adic integers and `𝔪_ℓ` for their positive-valuation ideal, componentwise, and put `J_ℓ=ℓ𝒪` for odd ℓ and `J₂=2𝔪₂`. Thus `mod 2𝔪₂` is stronger than `mod 2`; it distinguishes −1 from 1. Write `u^(−F)=(u^F)⁻¹`, let `v_Φ^Ψ α` denote α composed with group transfer from Ψ to Φ, and let `det χ` denote the linear determinant character of a representation with character χ.

The group H is a tame ℓ-group with cyclic inertia I and cyclic quotient `H/I`. Require the inertia sequence to split. When ℓ=2, also require the inversion companions in branch III to exist. Every tame ℓ-group quotient has a finite tame ℓ-power cover satisfying these two requirements: the split inertia sequence is obtained in a sufficiently large unramified cover, and the inversion companion in a further tame 2-power cover. Prove this existence and the compatibility of f under inflation. A group quotient sends group-ring units to units, so integrality on such a cover descends. These cover comparisons are part of this target (Taylor §3, p.50, and §7, p.57).

For degree-two characters at ℓ=2 write `2^r=order(α|I)`, and let a be the residue cardinality of the local field fixed by H, so an arithmetic Frobenius lift acts on inertia by its a-th power. The three types have respectively `a≡1 mod 4`, `a≡−1 mod 2^r`, and `a≡−1+2^(r−1) mod 2^r` with r≥3. The first case has nontrivial order-two action on `α(I)` as well; the identity action would give no irreducible degree-two χ.

1. Degree greater than two. For `χ=Ind_Φ^H α` let Ψ be the unique subgroup above Φ with `[Ψ:Φ]=ℓ`, put `β=v_Φ^Ψ α` and `χ′=Ind_Ψ^H β`. The inertia order of β is strictly smaller than that of α. Require

       `f(χ) f(χ′)^(−F) ≡ 1 mod J_ℓ`,
       `d_b(χ) d_b(χ′)^(−F) ≡ 1 mod J_ℓ`.

2. Semiabelian degree two. There are Ψ and a linear λ of Ψ with `[H:Ψ]=[I:I∩Ψ]=2`, `χ=Ind_Ψ^H λ` and `χ′=Ind_Ψ^H(λ²)`. Put `β=v_Ψ^H λ` and `γ=v_Ψ^H(λ²)`; for `s∈I`, `β(s)=λ(s²)`. Require the exact Gauss identity and determinant congruence

       `f(χ) f(β)^(−F) = f(χ′) f(γ)^(−F)`,
       `d_b(χ) d_b(β)^(−F) ≡ d_b(χ′) d_b(γ)^(−F) mod 2𝔪₂`.

3. Inversion degree two. There is an irreducible `χ̃=Ind_Φ^H α̃` of inversion or semidihedral type with `α̃²|I=α|I`, and an automorphism ω fixing L pointwise, with the induced action on characters, such that

       `f(χ̃+χ̃^ω) f(χ)^(−F) ≡ 1 mod 4𝒪`,
       `d_b(χ̃+χ̃^ω) d_b(χ)^(−F) ≡ 1 mod 2𝔪₂`.

4. Semidihedral degree two. Put `E=L(α|I)` and let `Tr_E/L` be the field trace, extended to the completed coefficient algebras. Let φ range over all linear characters of `I/ker(α²|I)`, each extended to Φ, and put `φ_*=Ind_Φ^H φ` and `ε_*=Ind_Φ^H 1`. For `h=f,d_b` define the additive expressions

       `A_h = 2^(1−r) Tr_E/L(h(χ)) − h(det χ)^F`,
       `B_h = 2^(1−r) Σ_φ h(φ_*) − h(det ε_*)^F`.

   Require `A_f≡B_f mod 4B`, `A_(d_b)≡B_(d_b) mod 4B`, and `A_f,B_f∈2B`. These include integrality of the normalized traces and sums. In particular `2^(1−r) Tr_E/L(f(χ))` is a 2-adic unit: its difference from the unit `f(det χ)^F` is in 2B. Omitting this parity assertion would lose detection of the residual sign.

Prove that these hypotheses imply `q=1` and hence `f=Det(zT′)∈D_B(H)`. Then verify every hypothesis for the constructed adjusted Gauss factor f. The residue assertion is §7.112, and the field-of-values assertion is Taylor Proposition3.10(iv) together with the character-component scalar comparison of §7.115. For `d_b`, inertia support gives the same field of values and Proposition3.8 gives the residue assertion. Prove the f identities from the finite conductor sums: branch I includes the Fröhlich–Taylor (1980), §5.1 local unit congruence, with the modulus `J_ℓ`, as in Taylor §9(Ia), p.66; branches II–IV are Taylor §9, pp.67–71. Prove the paired determinant congruences for all `b∈B[I]×` by the coefficient computations of Taylor §10, pp.71–75. Thus the identities are specified local targets here, rather than assumed integral-determinant membership of f.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), §4 (4.5), p.51; §7 (7.10), Theorem4(Ia–IVb) and its detection argument, pp.59–61; §§9–10, pp.65–75.) The theorem compares the Gauss homomorphism and an inertia-supported determinant in the ambient unit-valued character group.

To prove detection, induct on `order(α|I)`. Linear characters start the induction. The residue condition makes q's values ℓ-primary roots of unity. For degree two of inversion or semidihedral type the field-of-values assertion restricts these roots to ±1: adjoining unramified coefficients to the relevant 2-power cyclotomic fixed field introduces no further 2-primary roots. Branch II compares with smaller inertia order modulo `2𝔪₂`. In branch III, equivariance makes the two companion signs equal, so their product is 1; the displayed congruence then kills `q(χ)`. In branch IV, the induced φ characters have smaller inertia order, and linear determinant characters already have q-value 1. Subtracting the paired congruences gives

    `(q(χ)⁻¹−1) · 2^(1−r) Tr_E/L(f(χ)) ≡ 0 mod 4B`.

The trace factor is a unit, so the sign is 1. Finally branch I compares with smaller inertia order modulo `J_ℓ`, which distinguishes all ℓ-primary roots from 1 at the required precision. None of these steps uses the integral-determinant kernel theorem on q.

**Checks.**

- Rejection of unrestricted logarithm-plus-abelianization detection: for `B=ℤ₂`, `H=Q₈`, let h have value 1 on the four linear irreducibles `1,λ₁,λ₂,λ₃` and −1 on the faithful degree-two χ, and extend multiplicatively to virtual characters. This rational assignment is equivariant, torsion, and trivial on the abelian quotient. Both its characterwise logarithm and `ν_char` vanish; `ψ²χ=λ₁+λ₂+λ₃−1` does not detect it. In the faithful representation the generators `diag(i,−i)` and `[[0,1],[−1,0]]` have determinant 1, so every group element has determinant 1 at χ, while `h(χ)=−1`. Thus `h∉Det(Q₈)`. These data alone cannot justify the residual membership or equality; no claim that h is a Gauss factor is part of this example.
- `groupElement_determinant_eq_one_of_linear_characters`: if a group-element determinant is 1 on all linear characters, it is 1 on every representation, since `g↦det(ρ(g))` is itself a linear character. The four congruence branches therefore concern the larger carrier torsion, not an element of `Det(H)` already trivial on the abelian quotient.
- At ℓ=2 the sign −1 is congruent to 1 modulo 2 and modulo `𝔪₂`, but not modulo `2𝔪₂` or 4. Residue congruences alone cannot replace branches II–IV.
- In branch IV with r=3 and L unramified at 2, `[L(ζ₈):L]=4` and `2^(1−r)Tr_(L(ζ₈))/L(1)=1`. The factor 1/4 is essential to both parity and the unit trace conclusion.
- H abelian: the lift of §7.115 already gives q=1, without any nonlinear branch.

*Needs:* [The Gauss logarithm lifts through the commutator ideal](#layer-7-topic-115); [Adjusted tame Gauss homomorphisms](#layer-7-topic-112); [Local rational Brauer reduction for determinant quotients](#layer-7-topic-63).

<a id="layer-7-topic-119"></a>

### 7.119 The off-diagonal local Gauss factor is an integral determinant

For a tame local G-Galois extension over `F/Q_p` and ℓ≠p, put `K=Q(ζ_p)`. The local off-diagonal factor `y_p⁻¹τ_p` of §7.112 lies in `Det(O_(K,ℓ)[G]×)`, where `O_(K,ℓ)` is the product of completed integer rings over ℓ. Its local unramified factors retain the normalization `τ_F(χ)=χ(D_F/Q_p)⁻¹` and `y_p(χ)=−χ(P_F)` for rank-one χ. The assertion is membership in the integral-unit determinant subgroup, stronger than having unit character values.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Theorem2(b), p.45; Theorem3, p.49, proved in §§5–10, pp.52–75.) Away from the ramified prime, the Gauss homomorphism modulo its root-of-unity correction is a determinant unit.

To prove this, reduce by integral-character twisting and ℚ-elementary induction (Taylor (1981), §5: an integral identity over ℚ-elementary subgroups, and for ℚ-ℓ-elementary subgroups a multiplier prime to ℓ). Realize each ℚ-rational virtual character by finite free Z-lattices and extend along `Z→O_(K,ℓ)`, with the compatible local splitting fields; §7.47 applies with B=Z, independently of the ramification prime p. For a ℚ-q-elementary subgroup with q≠ℓ write `G=(C_ℓ × C′) ⋊ P_q`, where `C_ℓ` is cyclic of ℓ-power order, `|C′|` is prime to both ℓ and q, and `P_q` is a q-group. The subgroup `C_ℓ` is characteristic in the normal cyclic prime-to-q subgroup, hence normal in G. The quotient `G/C_ℓ` has order prime to ℓ, so its group ring over `O_(K,ℓ)` is a maximal order. Use the maximal-order and lifting/congruence inputs of [Determinant descent for `Q_p-ℓ`-elementary groups](#layer-7-topic-93), with its coefficient prime p replaced by ℓ and its auxiliary prime ℓ replaced by q. Taylor’s congruence Proposition3.10(v), resting on his Propositions3.7–3.8, shows that an ℓ-power of the adjusted Gauss factor is a unit determinant (Taylor (1981), §6, Propositions5.3 and6.1). On the ℚ-ℓ-elementary pieces use [The Gauss logarithm lifts through the commutator ideal](#layer-7-topic-115) and [Taylor’s congruences detect the pre-integrality character torsion](#layer-7-topic-118), then reassemble the cyclic crossed-product pieces (Taylor (1981), §§7–10). `Det(c_p)` is already an integral unit determinant and can be removed. Descent of invariant determinants uses [Fixed-point descent for integral determinant units](#layer-7-topic-109).

**Checks.**

- For G={1} over `ℚ_p`, `y_p(1)=−1` and `τ_p(1)=1`, so `y_p⁻¹τ_p` is Det(−1), an integral-unit determinant.
- For unramified rank-one χ over F, the different and uniformizer remain in `τ_F(χ)=χ(D_F/Q_p)⁻¹` and `y_p(χ)=−χ(P_F)`; unramifiedness alone does not set these two values to 1.
- At the zero virtual character the factor is 1, since both homomorphisms are multiplicative on the virtual character group.
- For q=3, ℓ=2 and `G=C₂×C₃`, quotienting by `C_ℓ=C₂` gives C₃ of odd order. Quotienting by the 3-part gives C₂ instead: for its generator s, `e=(1+s)/2` satisfies `e²=e` in `ℚ₂[C₂]`, hence is integral over ℤ₂, but lies outside `ℤ₂[C₂]`. Thus `ℤ₂[C₂]` is not a maximal order.

The logarithmic lift supplies a quotient in the torsion of `ℋ_L(H)`. The paired congruences of §7.118, including the local unit identities specified there and in §7.112, prove this quotient trivial before any claim of integral-determinant membership. The crossed-product comparison then transports the constructed integral determinant back to the elementary factor.

<a id="layer-7-topic-119a"></a>

### 7.119a Tame-inertia descent for local determinant units

Let ℓ be prime, `T/ℚ_ℓ` a finite tame Galois extension, Δ its Galois group, I its inertia subgroup, `U=T^I`, `S=𝒪_T` and `R=𝒪_U`. Thus S/R is totally ramified Galois of degree e=|I| prime to ℓ, R and S have the same finite residue field, and `U/ℚ_ℓ` is unramified. For every finite group G, let `D_S=Det(S[G]×)` and `D_R=Det(R[G]×)`, embedded in the same splitting-field character homomorphisms of §7.28. Inertia acts on coefficients, σ·Det(u)=Det(σu), fixing the group basis. Then `D_S^I=D_R`; equivalently the determinant obstruction quotient `Q_I=D_S^I/D_R` is trivial. This assertion requires no Frobenius lift on S. It also holds for any totally ramified tame Galois extension T/U of finite extensions of `ℚ_ℓ`.

The supporting API comprises:

- `GaloisModules.groupRingDeterminant`: For an embedding ι of coefficients into an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field Ω and a representation ρ on Ωⁿ, evaluate a group-ring element through ρ and take its determinant. On units these values determine the character determinant of §7.28; equality for all n and ρ is equality of those determinants.
- `GaloisModules.tameInertia_determinant_descent`: An S[G]-unit whose determinant is fixed by every R-automorphism of S has the same determinant as an R[G]-unit. Here R⊂S are complete characteristic-zero DVRs, S is finite free Galois over R, the residue fields are finite of characteristic ℓ and identified by inclusion, and [Frac(S):Frac(R)] is prime to ℓ.
- Restriction of scalars along R→S defines a determinant transfer `N_S/R`:`D_S→D_R`. After inclusion into `D_S` its value is `∏_(σ∈I)σd`. This includes independence of the unit representative: equality of all splitting-field determinants is preserved by transfer. Finite freeness gives the transfer matrix over R[G]; semilocal elimination replaces its determinant by that of a single unit.
- Put `P=Det(1+𝔪_S S[G])`. This is an abelian pro-ℓ group, and reduction gives `D_S=D_R·P`. The power map `b↦b^e` is an automorphism of `P^I`. Hence the image of `P^I` in `Q_I` is both killed by e, by transfer, and e-divisible through that power automorphism; in fact every `b∈P^I` is `N_S/R(c)` for its unique e-th root `c∈P^I`, so `Q_I=1`. These transfer and power assertions are part of this target.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), §12, Theorem6, inertia step (12.2)–(12.3) and norm argument, p.78.) The tame-inertia fixed-point statement follows from the coefficient norm on principal-unit determinants; the unramified step of Theorem6 is separate.

To prove this, the isomorphism of residue fields lifts each residue group-ring unit to R[G]×, since the maximal-ideal group-ring ideal lies in the Jacobson radical. Thus every determinant is a product of a determinant over R and one in P. The congruence filtration on `1+𝔪_S S[G]` has finite ℓ-group quotients; its determinant image is compact, hence a pro-ℓ group. Restriction of scalars and the product formula give the stated norm into `D_R`, using [Semilocal elimination preserves the determinant image](#layer-7-topic-27), without a group logarithm. For `d∈D_S^I` write d=ab with `a∈D_R` and b∈P; then `b∈P^I`. Since (e,ℓ)=1, the unique e-th root c of b in P is also I-fixed. Its norm is `c^e=b`, which lies in `D_R`, proving `d∈D_R`. The reverse inclusion follows from the coefficient action.

**Checks.**

- T=ℚ₃(√3), U=ℚ₃: S=ℤ₃[π], π²=3, I=C₂ and Tr(1)=2. There is no ordinary Frobenius lift on S: an endomorphism sends π to ±π, not to π³ modulo 3S. Nevertheless `D_S^I=D_ℤ₃` by this target, and squaring is an automorphism of `P^I`.
- G={1}: this is `(S×)^I=R×`; an invariant principal unit is the norm of its unique e-th root in `P^I`.
- I={1}: U=T, R=S, e=1 and the norm and power maps are identities.
- The prime-to-ℓ condition is used in the power assertion. Already on 1+3ℤ₃ the cube map misses 4, since every cube is 1 modulo 9; the argument cannot be applied to a wild degree-three inertia step.

*Needs:* [Determinants indexed by virtual characters](#layer-7-topic-28); [Semilocal elimination preserves the determinant image](#layer-7-topic-27); [TauCetiRoadmap.LocalFieldsRamification, layer 2 unramified extensions and frobenius](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/main/TauCetiRoadmap/LocalFieldsRamification/README.md#layer-2-unramified-extensions-and-frobenius); [TauCetiRoadmap.LocalFieldsRamification, layer 3 ramification the tame and wild cases and the filtration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/main/TauCetiRoadmap/LocalFieldsRamification/README.md#layer-3-ramification-the-tame-and-wild-cases-and-the-filtration).

<a id="layer-7-topic-120"></a>

### 7.120 The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality

For every tame finite G-Galois extension L/F of number fields, with d=[F:Q], `[O_L]−d[Z[G]]=t(W_L/F)` in Cl(Z[G]), under the compatible Hom-description and embedding-norm conventions. This is the equality of the full stable module class with the symplectic root-number class, not just a two-torsion assertion.

(Martin J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich’s conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Theorem1, pp.41–42; reduction(2.1)–(2.2), pp.44–45; §12 Theorem6 and conclusion, pp.78–79.) Taylor identifies the integer-ring stable class with the root-number obstruction through local determinant factors and descent.

To prove this, represent the class by the norm-resolvent/Gauss homomorphism from [The tame integer-ring class lies in the maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-114). At each ℓ separate the diagonal factor supplied by [The diagonal tame norm-resolvent factor is a determinant unit](#layer-7-topic-116) and the off-diagonal factors supplied by [The off-diagonal local Gauss factor is an integral determinant](#layer-7-topic-119). The assembled corrected factor differs from W by a determinant over a finite tame Galois coefficient extension `T/ℚ_ℓ`; a common tame Galois compositum contains the coefficients from both local targets. Apply [Gauss sums have the resolvent Galois transformation law](#layer-7-topic-107) with the correction factors to obtain Δ-invariance of this assembled determinant, where `Δ=Gal(T/ℚ_ℓ)`; invariance is required of the product, not of each local factor. Put `I=I(T/ℚ_ℓ)` and `U=T^I`. First [Tame-inertia descent for local determinant units](#layer-7-topic-119a) descends from `𝒪_T` to `𝒪_U`. Then [Fixed-point descent for integral determinant units](#layer-7-topic-109) descends the Δ/I-invariant determinant from `𝒪_U` to `ℤ_ℓ`: these are unramified integer rings with ordinary Frobenius lifts (the identity on `ℤ_ℓ` and arithmetic Frobenius on `𝒪_U`), finite free Galois coefficients and surjective trace. Normality, noetherianity and ℓ-adic completeness hold for both rings. For a product of local coefficient rings, take a decomposition-group component and recover the other components by Galois transport. The positive principal denominator absorbs the rational basis choices. The remaining quotient is exactly t(W).

**Checks.**

- G abelian, or of odd order: there is no symplectic character, t(W) = 0, and `[O_L] − d[ℤ[G]] = 0`.
- Martinet's tame Q₈-extension of ℚ (Checks of [Taylor's theorem: the Galois module class has order at most two](#layer-7-topic-121)): t(W) ≠ 0, so `𝓞_L` is not stably free over ℤ[Q₈] and has no normal integral basis.
- In particular `2([O_L] − d[ℤ[G]]) = 0`, Taylor's theorem ([Taylor's theorem: the Galois module class has order at most two](#layer-7-topic-121)).

*Needs:* [The tame integer-ring class lies in the maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-114); [The root-number class in the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-113); [The diagonal tame norm-resolvent factor is a determinant unit](#layer-7-topic-116); [The off-diagonal local Gauss factor is an integral determinant](#layer-7-topic-119); [Fixed-point descent for integral determinant units](#layer-7-topic-109); [The Hom quotient is the actual maximal-order kernel](#layer-7-topic-106); [Tame-inertia descent for local determinant units](#layer-7-topic-119a); [Gauss sums have the resolvent Galois transformation law](#layer-7-topic-107).

<a id="layer-7-topic-121"></a>

### 7.121 Taylor's theorem: the Galois module class has order at most two

Let M/N be a tame Galois extension of number fields with group Γ. Then `2·[𝓞_M]_ℤ = 0` in Cl(ℤΓ). (Taylor's Theorem 1: `[𝓞_M]_ℤ = t(W)`, the Cassou-Noguès–Fröhlich root number class, whose values are signs of Artin root numbers of symplectic characters.)

M/N tame Galois.

(M. J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich's conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Theorem 1 (printed p. 41).) The target is part (a); the source writes Cl(ℤΓ) multiplicatively.

(Henri Johnston, [Notes on Galois Modules](#reference-johnston-galois-modules-2016), Theorem 15.3 (printed p. 29).) The same statement.

To prove this, Taylor's proof (Fröhlich's Hom-description (2.1), the representative `u = Det(A)·W′·τ_Γ⁻¹` of the class, Galois Gauss sums and the group logarithm, Sections 2–12 of Taylor 1981) is decomposed in [The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality](#layer-7-topic-120) and [The root-number class in the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-113), with the boundaries the virtual-character local-constant laws below, the field-of-definition induction theorem below, [the integral crossed-product matrix comparison](#layer-7-topic-86), [the adjusted Gauss congruences](#layer-7-topic-112) and [the elementary determinant congruence and maximal-order inputs](#layer-7-topic-93).

**Checks.**

- For Γ abelian the class is zero (Hilbert–Speiser over ℚ; for general N, Taylor's theorem with no symplectic characters).
- Martinet's quaternion example: for Γ = Q₈ and N = ℚ the class can be nonzero, so "order two" cannot be improved to "zero".

*Needs:* [The Galois module class of the ring of integers](#layer-7-topic-110); [The locally free class group of an order](#layer-7-topic-77); [The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality](#layer-7-topic-120); [The root-number class in the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-113).

<a id="layer-7-topic-122"></a>

### 7.122 Taylor: without symplectic characters the ring of integers is stably free

Let M/N be a tame Galois extension of number fields with group Γ. If Γ has no irreducible symplectic (quaternionic) character, that is no irreducible complex representation carries a nonzero Γ-invariant alternating form (Frobenius–Schur indicator −1), then `[𝓞_M]_ℤ = 0`: `𝓞_M` is stably free over ℤΓ.

M/N tame Galois; every irreducible character of Γ has Frobenius–Schur indicator 0 or 1.

(M. J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich's conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Theorem 1(b) (printed p. 41).) Part (b) says the root-number signs of the symplectic characters are the only obstruction; the target is the case with no symplectic characters, where there is none.

(Henri Johnston, [Notes on Galois Modules](#reference-johnston-galois-modules-2016), Section 15.4 (printed p. 29).) The hypothesis.

To prove this, t(W) is defined from the Artin root numbers of the irreducible symplectic characters only; with none, t(W) = 1 (Taylor Section 2).

Apply Taylor's Theorem 1, the Fröhlich–Taylor equality [The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality](#layer-7-topic-120).

The characterisation of symplectic characters by invariant alternating forms is the Frobenius–Schur trichotomy (CharacterTheory Layer 7).

**Checks.**

- Abelian, dihedral, symmetric groups and groups of odd order have no symplectic characters.
- Q₈ has one (its two-dimensional representation).

*Needs:* [Taylor's theorem: the Galois module class has order at most two](#layer-7-topic-121); [The Galois module class of the ring of integers](#layer-7-topic-110); [The root-number class in the kernel group](#layer-7-topic-113); [The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality](#layer-7-topic-120); [Stable equality in the existing split K₀](#layer-7-topic-23).

<a id="layer-7-topic-123"></a>

### 7.123 Taylor: for groups of odd order the ring of integers is free over ℤΓ

Let M/N be a tame Galois extension of number fields with group Γ of odd order. Then `𝓞_M` is a free ℤΓ-module of rank [N : ℚ].

M/N tame Galois; |Γ| odd.

(M. J. Taylor, [On Fröhlich's conjecture for rings of integers of tame extensions](#reference-taylor-froehlich-conjecture-1981), Corollary and its proof (printed pp. 41–42).) The mathematical contract, with the conventions stated here; the rank is [N : ℚ] by local freeness.

To prove this, a group of odd order has no nontrivial real-valued irreducible character (CharacterTheory Layer 7: real characters count real classes, and an odd-order group has only the identity as a real class), hence no symplectic character; so `[𝓞_M]_ℤ = 0` ([Taylor: without symplectic characters the ring of integers is stably free](#layer-7-topic-122)).

ℚΓ satisfies the Eichler condition (no totally definite quaternion component), so ℤΓ has locally free cancellation (Jacobinski's cancellation theorem, [Jacobinski cancellation under Eichler’s condition](#layer-7-topic-98)).

Stably free and locally free of rank [N : ℚ] with cancellation gives free of that rank.

**Checks.**

- Γ cyclic of odd order: consistent with Hilbert–Speiser when N = ℚ.
- The hypothesis "odd order" cannot be dropped: Cougnard's example over Q₃₂ is stably free but not free (quoted by Johnston).

*Needs:* [Taylor: without symplectic characters the ring of integers is stably free](#layer-7-topic-122); [The ring of integers is locally free over ℤ[G]](#layer-7-topic-103); [Odd-order group algebras satisfy Eichler’s condition](#layer-7-topic-31); [Jacobinski cancellation under Eichler’s condition](#layer-7-topic-98); [The Fröhlich–Taylor obstruction equality](#layer-7-topic-120).

### Examples

The Gaussian integer extension has a rational normal basis and no integral normal basis. A nonprincipal norm-two ideal in ℤ[√−5] tests local freeness against freeness. The trivial group and zero stabilisation test the identity arithmetic class. Every computed value and negative control attached to a result above is part of its required interface.

## Downstream consumers

The scope boundaries give the direction of each cross-roadmap import. In particular the power-residue and Gauss APIs feed reciprocity and character-sum developments, the automatic-sequence interfaces feed algebraic power-series work, the polynomial comparisons feed arithmetic algorithms and factor bounds, the formal products feed q-series identities, and the integral determinant and group-logarithm APIs feed equivariant Iwasawa theory. A consumer must cite the result with the hypotheses and normalisation stated here.
